# Additional information

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/prerelease/main/additional-information/

This page gathers what does not fit under Guides or Reference: licensing of the default stack, how to reach the people behind a Kumoss deployment, where release notes and the changelog will be published, where the FAQ lives, and where to find the roadmap.

## Licensing of the default stack

Every component that runs by default in the checked-in Compose stack is open source, with one source-available exception that is disclosed rather than hidden (the bundled but inactive Terraform binary is a second, opt-in exception). Identity has no licensing footprint at all: Kumoss speaks standard OpenID Connect and trusts any spec-faithful issuer, so a fully open-source deployment can pair it with Keycloak (Apache-2.0, CNCF Incubating) while an enterprise can point it at Entra ID, Auth0, or Okta without changing a line of code.

| Component | Role | License | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kumoss (core, sidecars, SPA, contracts) | The platform | Apache-2.0 | REUSE-compliant SPDX headers |
| OpenTofu 1.12.6 | Default IaC engine in the iac sidecar | MPL-2.0 (Linux Foundation) | Digest-pinned. The same image also bundles HashiCorp Terraform 1.16.0 (BUSL-1.1, not OSI), downloaded and checksum-verified at build time and selectable via `IAC_BINARY=terraform`; running it makes your use subject to its license terms |
| RustFS | Default, bundled S3-compatible object storage for artifacts (and for Terraform state where that is enabled) | Apache-2.0 | Rust implementation of the S3 API; AWS S3 or Azure Blob Storage selectable via `storage.provider`, or any other S3-compatible endpoint via the `RUSTFS` provider |
| PostgreSQL 17 | core-db and langfuse-db | PostgreSQL License | — |
| Redis 8 | Fail-open cache | Tri-licensed: AGPLv3 (OSI) / RSALv2 / SSPLv1 | AGPLv3 option restored in Redis 8.0 |
| nginx | Reverse proxy and SPA host | BSD-2-Clause | — |
| FastAPI, LiteLLM, React, oidc-client-ts | Framework, model router, portal, OIDC client | MIT | — |
| OpenTelemetry | Tracing standard | Apache-2.0 | OpenTelemetry is CNCF Graduated (2026-05-21) |
| Langfuse | Trace UI and runtime prompt registry | MIT | Self-hosted open-source edition. Code under its `ee` directories is under a commercial license and stays inactive without a license key; Kumoss uses none of it |
| ClickHouse | Langfuse’s trace store | Apache-2.0 | — |
| OpenID Connect | Authentication protocol | Open standard (OpenID Foundation) | No component shipped; any compliant IdP |

## Contact and support

Three channels, each with its own purpose:

- **Support request in the web application** — questions about your own Kumoss deployment or about one of your sessions. It reaches the reviewers in your deployment, not the Kumoss project.
- [Issue tracker](https://github.com/InditexTech/kumoss/issues) — bugs and feature requests in Kumoss itself. Check the existing issues first; [Contributing](../contributing/) covers what happens next.
- [Disclosure submission program](https://vdp.inditex.com) — security vulnerabilities, reported privately and never through a public GitHub issue.

### Support requests

Any signed-in user can send a support request from inside the web application. It goes to the people who hold the reviewer roles in your own Kumoss deployment — colleagues on your platform team, not the Kumoss project — through the channel your platform team connected (Slack in the reference setup), with a copy addressed to you.

From the browser, the chat-bubble **Support** icon in the header opens a form for up to 500 characters, plain text only — HTML and code formatting are rejected. The message carries your e-mail, the session id, the repository, branch, request, status, and a link to the session automatically, so you do not need to copy those in yourself. **Contact Team** (on a locked session) and **Request Review** (on the apply confirmation) send the same kind of message, pre-filled for that session, and flagged as a warning when the plan deletes or recreates resources. "Your question has been sent successfully" confirms delivery; "Your question could not be sent. Notifications are disabled." means your deployment has not connected a notification channel — use your organization’s usual support route and quote the session id.

The form calls `POST /api/v1/notifications`. The core forwards the request to the notifications sidecar with an audience made of the caller’s e-mail plus every user holding a panel role of `editor` or higher, and the bundled sidecar posts it to Slack. When `services.notifications.enabled` is `false` the route answers `503 Notifications are disabled.`; when delivery fails it answers `502 Notification was not delivered.`

### Security

Report a security vulnerability through the [disclosure submission program](https://vdp.inditex.com), in English — never through a public GitHub issue. The security team acknowledges a report within 48 hours, investigates its severity, and develops, tests, and publishes a fix and an advisory. See the [security policy](https://github.com/InditexTech/kumoss/blob/main/SECURITY.md) for the full process and the safe-harbor terms covering researchers who report in good faith.

## Release notes

Kumoss publishes tagged releases. The curated highlights of each release — what is new and what it changes for the people using it — are available on the project’s [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/InditexTech/kumoss/releases) page.

## Changelog

The unabridged, commit-level record of changes is the repository’s [commit history](https://github.com/InditexTech/kumoss/commits/main); it is not duplicated here. Each GitHub Release carries the complete list of additions, changes, fixes, and deprecations since the previous one.

# Contributing

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/prerelease/main/contributing/

Thank you for your interest in contributing to Kumoss. Any contribution is valued and appreciated; the guidelines below keep the project collaborative and respectful. For the local development loop — running the stack, the test suites, type checking, and linting — see [Development](../guides/development/).

## Prerequisites

- Before contributing code, sign the Contributor License Agreement (CLA). Instructions are at [InditexTech/foss](https://github.com/InditexTech/foss/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).
- By participating in the project you agree to abide by the rules and principles set out in the [code of conduct](https://github.com/InditexTech/kumoss/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Kumoss adheres to the general [Inditex Tech Code of Conduct](https://github.com/InditexTech/foss/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md); direct any inquiry about it to [oso@inditex.com](mailto:oso@inditex.com).
- Check existing [issues](https://github.com/InditexTech/kumoss/issues) and [pull requests](https://github.com/InditexTech/kumoss/pulls) before starting work, to avoid duplication. If you take on an existing issue, comment on it so other contributors know it is in progress.
- Discuss and gather feedback from the community before making significant changes to the project’s structure or architecture.

## How to contribute

1. Open an issue to discuss and gather feedback on the feature or fix you wish to address. Security vulnerabilities are the exception: report them through the [disclosure submission program](https://vdp.inditex.com) as described in the [security policy](https://github.com/InditexTech/kumoss/blob/main/SECURITY.md), never through a public issue.
2. Fork the repository and clone it to your local machine.
3. Create a new branch to work on your contribution: `git checkout -b your-branch-name`.
4. Make the necessary changes in your local branch, following [Development](../guides/development/) to run the stack and its checks.
5. Ensure that your code follows the established project style and formatting guidelines.
6. Perform testing to ensure your changes do not introduce errors.
7. Make clear and descriptive commits that explain your changes.
8. Push your branch to the remote repository: `git push origin your-branch-name`.
9. Open a pull request describing your changes and linking the corresponding issue.
10. Await comments and discussions on your pull request. Make any necessary modifications based on the feedback you receive.
11. Once your pull request is approved, your contribution is merged into the main branch.

## Pull requests

Fill in the pull-request template ([.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md](https://github.com/InditexTech/kumoss/blob/main/.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md)) and link the issue it addresses. Include UI screenshots for visible changes. Document any new changes or features you add, so other contributors and users understand your work and its purpose.

Keep the commit history clean and organized: divide your changes into logical, descriptive commits. Commit subjects must follow the [Conventional Commits Specification](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) (for example `fix(core): release session lock`); CI rejects other subjects. Sign your commits (`git commit -S`) — signing is required by policy and checked in review, not enforced by any CI workflow.

Every new file starts with an SPDX header following the [REUSE Specification](https://reuse.software/spec-3.3/#licensing-information) (`SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 INDUSTRIA DE DISEÑO TEXTIL S.A. (INDITEX S.A.)` and `SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0`). CI runs the REUSE check on every pull request, alongside Repolinter and the Conventional Commits check above.

# Quickstart

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/prerelease/main/quickstart/

In this quickstart, you install Kumoss on one machine with Docker Compose, using the bundled stack as shipped, and open the running web application. To see what a session looks like before you install anything, watch [Kumoss in action](../see-it-in-action/).

> **Tip**
> Prefer Kubernetes? Each release also publishes a Helm chart,
> `oci://ghcr.io/inditextech/charts/kumoss`. To install it, or to try it on
> a local kind cluster, see [Deploy with Helm](../guides/deploy-with-helm/).

## Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you meet the [prerequisites](../prerequisites/).

## Steps

### 1. Clone the repository and create the environment files

```
git clone https://github.com/InditexTech/kumoss.git
cd kumoss

cp core/env.sample core/.env
cp services/iac/env.sample services/iac/.env
cp services/mapping/env.sample services/mapping/.env
```

Each `env.sample` documents its own variables and is the source of truth for their names. Every `.env` file is gitignored; never commit one.

### 2. Write `config.yaml`

`config.yaml` at the repository root is the single configuration file. Compose mounts it into the core container, and the core reads it at startup, so every edit needs `docker compose restart core`.

#### What to edit and what to keep

- **Must Modify / Verify:** - `llm.model`: set your primary LLM provider model string. - `llm.small_model`: set your lightweight model string.

The `llm` values below are only an example: replace both model strings with the models you prefer. Model strings per provider: [LLM providers and models](../reference/llm-providers/).

```
llm:
  model: "vertex_ai/claude-sonnet-5-5"
  small_model: "vertex_ai/gemini-3.8-flash"
```

- **Optional / Conditional:** - `git.provider`: only modify if you are using GitLab (`"GITLAB"`) or Azure DevOps (`"AZURE_DEVOPS"`). Defaults to `"GITHUB"`. Accepted values and the supported hosts: [`git` configuration](../reference/configuration/#config-git).

```
git:
  provider: "GITHUB"  # or "AZURE_DEVOPS", "GITLAB"
```

- **Keep as Default:** - All unmentioned configuration fields automatically fall back to core code defaults.

### 3. Fill in `core/.env`

The `core/.env` passes mandatory runtime secrets such as LLM API keys and Git access tokens. The core will not run without them.

> **Warning**
> every `.env` file is gitignored by default. Never commit a `.env` file containing real credentials to version control.

#### What to edit and what to keep

- **Variables you MUST set:** - **LLM provider credentials:** set the specific API key or authentication variables required by LiteLLM for the provider prefixes configured in `llm.model` and `llm.small_model`. See examples below. For more info see [provider credential variables](../reference/llm-providers/#provider-credentials). - `GIT_USER`, `GIT_TOKEN`: the account username and personal access token for the provider named by `git.provider` defined in `config.yaml`. See examples below.
- **Variables to Keep as Default:** - **All other sample values in `core/env.sample`:** leave all pre-populated values intact (such as internal tokens, container URLs, and service connection details). These are pre-configured to match the bundled Docker Compose setup. For a complete reference of every variable, see [environment variables and secrets](../reference/environment-variables/).

> **Tip**
> if you modify `core/.env` after the stack is already running, recreate the container using `docker compose up -d core` to apply changes. Running `docker compose restart` will **not** reload `.env` variables.

#### Examples

**Anthropic example:**

```
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"
```

**Google Vertex AI example::**

```
VERTEXAI_PROJECT="your-gcp-project-id"
VERTEXAI_LOCATION="us-central1"
VERTEXAI_CREDENTIALS='{"type": "service_account", "project_id": "my-project", ...}'
```

**Azure OpenAI example:**

```
AZURE_API_KEY="xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"
AZURE_API_BASE="https://your-resource.openai.azure.com"
AZURE_API_VERSION="2025-01-01-preview"
```

**Git Credentials example:**

```
GIT_USER="your-git-username"
GIT_TOKEN="ghp_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"
```

### 4. Fill in `services/iac/.env`

The `services/iac/.env` file passes your cloud provider access keys and execution engine settings directly to the IaC sidecar.

> **Note**
> missing or invalid cloud credentials in `services/iac/.env` do not stop the container. The engine runs anyway, but authentication errors will appear inside the session as a failed `init`, `plan`, or `apply` operation.

#### What to edit and what to keep

- **Variables you MUST set:** - **Cloud provider credentials:** set the specific authentication variables required by your OpenTofu or Terraform providers. See [terraform providers](../reference/terraform-providers/) for the minimum set per cloud and authentication method.
- **Optional / Conditional Settings:** - `IAC_BINARY`: the sidecar runs OpenTofu 1.12.6 by default. Set `IAC_BINARY=terraform` only if you explicitly want to use the bundled HashiCorp Terraform 1.16.0 instead (selecting Terraform makes your use subject to its BUSL-1.1 license).
- **Variables to Keep as Default:** - **Internal service settings (e.g., `KUMOSS_IAC_TOKEN`):** leave these pre-populated values intact so they remain synchronized with `core/.env` and the container stack.

> **Tip**
> recreate the sidecar using `docker compose up -d iac` whenever you update `services/iac/.env`.

#### Examples

**AWS Credentials Example:**

```
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="AKIAXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX"
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"
AWS_REGION="us-east-1"
```

**GCP Credentials Example:**

```
GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS='{"type": "service_account", "project_id": "my-project", ...}'
```

**Azure Credentials Example:**

```
ARM_CLIENT_ID="xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"
ARM_CLIENT_SECRET="xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"
ARM_TENANT_ID="xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"
```

### 5. Start Kumoss

```
docker compose up
```

Add `-d` to run in the background. Compose pulls the Kumoss images for the checked-out release from `ghcr.io/inditextech/kumoss-*` (`linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`). To run code changes from your checkout instead, add `--build`; the first build downloads the base images, installs the Python dependencies, downloads both IaC engines, and compiles the web application.

After a later change to `config.yaml`, restart the core:

```
docker compose restart core
```

A change to a `.env` file needs the affected container recreated (`docker compose up -d core`, `docker compose up -d iac`); `docker compose restart` does not reload it.

### 6. Verify the services

```
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f core
```

Wait for `Application startup complete` in the core log. Boot is strict: if a start-up step fails, the container exits with the reason in the log. A `notifications` container that has exited is expected while that optional sidecar is unconfigured.

```
curl http://localhost/api/v1/auth/config
```

With authentication disabled this returns a JSON document with an empty `issuer_url`.

## Where Terraform state lives

By default, Kumoss keeps Terraform state in the bundled RustFS object storage, in the `kumoss-terraform-state` bucket. Each project (repository and root-module path) gets its own state file, which starts **empty** the first time Kumoss works on it. Any `backend` block in the repository is ignored.

To use your own external state instead, new or already existing, in AWS S3, Azure Storage, or Google Cloud Storage, see [Configure state backends](../guides/configure-state-backends/).

## See it working

| URL | What it serves |
| --- | --- |
| `http://localhost` | Kumoss web application and the API under `/api/v1/…​` |
| `http://localhost:3000` | Langfuse: traces of every run and the prompt registry |

Port 80 serves the unauthenticated Kumoss application by default, port 9000 exposes presigned artifact downloads, and port 3000 serves Langfuse, on every interface of the host. Keep the stack on a machine only you can reach. The RustFS web console is disabled; to enable it, see [RustFS console](../guides/production/operations/#rustfs-console).

> **Warning**
> Use a **test repository and a sandbox cloud scope** for this first
> run. Because every project starts with
> [empty state](#default-state), a repository whose infrastructure already
> exists gets a plan that creates it all again.

Open `http://localhost`. With authentication disabled you land directly in the wizard as the local developer. Enter a repository your Git token can push to, pick the root module, describe the infrastructure you need, answer the module’s scopes and variables if Kumoss asks for them, and follow the session. What each mode does is explained in [Guides](../guides-overview/); your sessions and the admin panel are described in [Administer users and locks](../guides/administer-users-and-locks/).

Open `http://localhost:3000` and sign in as `admin@example.com` with the password `kumoss-admin-1` (the development defaults the stack provisions) to see the run under **Sessions** and **Tracing**, and the seeded prompts under **Prompts**. Langfuse receives prompts, plans, and generated code in clear text; change those defaults before anyone else can reach the machine. See [Monitor with Langfuse](../guides/monitor-with-langfuse/).

## Stop or reset the stack

```
docker compose down            # stop; named volumes are kept
docker compose down -v         # stop and delete all volumes
```

`down` keeps the databases, artifacts, and workspaces, so sessions and prompts survive a restart.

**`down -v` deletes the session database, the artifacts, the Langfuse traces and prompts, any in-progress workspaces, and the Terraform state** kept in RustFS.

## Next steps

- Hand the [Make a request](../guides/make-a-request/) and [FAQ](../faq/) to the people who will make requests.
- Review and adapt the seeded prompts; they encode a generic policy, not yours: [Customize prompts](../guides/customize-prompts/).
- Try a real login flow with your identity provider: [Enable authentication](../guides/enable-authentication/).
- Learn the role model and the admin panel: [Administer users and locks](../guides/administer-users-and-locks/).
- Decide where Terraform state should live before you point Kumoss at anything real: [Configure state backends](../guides/configure-state-backends/).
- Set `MAPPING_PREFIX_IDENTIFIER` in `services/mapping/.env` so users can type a repository name instead of its URL, and turn on the optional sidecars — Slack notifications, external authorization (it needs an implementation you provide) — from [`services`](../reference/configuration/#config-services) and [Environment variables and secrets](../reference/environment-variables/).
- Before sharing the instance with anyone, switch to the production deployment model: [Deploy to production](../guides/deploy-to-production/). On Kubernetes, the Helm chart does most of the work: [Deploy with Helm](../guides/deploy-with-helm/).

## Troubleshooting

- **The core exits during boot.** Boot is strict and the reason is in `docker compose logs core` — most often missing LLM credentials, an empty `KUMOSS_IAC_TOKEN` or database URL in `core/.env`, or a Langfuse key pair (`LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY` / `LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY`) that does not match the one the stack provisions. Apart from the Langfuse services the stack has no healthchecks, so a dependency that was simply slower to start leaves the core stopped rather than retrying: run `docker compose up -d core` again.
- **Every session fails at validation with a `401` from the IaC sidecar.** `KUMOSS_IAC_TOKEN` differs between `core/.env` and `services/iac/.env`.
- **A `config.yaml` change has no effect.** Restart the core with `docker compose restart core`; the file is read only at startup.
- **`plan` or `apply` fails with a provider authentication error.** The cloud credentials in `services/iac/.env` are absent, invalid, or insufficient.
- **`plan` fails with `permission denied` on a file in the workspace.** The `workspaces` volume predates the current non-root containers. Run `docker compose down`, then `docker run --rm -v kumoss_workspaces:/workspaces alpine chown -R 10001:10001 /workspaces`, and start again.
- **`init` fails on the state backend, or every plan wants to recreate existing resources.** [Troubleshooting state backends](../guides/configure-state-backends/#state-troubleshooting).
- **Push or pull-request creation fails.** Check `GIT_USER`, `GIT_TOKEN`, that `git.provider` matches the repository host, and the token’s permissions.
- **A session aborts because a prompt is missing.** The prompt is absent from Langfuse or has no version labeled with the `environment` value. See [A session stops without an error](../guides/customize-prompts/#session-stops).
- **The browser cannot download an artifact.** Port 9000 must be reachable from the browser under the host in `storage.public_endpoint_url`.
- **LLM calls fail although the core booted.** Not every provider can be validated at boot. See [LiteLLM troubleshooting](../reference/llm-providers/#llm-troubleshooting).

# Reference

This section is the lookup material for Kumoss, described exhaustively and grouped by what you are looking up. For step-by-step tasks, see [Guides](../guides-overview/).

## Configure

[Configuration](../reference/configuration/)

Every `config.yaml` section and field: type, default, validation rule, and effect.

[Environment variables and secrets](../reference/environment-variables/)

Every variable in `core/env.sample` and the IaC and notifications sidecar `env.sample` files, plus the IaC engine and LLM provider variables.

How Kumoss selects LiteLLM models, provider credential tables, and the `llm.model_list` router escape hatch.

Minimum environment variables per cloud and state backend, plus the exhaustive variable reference.

## Behavior

[Operating modes](../reference/operating-modes/)

What each operating mode does today, the inputs every session takes, and how a session runs.

[Compliance policy](../reference/compliance-policy/)

The Rego policy OPA evaluates on every generate round’s plan: input, decision contract, failure semantics, and testing commands.

[Prompt registry](../reference/prompt-registry/)

How prompts are stored, seeded, and fetched in Langfuse, which agent reads which prompt, and the prompts that ship with each provider.

[Root module manifest](../reference/root-module-manifest/)

How Kumoss reads a root module’s providers and inputs, asks for its scopes and variable values once, and keeps them in `kumoss.yaml`.

[Repository layout](../reference/repository-layout/)

How Kumoss finds Terraform roots in a repository: the detection rules and the wizard’s zero/one/many behavior.

[Roles and permissions](../reference/roles-and-permissions/)

The two independent role groups, the complete permission matrix, and who gets which role by default.

## Data and APIs

[Database schema](../reference/database-schema/)

The thirteen tables of core-db, what each records, the enumerated columns, and how rows are deleted.

[HTTP APIs](../reference/api/)

Every route the core exposes under `/api/v1`, and the sidecar OpenAPI contracts it consumes as a client: IaC, the SearXNG search engine, notifications, repository mapping, and authorization.

## Limits at a glance

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Request and follow-up text | 500 characters |
| Provider scope (subscription, project, account, compartment) | 1024 characters |
| Support message | 500 characters |
| Generate-and-validate attempts per request | 5 in the shipped `config.yaml` (`orchestration.max_validation_iteration`) |
| Drift check inside a generate round | 2 passes |
| Drift remediation session | 3 iterations (`orchestration.max_drift_reports`) |
| One operation per session at a time | A second request while one is running is ignored until it finishes |
| Live progress stream | About 3 hours per connection; reopen the session afterwards |
| [Roles](../reference/roles-and-permissions/) | `developer`: generate, pull request, apply. `devops`: also drift remediation. |

# Architecture

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/prerelease/main/architecture/

This page introduces Kumoss’s runtime components and how they fit together. The rest of this section goes deeper: the end-to-end request flow, the data and state each component owns, and the deployment topology.

## Overview

![Kumoss system architecture: the browser and Nginx edge, the layered core inside its container boundary, the bundled iac and notifications sidecars with the optional mapping and authz contracts, and the data and observability containers on one Compose network](../_images/system-architecture.png)

Pan, zoom, search, trace a relationship, switch themes. [Open in a new tab](../_attachments/system-architecture.html)

/* Progressive enhancement for the block above. Guarded so that a page holding
   several diagrams runs this once, and deferred to DOMContentLoaded because a
   parse-time script cannot yet see the diagrams below it. */
(function () {
  if (window.__archifyEmbed) return
  window.__archifyEmbed = true

  /* The viewer's own interactive chrome. Its toolbar and zoom bar are
     position:fixed, so they always reach the bottom of whatever viewport the
     iframe gives them -- measuring them would make the height measurement
     below a fixpoint that can never shrink. Same selector list as
     docs/diagrams/capture-png.mjs, which hides them instead; here they stay
     visible and are only excluded from the measurement. */
  var CHROME = '.toolbar, .diagram-nav, .focus-chip, .guided-views, .archify-toast, .no-print'

  var style = document.createElement('style')
  style.textContent = [
    '.archify-actions{display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:.35rem .9rem;align-items:baseline;',
    'margin-block:-.65rem 1.5rem;font-size:.875rem;line-height:1.5}',
    '.archify-hint{opacity:.72}',
    '.archify-frame{width:100%;border:0;display:block}',
    /* A viewer is ~800KB and takes real time to arrive, so it loads out of
       the way while the still stays on screen, and is only swapped in once
       it has something to show. Off-screen rather than display:none: a
       display:none iframe has no viewport, so the application inside would
       not lay out, and revealing it would show an empty frame anyway --
       which is the whole failure this avoids. */
    '.archify-frame[data-archify-loading]{position:absolute;left:-99999px;top:0}',
    /* Only while the viewer is live. The still image is centred by the theme
       inside the narrower .imageblock; the frame is centred by this margin
       inside the wider one. */
    '.imageblock.archify-live{margin-inline:auto}',
    /* The theme insets an image block's contents by 40px, which puts the
       diagram 40px right of every heading and paragraph on the page. Those
       do line up with each other: a heading's box starts 64px further left
       than its text, because the theme carves that gutter with a negative
       margin and an equal padding to hold the hover anchor. So the column
       edge is where the text sits, and the diagram was the one thing off it.
       Dropped on both forms, so activating a block does not shift it. */
    '.imageblock.archify-block > .content{padding-inline:0}',
  ].join('')
  document.head.appendChild(style)

  /* The .imageblock wrapper is what escapes the 820px .sectionbody cap
     (`width: min(calc(var(--content-max-width)*1.25), var(--doc-inset-cap))`),
     so the viewer is swapped in inside it rather than in place of it. */
  function blockFor (actions) {
    var el = actions.previousElementSibling
    while (el && !el.classList.contains('imageblock')) el = el.previousElementSibling
    return el
  }

  /* Width is the only lever on how large the viewer draws: its SVG comes out
     at roughly 0.9x the viewport width it is given, and viewport height barely
     moves it. But --doc-inset-cap holds .imageblock at 1025px however wide the
     window gets, which on a large display leaves the whole right half of the
     article column unused. Track the column instead, so a 2560px screen gets
     a 1490px frame rather than the still's 945px. */
  function columnWidth (block) {
    var column = block.closest('.doc')
    return column ? column.clientWidth : 0
  }

  function widen (block) {
    var width = columnWidth(block)
    if (width) block.style.width = width + 'px'
  }

  /* Height of the real content, which is not the same as the document height:
     the viewer is a full-viewport application, so both scrollHeight and body
     height just echo back the height we set. Measure the lowest visible
     content edge instead, ignoring the fixed chrome. */
  function contentHeight (frame) {
    var doc = frame.contentDocument
    if (!doc) return 0
    var view = doc.defaultView
    var root = doc.querySelector('.container') || doc.body
    var nodes = root.querySelectorAll('*')
    var bottom = 0
    for (var i = 0; i < nodes.length; i++) {
      var node = nodes[i]
      var computed = view.getComputedStyle(node)
      if (computed.display === 'none' || computed.visibility === 'hidden' || computed.opacity === '0') continue
      if (computed.position === 'fixed' || node.closest(CHROME)) continue
      var rect = node.getBoundingClientRect()
      if (!rect.width || !rect.height) continue
      bottom = Math.max(bottom, rect.bottom)
    }
    return bottom ? Math.ceil(bottom + 24) : 0
  }

  /* A wider frame makes the viewer draw a larger diagram, which makes it
     taller, which is the measurement that sized the frame. Settle it over a
     few bounded passes instead of assuming one is enough, and stop once the
     change is not worth another reflow.

     A measurement of zero means the viewer has not laid itself out yet, not
     that it never will: each one is a whole application, and end-to-end-flow
     loads five of them at once over a cold cache. Keep waiting, because
     giving up here strands the frame at its seeded height for good. */
  function fit (frame, pass, waits) {
    var height = contentHeight(frame)
    if (!height) {
      if ((waits || 0) < 60) setTimeout(function () { fit(frame, pass, (waits || 0) + 1) }, 250)
      return
    }
    var current = parseInt(frame.style.height, 10) || 0
    if (Math.abs(height - current) < 8) return
    frame.style.height = height + 'px'
    if ((pass || 0) < 3) setTimeout(function () { fit(frame, (pass || 0) + 1, 0) }, 250)
  }

  /* Replaces one still with its viewer, then calls `done` to free the slot for
     the next one -- on load, or on the breaker below, whichever comes first.

     The still stays on screen for the whole download. An earlier version put
     the frame in place the moment it was created, which left a blank grey
     panel where the diagram had been until ~800KB arrived: on a fast static
     server that is a flicker, on anything slower it is the whole reading
     experience. So the frame loads off-screen, at the size it is about to
     occupy, and the swap happens in one synchronous block. */
  function activate (actions, done) {
    var block = blockFor(actions)
    if (!block || block.classList.contains('archify-live')) return done()
    var content = block.firstElementChild || block
    var still = content.querySelector('img')

    var frame = document.createElement('iframe')
    frame.className = 'archify-frame'
    frame.title = actions.dataset.archifyTitle || 'Interactive diagram'
    /* Load it at the size it will be revealed at, so the viewer lays out for
       the real column and appearing costs no second reflow. Antora writes no
       width/height on the still, so one that has not decoded yet measures
       zero: fall back to a nominal height rather than a collapsed frame. */
    var seed = still ? Math.round(still.getBoundingClientRect().height) : 0
    frame.style.height = (seed > 120 ? seed : 620) + 'px'
    frame.style.width = (columnWidth(block) || block.clientWidth || 900) + 'px'
    frame.setAttribute('data-archify-loading', '')

    /* Everything that makes the frame visible, in one go, so no intermediate
       state is ever painted. The frame is never moved in the DOM --
       re-inserting an iframe reloads it, which would throw away the wait --
       so the still is removed around it instead. */
    function reveal () {
      frame.removeAttribute('data-archify-loading')
      frame.style.width = ''
      /* .imageblock is display:flex and .content is a shrink-wrapping flex
         item: the image sized it by its own intrinsic width, but an iframe
         has none, so .content would collapse to the UA's 300px iframe default
         and the frame's width:100% would resolve against an indefinite
         container. Pin .content to the flex container's width so the
         percentage has something definite to resolve against. */
      content.style.width = '100%'
      block.classList.add('archify-live')
      widen(block)
      for (var i = content.children.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        if (content.children[i] !== frame) content.children[i].remove()
      }
    }

    /* One viewer loads at a time, so a frame that never fires load would hold
       the queue for good and strand every diagram below it as a still.
       Release the slot after a generous wait; this frame still reveals itself
       if it turns up late. */
    var settled = false
    function settle () {
      if (settled) return
      settled = true
      done()
    }
    setTimeout(settle, 15000)

    frame.addEventListener('load', function () {
      /* The viewer repeats its own title as an <h1> above the diagram, and
         every page that embeds one already carries that line as the section
         heading right above the frame. Two of the same sentence is one too
         many, and at column width the repeat wraps onto a second line and
         runs into the viewer's own toolbar. Hidden here rather than removed
         from the specification: a title is required there, and the "Open in a
         new tab" page has no surrounding heading to make it redundant. Same
         document, same origin, so this is a stylesheet and not a message. */
      var inner = frame.contentDocument
      if (inner) {
        var hide = inner.createElement('style')
        hide.textContent = '.container > .header{display:none}'
        inner.head.appendChild(hide)
      }

      /* `load` means the viewer's assets arrived and its scripts ran, not that
         it has drawn: the SVG appears in a later layout pass. Revealing on
         load alone shows the viewer's own empty panel for a frame or two, so
         wait for the drawing to exist -- briefly, and then reveal anyway,
         because a viewer that never draws must not keep the still forever. */
      var tries = 0
      ;(function ready () {
        var drawn = false
        try { drawn = !!(inner && inner.querySelector('svg')) } catch (e) { drawn = true }
        if (!drawn && ++tries <= 20) return void setTimeout(ready, 100)

        reveal()
        settle()

        /* Only now is the frame in the flow at its final width, so this is
           where the height measurement belongs. */
        setTimeout(function () { fit(frame, 0) }, 400)
        var width = 0
        new ResizeObserver(function () {
          /* Width only: observing our own height would loop against fit(). */
          var next = Math.round(frame.getBoundingClientRect().width)
          if (next === width) return
          width = next
          fit(frame, 0)
        }).observe(frame)
      })()
    })

    content.appendChild(frame)
    frame.src = actions.dataset.archifySrc
  }

  /* A page can hold five of these and each is a whole application of roughly
     800KB, so they are loaded strictly one at a time.

     Serial, not merely staggered. An earlier version started one every 900ms,
     which on a slow origin simply put all five in flight together: a browser
     opens about six connections per origin, five long downloads take nearly
     all of them, and the next click on the navigation sidebar gets no socket
     at all. That is not a slow page, it is a page that has stopped answering
     -- the network panel shows the navigation cancelled with zero bytes
     transferred. One viewer at a time bounds the cost to a single connection
     however slow the origin is, and the reader keeps a still until its
     replacement is ready, so nothing is lost by waiting.

     Proximity decides the order and never whether. Two earlier versions let it
     decide whether, and both stranded the lower diagrams as stills for good:
     the reader saw a tiny illegible image where a viewer should be. The cause
     outlives either mechanism. Antora writes no width or height on a still, so
     every image reflows everything below it as it decodes -- which means a
     block can be carried into range with no event to announce it. An
     IntersectionObserver's one-shot entry arrives against a position the block
     no longer holds; a rect read on scroll is never stale, but nothing reads it
     once the reader stops scrolling. Working through the whole queue removes
     that class of failure instead of widening the window it hides in: being
     near a diagram only brings it forward. */
  function enhance () {
    var pending = []
    var actions = document.querySelectorAll('.archify-actions[data-archify-src]')
    for (var i = 0; i < actions.length; i++) {
      var block = blockFor(actions[i])
      if (!block) continue
      /* Marks the blocks this script owns, so the stylesheet above can reach
         them while they are still stills. */
      block.classList.add('archify-block')
      pending.push(actions[i])
    }
    if (!pending.length) return

    var queued = false
    var running = false

    function stop () {
      window.removeEventListener('scroll', schedule)
      window.removeEventListener('resize', schedule)
    }

    /* Leaving the page ends the queue. Without this, a click on the navigation
       sidebar races a pump that is about to start another ~800KB viewer: the
       browser asks for the next document while this page opens one more
       connection for a viewer nobody will ever see, and on a slow origin the
       navigation is what waits. The reader reads that as a page that has
       stopped answering. Nothing below needs the queue once the document is
       on its way out. */
    window.addEventListener('pagehide', function () {
      pending.length = 0
      stop()
    })

    /* One observer for the whole column, not one per diagram. Every live block
       tracks the same element, so five separate observers on it did the same
       work five times over on every resize. */
    var column = document.querySelector('.doc')
    if (column) {
      new ResizeObserver(function () {
        var live = document.querySelectorAll('.imageblock.archify-live')
        for (var i = 0; i < live.length; i++) widen(live[i])
      }).observe(column)
    }

    /* The one place a viewer is ever started. Nothing else calls activate, so
       there is exactly one download in flight no matter what triggers a
       pump -- scroll, resize, or the previous one finishing. */
    function pump () {
      if (running || !pending.length) return
      running = true
      activate(pending.shift(), function () {
        running = false
        if (pending.length) setTimeout(pump, 250)
        else stop()
      })
    }

    /* Reorders what is left so anything the reader can nearly see goes next,
       and never activates anything itself. A diagram already passed keeps its
       place in the queue: the saving worth having is not loading five viewers
       at once, not reclaiming one that has scrolled off the top. */
    function promote () {
      queued = false
      var visible = []
      var rest = []
      for (var i = 0; i < pending.length; i++) {
        var block = blockFor(pending[i])
        var close = block && block.getBoundingClientRect().top <= window.innerHeight + 400
        ;(close ? visible : rest).push(pending[i])
      }
      pending = visible.concat(rest)
      pump()
    }

    function schedule () {
      if (queued) return
      queued = true
      requestAnimationFrame(promote)
    }

    window.addEventListener('scroll', schedule, { passive: true })
    window.addEventListener('resize', schedule)
    promote()
  }

  if (document.readyState === 'loading') document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', enhance)
  else enhance()
})()

Dashed edges are wiring that exists but is not exercised by the checked-in `config.yaml`: the identity provider is contacted only once `oidc.issuer_url` is set.

The diagram condenses some detail. The sidecars share one node: the bundled `iac :8082`, `notifications :8080` and `mapping :8081`, `searxng :8888`, plus the optional authz contract, whose implementation you provide yourself; the core appears as its API layer plus a single "application and adapters" node covering the other three layers; and Redis, the `workspaces` volume, Langfuse’s own stores and the notification and storage backends are carried in the notes beside it rather than drawn. The Langfuse UI is reachable through the proxy on port 3000, artifacts land in the `kumoss-artifacts` bucket, and the shipped configuration routes model calls through LiteLLM.

## Component responsibilities

| Component | Responsibility | Main relationships |
| --- | --- | --- |
| React SPA (`client/web`) | Session wizard, planning and results views, user page and admin panel. An OIDC public client: it calls `/api` with a bearer token and streams progress over Server-Sent Events. | Built into the Nginx image; reaches the API through Nginx, and the identity provider directly for login |
| Nginx (`proxy`) | Sole public entry point, on ports 80, 9000 and 3000: serves the built SPA and proxies `/api`, the events stream, object storage and the Langfuse UI. | Browser → core, object storage, Langfuse |
| Core API layer (`core/src/api/v1`) | Routes every request: IaC operations, the progress stream, session reads, repository and pull-request actions, identity and roles, the admin panel, and a passthrough to the notifications sidecar. One authentication dependency guards all of them but the public OIDC configuration. | Delegates to application handlers |
| Application layer (`core/src/application`) | The generate, drift and apply handlers, and the services they orchestrate — filtering, reporting, pull requests, session orchestration. A factory builds a fresh object graph per run. | Composes domain services |
| Domain layer (`core/src/domains`) | Entities, value objects and ports, and the services holding the behavior: the agent loop, session and user management, validation, targeting, the compliance check, artifact storage, persistence and tracing. | Depends only on interfaces |
| Infrastructure layer (`core/src/infrastructure`) | Adapters behind those ports: OIDC, the LiteLLM router, git and workspaces, the iac-sidecar driver, Jinja layouts, object storage, PostgreSQL, Redis and OpenTelemetry. The generated sidecar clients are **not** part of this layer — they live in `core/src/clients`, a sibling package. | Implements domain ports |
| authz service | AuthZEN policy decision point for organizational access control. Disabled by default and not bundled: deploy your own PDP implementing the 2-endpoint contract (evaluation + healthz). Disabled, the core treats every operation as authorized; enabled, the core consults the PDP on every write route and never fails open. | Called from every write route via the PEP helper with the caller’s identity |
| iac service | Runs one IaC engine command per asynchronous job — `init`, `validate`, `plan`, `show`, `apply` — returning a job id to poll. OpenTofu by default, selected with `IAC_BINARY`. A reference implementation; production deployments are expected to supply their own. | Shares the `workspaces` volume with the core |
| mapping service | Resolves what the user types in the wizard’s repository step (a repository name or URL) to the clone URL. Bundled and enabled by default: a bare name is appended to `MAPPING_PREFIX_IDENTIFIER`; replace it with your own catalog-backed implementation if you have one. Disabled, the core treats the input as the repository URL (identity passthrough). | Called by the core from `POST /api/v1/repository/parse` |
| notifications service | Channel-agnostic notify contract; the reference implementation posts color-coded Slack webhook messages. | Fire-and-forget from the core on compliance, apply and pipeline failures; request/response for the support requests the header’s chat bubble sends |
| searxng service | Self-hosted SearXNG metasearch with the JSON API enabled. Answers the core’s `web_search` tool so agents get live web results without the LLM provider needing native search support. The base image is pinned to a datetagged SearXNG build: the project is a rolling release, so the pinned tag makes rebuilds reproducible and upgrades deliberate. | Called synchronously by the core’s web-search facade, driven by `web_search.*` in `config.yaml` |
| OpenAPI contracts (`contracts/openapi`) | Source of truth for the four sidecar APIs (the searxng sidecar is not contract-based; it is plain SearXNG), with Schemathesis conformance suites. | Contracts → generated clients → sidecars |
| core-db (PostgreSQL 17) | System of record: thirteen tables covering users, sessions, workspaces, rounds, plans, pull requests, reports, compliance checks and artifacts. | Core, over asyncpg |
| Redis 8 | Fail-open cache for session facts, the last status and finished-session aggregates. No pub/sub, no locks. | Core only |
| object-storage (RustFS, Apache-2.0) | **Default, bundled** artifact store (`kumoss-artifacts`): reports, plans, drift JSON and code changes, served to the browser by presigned URL. `storage.provider` switches to AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage or any other S3-compatible endpoint. Engine state lives in the **separate** `storage.terraform_state_bucket` — on by default as shipped. | Core through the SDK, browser through Nginx :9000, and the iac sidecar for state |
| `workspaces` volume | Per-run git clones under `/workspaces/<session>/<call>`. A failed run’s directory is removed; a successful generate round **renames** its directory to `/workspaces/<session>/pinned`, which survives until apply discards it or the next generate round replaces it. | Mounted by core and iac |
| Langfuse (web, worker, langfuse-db, ClickHouse, its own Redis, a `langfuse` bucket) | Trace store and UI (OpenTelemetry), and the prompt registry seeded at core boot. One project; the deployment’s `environment` is Langfuse’s environment and the operation and providers are trace tags. | Core, over OTLP/HTTP and the public prompt API, with the project’s key pair |
| OIDC identity provider | Authenticates users and issues the JWT access tokens the core validates. Any provider with discovery, JWKS and JWT access tokens works; Entra ID, Keycloak, Auth0 and Okta are documented. | Browser for login, core for discovery and JWKS; configured under `oidc` |
| LLM providers | Model inference behind the LiteLLM router, in a main and a small role. | Selected by `llm.model` and `llm.small_model`; credentials in the core’s environment file |
| Git hosting | Clone and push over the git CLI; pull requests through the GitHub, Azure DevOps or GitLab REST APIs. Public SaaS hosts only — `github.com`, `gitlab.com` without subgroups, `dev.azure.com` — over HTTPS. GitHub Enterprise Server and self-managed GitLab are not supported today. | Selected by `git.provider` |

# See Kumoss in action

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/prerelease/main/see-it-in-action/

This page shows Kumoss working on a real cloud environment, from a developer’s first request to an applied change, and then a destructive request that Kumoss holds for review. Watch the four-minute video, then use the walkthrough below to jump to the guide behind each moment.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

## About this recording

- **One unscripted session.** The run was recorded against a real cloud subscription with the default Kumoss stack. Waiting times are shortened; the generated code, plans, reports, and applied results are not edited.
- **Captions and step cards are added in editing.** They explain what happens on screen while the agent works.
- **Sensitive data is blurred.** Subscription identifiers, accounts, and user names are masked. The request was typed in Spanish and is shown in English; Kumoss accepts requests in the language your team uses.
- **The notification cards are a recreation.** They follow the messages Kumoss sends when it locks a session; in the recording, those messages went to a chat channel off screen.

## What you see

| Time | Moment | Learn more |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0:04 | **The starting point.** An existing cloud environment with an app runtime, secrets, storage, and networking, all managed as code in a repository. | [About Kumoss](../about/) |
| 0:10 | **The request.** A developer writes *My app needs to store images and use a fixed outbound IP* and picks the repository. No tickets, no infrastructure code. | [Make a request](../guides/make-a-request/) |
| 0:23 | **Context first.** Kumoss reads the repository, the infrastructure deployed in the cloud, and the organization’s guidelines for that cloud. | [Generate infrastructure](../guides/generate-infrastructure/) |
| 0:38 | **Standards built in.** The generated code follows the organization’s conventions: private networking, secrets in a vault, least-privilege roles, and deletion locks. | [Customize prompts](../guides/customize-prompts/) |
| 0:54 | **Drift fixed on the way.** Kumoss finds network rules that were changed outside the code and updates the code to match, in the same pull request. | [Remediate drift](../guides/remediate-drift/) |
| 1:10 | **A plan that passes.** Kumoss runs a real OpenTofu or Terraform plan, feeds any errors back to the agent, and checks the result for compliance. | [Generate infrastructure](../guides/generate-infrastructure/) |
| 1:25 | **A report anyone can read.** The summary, the impact, and the estimated monthly cost, followed by the explanation of the drift fix and the generated code. | [Follow a session](../guides/follow-a-session/) |
| 2:00 | **Pull request and apply.** The developer opens the pull request, approves it, and confirms the apply. Kumoss applies exactly the plan that was reviewed. | [Merge and apply](../guides/merge-and-apply/) |
| 2:15 | **Live in the cloud.** The new resources appear in the cloud console, and every agent step is recorded as a trace. | [Monitor with Langfuse](../guides/monitor-with-langfuse/) |
| 2:34 | **Rules defined once.** The platform team keeps its security and architecture rules as versioned prompts that apply to every request. | [Customize prompts](../guides/customize-prompts/) |
| 2:46 | **A destructive request.** The same developer asks to delete the storage account. Kumoss flags the change as high impact. | [Generate infrastructure](../guides/generate-infrastructure/) |
| 3:08 | **Deployment blocked.** The deletion breaks policy, so the session is locked and apply is refused, whoever asks. The platform team is notified. | [Resolve a locked session](../guides/resolve-a-locked-session/) |
| 3:27 | **Humans approve.** An administrator with the editor role reviews the locked session in the admin panel and removes the lock. | [Session locks](../guides/administer-users-and-locks/#session-locks) |
| 3:44 | **Reviewed, applied, recorded.** The developer applies the reviewed plan, and the resources are removed with a full audit trail. | [Merge and apply](../guides/merge-and-apply/) |

# Frequently asked questions

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/prerelease/main/faq/

Short answers for people using the Kumoss web application. The longer explanations are in the [Make a request](../guides/make-a-request/) guide; mode-by-mode behavior is in [Comparing the operating modes](../reference/operating-modes/#compare-modes). If the answer you need is not here, see [Support requests](../additional-information/#support-requests).

## FAQ

### Access and roles

Why are the drift and import modes grayed out?

They require the `devops` operation role. New users start as `developer`. Ask your administrator to change your role in the admin portal; it takes effect on your next page load.

Can other people see my sessions?

Only reviewers who hold a panel role (viewer, editor, or admin) can read them, including the conversation. Nobody but you can continue, merge, or apply your sessions.

Why does the login page say my session has expired?

Your identity token expired and the application signed you out. Sign in again. Any Kumoss session that was running continues on the server; reopen it from the footer or your user page.

### Requests

Do I have to specify every parameter?

No. Missing parameters never block a creation request. Kumoss applies your organization’s naming conventions, resource defaults, and the placement it finds in the workspace, and it states the assumptions it made in the response.

My request was declined. Why?

The filter explains the reason in the chat. The three causes are: out of scope (not a Terraform-managed change), an ambiguous target (name the resource), or a missing referent (the thing you refer to does not exist in that repository and path).

Can I ask questions instead of requesting changes?

Yes. Inventory, improvement, and impact questions are answered in the chat; the round ends without changes and you can continue with a change request in the same session.

Can I request several changes at once?

You can, but one intent per request produces better results and clearer reports. Use follow-ups for the next step; they run on the same branch.

Why was my repository URL rejected?

Only `https://` URLs are accepted: SSH (`git@host:path`, `ssh://`), `git://`, `http://`, `file://` and local paths are refused, and so are URLs that embed a password or token. Enter the plain HTTPS URL. Azure DevOps users: the portal’s clone URL starts with `https://<org>@dev.azure.com/…​`; that `<org>@` prefix is accepted, but it must match `GIT_USER` (see [Git credentials](../guides/production/secrets-and-credentials/#git-credentials)), so removing it is the safe choice. Only `github.com`, `gitlab.com` (no subgroups), and `dev.azure.com` are supported for pull requests. The repository must also be reachable by Kumoss’s service account; when it is not, the answer is always "Repository is not reachable or access was denied." whatever the cause, and the exact git error is only in the core log.

Why does Kumoss say it found no root module paths?

It only sees files committed on the repository’s default branch, and it offers a directory only when it contains `.tf` files and no part of its path is `modules`, `examples`, `example`, or `.terraform`. Commit the Terraform files to the default branch, or move them out of an excluded directory. The rules are in [Repository layout](../reference/repository-layout/#terraform-roots).

Why is my directory not offered as a root module path?

Either it sits under an excluded directory name, or it is nested under another directory that already qualifies as a root (for example `platform/network/` under a `platform/` that has a `main.tf`); in that case pick the parent, Kumoss works from there.

Why am I not asked which cloud provider to use?

Kumoss reads the providers from the root module’s `required_providers`, so a module that uses several (say `azurerm` and `kubernetes`) gets all of them in one session. It asks only what the code cannot tell: the subscription, project, account or compartment of each `azurerm`, `google`, `aws` or `oci` provider, and values for required variables, once per root module. The answers are kept in a `kumoss.yaml` file next to the module. See [Root module manifest](../reference/root-module-manifest/).

Why does Kumoss ask for the module’s inputs again?

The inputs form only appears when the module needs something its `kumoss.yaml` does not cover. Either the pull request that committed `kumoss.yaml` has not been merged yet (Kumoss reads the default branch), or the module changed: a new required variable, a new cloud provider, a deleted var file you had picked, or a secret whose stored value is gone. Only what is missing is asked.

### Sessions

How long does a session take?

From a couple of minutes for a small change to considerably longer for large roots: generation and up to five validation attempts run first, then a drift check and the report. The progress screen shows what is happening at each moment.

Can I close the browser?

Yes. The session runs on the server. Reopen it from the **Sessions** panel in the footer or from **View all sessions** on your user page.

Why can I not continue a failed session?

A failed round ends the session for good. Start a new session; if the failure was "Validation loop exceeded.", make the request more specific or split it.

Why does nothing happen when I send a second request while one is running?

Only one operation runs per session at a time. Wait for the current round to finish; the input is disabled during a run.

What is the branch called?

`Kumoss/YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS` in UTC, created on the first request of the session. Every round pushes to it.

### Results

What do Low, Medium, and High impact mean?

With the default criteria: high is destructive actions, restarts, downtime, or critical networking changes; medium is a significant configuration update that changes behavior without guaranteed downtime; low is isolated new resources or non-disruptive updates such as tags.

Is the estimated cost accurate?

It is an approximation of fixed monthly prices for the resources in the plan, taken from public pricing pages when the report was written. Usage-based and free resources are listed but not included in the total. Use it to compare options, not as a quote.

Where are the compliance findings?

In the session details, as the round’s **Compliance Check** artifact: a summary, each violation with its severity, rule id, and resource, and the rules that passed. When a finding locks the session, the same findings appear under **Why** on the **Deployment Blocked** screen. Findings from the compliance policy carry a **policy** badge, and findings from the intent check an **intent** badge. See [Compliance findings](../guides/follow-a-session/#compliance-findings).

Can I download the plan or the report?

Not as files. The plan, report, and changed files are shown inline in the results view and in the session details; the code itself is on the session branch in your repository.

### Locks and approvals

Why is my session locked?

The compliance check found an error-level or critical violation (with the default rules: from the intent check, changes outside the scope of your request or parts of the request left undone; from the compliance policy, a standalone deletion, a removed customer-managed encryption key, a `null_resource`, provisioner or `data "external"`, or one of the provider policies' prohibitions such as a port open to the internet), a compliance policy could not be evaluated, or the impact was rated High in a deployment that locks on high impact. See [Why a session is locked](../guides/resolve-a-locked-session/#why).

What can I do while locked?

Read everything, continue the conversation, and create the pull request so reviewers can see the diff. Merging and applying are refused.

How is a lock released?

A reviewer with the editor or admin panel role unlocks the session from the admin panel, or a new request in the same session produces a result that passes cleanly. A reviewer’s unlock lasts until your next generate round. See [Unlock the session](../guides/resolve-a-locked-session/#unlock).

Why is a deletion I explicitly asked for flagged?

The compliance policy denies any standalone deletion as a critical violation regardless of the request; only a recreate of the same resource is allowed. The check is deterministic, so rephrasing does not help. A reviewer can unlock the session after looking at it, and your organization can adapt the policy; see [Write a policy rule](../guides/write-a-policy-rule/).

### Pull requests and apply

Do I have to open a pull request?

The API allows a direct apply, but the web application does not offer a standalone Apply button. You reach apply through **Approve PR and Apply**, which merges the pull request and then applies, so in the web application the pull request is the route to apply — which is also the recommended one, because it brings your team’s review and CI into the decision.

Reviewers asked for changes. What now?

Type the changes as a follow-up request in the same session. The new round pushes to the same branch, so the pull request updates.

What exactly does Approve PR and Apply do?

After you confirm, it merges the pull request into the default branch and executes the plan you reviewed, without re-planning. The apply-results screen shows what happened.

The apply failed. Will Kumoss retry?

No. The session still closes as completed, with an apply report whose status is the model’s reading of the engine output (normally **Failed**) and a failure notification to your reviewers, which is the signal keyed to the exit code; nothing is rolled back and nothing is re-run. Read the error in the apply results, fix the cause (often cloud permissions or a resource that changed since the plan), and send a new request, which produces a fresh plan to review.

Do the import modes import my existing resources?

Yes, in the Azure subscriptions, GCP projects and AWS accounts the root module’s `azurerm`, `google` and `aws` providers point at. OCI, Kubernetes and VMware vSphere scopes cannot be listed, so an import round on a module that uses only those finds nothing to import. Partial Import and Full Import find the resources in your scopes that Terraform does not manage, write resource blocks for them, and run `terraform import` during the round, so they are in the state before the pull request is reviewed. Rejected imports are fed back to the generator and retried. Merging the pull request ends the session; nothing is applied. See [Import infrastructure](../guides/import-infrastructure/).

Where does Terraform state live?

Not in the repository, and not in the working copy Kumoss creates. Out of the box, Kumoss keeps state for you, in a bucket dedicated to state with one state file per project (repository + root-module path), and ignores any `backend` block your repository declares. Your platform team can instead configure Kumoss to leave it in the remote backend your repository’s own Terraform files declare, exactly as it would if you ran the engine yourself. Either way your pull request contains only your infrastructure code — no state file and no backend file — and there is nothing for you to set per session; the details are in [Configure state backends](../guides/configure-state-backends/).

My plan wants to create resources that already exist. Why?

The session is planning against empty state. The most common cause is that your repository keeps its state in its own backend while Kumoss manages state, which is the default: Kumoss then ignores that backend. Other causes are that your platform team turned off Kumoss-managed state and your repository declares no remote backend of its own, that the project’s identity changed — the root-module path moved or the repository was renamed — that your platform team changed the state backend, which Kumoss never migrates, or that Kumoss was upgraded from a release whose state keys also included the cloud scope and the state was not moved (see [Upgrade notes](../guides/upgrade-notes/)). Report it with the session id; an operator can check the state location.

### Data and privacy

What data leaves Kumoss when I make a request?

Your request text, the conversation, the repository files the agent reads, the plan, and validation errors are sent to the language model your platform team configured and stored in the tracing system for review. Do not paste secrets into requests or commit them to the repository.

Which cloud credentials does Kumoss use?

The identity your platform team configured for the execution engine, never yours. Your deployment can also plug in an external authorization service that is asked, at the start of each session, whether you may work on that cloud, repository, and root module path; in the shipped configuration that service is switched off and no such check runs.

### Getting help

How do I contact support?

Use the chat-bubble **Support** icon in the header, or **Contact Team** on a locked session. The message carries your e-mail, the session id, and the session context automatically and reaches the reviewers of your deployment.

Support says notifications are disabled.

Your deployment has not connected a notification channel. Use your organization’s usual support route and quote the session id from the session details.

What should I include when reporting a problem?

The session id, the mode, the repository and path, what you asked, and what you expected instead. Reviewers can then open the session’s history, artifacts, and traces.

See [Support requests](../additional-information/#support-requests) for the full detail on what each support channel carries and how it is routed.

# Guides

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/prerelease/main/guides-overview/

These guides show how to accomplish specific tasks with Kumoss. Pick the group that matches your role, then the guide that states your goal. To watch the main guides play out in one real session, see [See Kumoss in action](../see-it-in-action/).

## Use Kumoss

For developers who ask Kumoss for infrastructure changes.

[Make a request](../guides/make-a-request/)

Open a session and phrase a request the filter accepts.

[Follow a session](../guides/follow-a-session/)

Track progress and read the report, plan, and code.

[Merge and apply](../guides/merge-and-apply/)

Open, merge, and apply the pull request of a session.

[Resolve a locked session](../guides/resolve-a-locked-session/)

Find out why a session is locked and get it unlocked.

## Operating modes

What each kind of session does, from the request to the merge. For the three side by side, see [Operating modes](../reference/operating-modes/).

[Generate infrastructure](../guides/generate-infrastructure/)

Turn a request into validated Terraform code, reviewed as a plan and report before you apply it.

[Remediate drift](../guides/remediate-drift/)

Detect and reconcile drift for a set of resources or a whole Terraform root.

[Import infrastructure](../guides/import-infrastructure/)

Bring existing, unmanaged cloud resources under Terraform management, for a specific set of resources or across a whole scope.

## Review and administer

For reviewers and administrators with a panel role.

[Administer users and locks](../guides/administer-users-and-locks/)

Review any user’s sessions, and manage session locks and roles from the admin panel.

## Customize

For platform and security teams adapting Kumoss to their standards.

[Customize prompts](../guides/customize-prompts/)

Adapt Kumoss to your organization’s standards by editing its prompts in Langfuse.

[Write a policy rule](../guides/write-a-policy-rule/)

Add a deterministic rule to a compliance policy, test it, and publish it.

## Deploy and operate

For operators who install and run Kumoss.

[Deploy to production](../guides/deploy-to-production/)

Plan a production deployment, then work through [secrets and credentials](../guides/production/secrets-and-credentials/), [networking and TLS](../guides/production/networking-and-tls/), [hardening](../guides/production/hardening/), and [operations](../guides/production/operations/).

[Deploy with Helm](../guides/deploy-with-helm/)

Install Kumoss on Kubernetes with the bundled chart, try it on a local kind cluster, and bind cloud credentials through workload identity.

[Enable authentication](../guides/enable-authentication/)

Connect an OIDC identity provider and grant the first administrator access.

[Configure state backends](../guides/configure-state-backends/)

Choose who owns Terraform and OpenTofu state: [the repository](../guides/state-backends/repository-declared/), [Kumoss](../guides/state-backends/kumoss-managed/), or [the deployment](../guides/state-backends/sidecar-supplied/).

[Monitor with Langfuse](../guides/monitor-with-langfuse/)

Read Kumoss’s traces in Langfuse, and know what a trace contains and omits.

Before upgrading an existing deployment, read [Upgrade notes](../guides/upgrade-notes/).

## Develop

For contributors to Kumoss itself.

[Development](../guides/development/)

Run the stack for development, test, type-check, lint, and regenerate the sidecar clients.

# Roadmap

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/prerelease/main/roadmap/

This page describes the direction of Kumoss. It groups the planned work into themes and summarizes each initiative in a few lines, so that users, operators, and contributors can see where the project is going and plan around it.

> **Note**
> The roadmap states intent, not commitment. Priorities change as the project learns from the people using it, and no initiative carries a delivery date. Each feature is announced in the [release notes](https://github.com/InditexTech/kumoss/releases) when it ships; until then, the rest of this documentation describes only what Kumoss does today.

## How to read the roadmap

The initiatives are grouped into seven themes. Each initiative carries one of three statuses:

- Done: the initiative has shipped and is documented; the section links to its documentation.
- In progress: active development is under way.
- Planned: the initiative is accepted into the roadmap, and work has not started.

The order of the themes and of the initiatives within them does not indicate priority.

| [Cloud and code lifecycle](#cloud-and-code) | [From cloud to code](#cloud-to-code) | Planned |
