# Core API

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/prerelease/main/reference/api/core/

The core exposes 20 routes across ten routers in `core/src/api/v1/`. This page is derived from those routers, which are the only source of truth: the core has no hand-written specification.

Every router is mounted under `/v1` on an application created with `root_path="/api"`, so the reverse proxy publishes the routes as `/api/v1/…​`. Paths below are written with that prefix.

## The authentication rule

**Authentication is a per-route dependency, not middleware.** Every route under `/v1` except `GET /v1/auth/config` declares the authentication dependency, or one of the two role wrappers built on it. A router added without one of these is public.

The dependency behaves in one of two ways:

- **Blank `oidc.issuer_url`** (the checked-in default) — authentication is disabled. Every request resolves to a fixed local development identity, provisioned as a real row in the users table with the top role of both groups.
- **`oidc.issuer_url` set** — the dependency requires an `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>`, validates it against the issuer’s JWKS, and maps the `(issuer, subject)` pair to a users row, creating it on first sight. A missing or invalid token is `401` with a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` challenge.

Two independent role groups gate the routes, and both live in the core database:

- The **operation role** (`developer` < `devops`) gates Infrastructure as Code work. Falling short is `403 Requires operation role '<role>' or higher`.
- The **panel role** (`viewer` < `editor` < `admin`, nullable) gates `/v1/admin/*`. Falling short is `403 Requires admin-panel role '<role>' or higher`.

Beyond the role check, a per-session access check applies: the owner may always read and write; a non-owner with any panel role may read only; everyone else receives `403 Not the session owner`. See [Roles and permissions](../../roles-and-permissions/) for the full matrix.

The whole surface is summarized here and then described router by router.

| Route | Requires | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/v1/auth/config` | nothing (public) | `200` OIDC settings |
| `GET /api/v1/users/me` | any signed-in user | `200` identity and roles |
| `POST /api/v1/iac/generate` | operation `developer` | `202` session id |
| `POST /api/v1/iac/drift` | operation `devops` | `202` session id |
| `POST /api/v1/iac/import` | operation `developer` | `202` session id |
| `POST /api/v1/iac/apply` | operation `developer` | `202` session id |
| `POST /api/v1/manifest/probe` | operation `developer` | `200` what the root module needs |
| `GET /api/v1/events/subscribe/{session_id}` | read access to the session | `200` event stream |
| `PUT /api/v1/repository/pr` | operation `developer`, owner | `201` pull request |
| `PUT /api/v1/repository/pr/merge` | operation `developer`, owner | `204` no content |
| `POST /api/v1/repository/parse` | operation `developer` | `200` resolved URL and Terraform roots |
| `GET /api/v1/sessions/list` | any signed-in user | `200` page of summaries |
| `GET /api/v1/sessions?id={session_id}` | read access to the session | `200` session aggregate |
| `GET /api/v1/admin/sessions/list` | panel `viewer` | `200` page of summaries |
| `GET /api/v1/admin/sessions?id={session_id}` | panel `viewer` | `200` session aggregate |
| `PATCH /api/v1/admin/sessions/{session_id}/toggle_lock` | panel `editor` | `200` lock state |
| `GET /api/v1/admin/users` | panel `admin` | `200` page of users |
| `PUT /api/v1/admin/users/{user_id}/roles` | panel `admin` | `200` updated user |
| `POST /api/v1/notifications` | any signed-in user | `202` delivery id |

## Infrastructure as Code

Prefix `/v1/iac`. Four routes, one per operation. All four are **asynchronous**: they validate the request, resolve or create the session, schedule the pipeline as a background task, and answer `202 Accepted` with nothing but the session id. Progress arrives over the event stream.

```
{"session_id": "917d0485-a0a2-4c34-8f33-a89d28aba9b0"}
```

| Route | Minimum role | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /api/v1/iac/generate` | `developer` | Generates, validates, and prepares IaC from a natural-language query. |
| `POST /api/v1/iac/drift` | `devops` | Detects and remediates drift. `is_partial: true` scopes the round to the resources named in the query. |
| `POST /api/v1/iac/import` | `developer` | Brings unmanaged resources under Terraform management. `is_partial: true` limits it to the resources named in the query. See [Import infrastructure](../../../guides/import-infrastructure/). |
| `POST /api/v1/iac/apply` | `developer` | Applies the plan pinned by the session’s last successful generate round. No re-plan happens at apply time. |

`generate`, `drift` and `import` share a request body. Exactly one of `repo_uri` (a first call, which opens a session) or `session_id` (an iteration call on an existing session) must be present; supplying both or neither is a validation error.

| Field | First call | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `q` | required | The user’s query for this call. At least one character. |
| `repo_uri` | required | `https://` repository URI with a host; SSH (`git@host:path`, `ssh://`), `git://`, `http://`, `file://` and local paths are `422`. May carry a userinfo username (for example `https://org@dev.azure.com/…​`) but must not embed a password or token; an empty password (`user:@host`) is rejected too. |
| `root_module_path` | optional | Repository-relative path to the root module, for example `environments/dev`. Defaults to the repository root. An absolute path or one containing a `..` segment is rejected. After the clone, the path must resolve, symlinks included, to an existing directory inside the repository, or the session ends `FAILED` with `runner failed: root_module_path '<path>' is not a directory inside the repository`. First call only — iteration calls inherit it from the session. The former name `iac_path` is still accepted as a deprecated alias; prefer `root_module_path`. |
| `manifest` | optional | Answers for the root module’s inputs: `{"variables": [{"name", "value", "sensitive"}], "var_files": […​], "scopes": {"<provider>": "<scope id>"}}`. Needed when [`POST /api/v1/manifest/probe`](#manifest) reports `needs_input`; the session saves them to the module’s manifest before running. First call only. |
| `project_identifier` | optional | What the user named the repository before it was resolved, for example `sistemas-kumoss-rsg-esc1-dev`: the `project_identifier` that `POST /api/v1/repository/parse` returned. 1 to 1024 characters, trimmed; dropped when empty or equal to `repo_uri`, and rejected when it embeds a password or token, since it is committed with the manifest. Before any session is created the core resolves it through the [mapping sidecar](../mapping/) and rejects it with `422` unless it resolves to `repo_uri`. The session records it, writes it to the module’s [manifest](../../root-module-manifest/) and sends it to the IaC sidecar as the [`Kumoss-Project` header](../iac/#project) on every command, apply included. First call only. |
| `session_id` | omit | On an iteration call, the session to continue. Only `q` (and `is_partial`) may accompany it; `root_module_path`, `project_identifier` and `manifest` are rejected. |
| `is_partial` | optional | `drift` and `import` only, and not gated on which call it is — a first call carrying `repo_uri` may set it. Defaults to `false`. When true, `q` must be non-empty: a blank query is rejected with `Partial drift detection requires a non-empty `q`.` (`Partial import requires a non-empty `q`.` for import). |

There is no provider or scope field. The session’s providers are the ones the root module’s `required_providers` declares, and their scopes come from the module’s [manifest](../../root-module-manifest/). The former `terraform_providers` and `scope_id` fields are gone; the request model ignores unknown fields, so a client that still sends them gets no error, and no effect either.

`apply` takes only `session_id`, which is required.

Failures on these three routes:

- `400` — the repository URI was rejected as unreachable or not allowed.
- `403` — the operation role is too low, the caller is not the owner of the session named by `session_id`, or, on an iteration call or `apply`, the authorization sidecar denied one of the session’s provider scopes.
- `404` — an iteration call referenced an unknown session, or the mapping sidecar cannot resolve a first call’s `project_identifier` (with the mapper’s own explanation).
- `409` — `apply` only, and only when the session’s plan is locked: `Session <id> is blocked; apply is not allowed.`
- `422` — the body failed the validation rules above, or a first call’s `project_identifier` does not resolve to its `repo_uri`. With `services.mapping` disabled the identifier resolves to itself, so any identifier other than `repo_uri` is `422`.
- `502`, `504` — the mapping sidecar failed or timed out while checking `project_identifier`, as for `POST /api/v1/repository/parse`.

A `202` is a promise that a round was scheduled, not that it succeeded. If the session is already running, or already finished, the background runner cannot take the session lock and exits without starting — the `202` has already been sent. Everything after the `202` is visible only on the event stream and in the session detail.

A first call is authorized after the `202`, inside the session: the providers and scopes to check are only known once the manifest has been read, so the session sets the manifest up, asks the authorization sidecar about every provider scope before saving anything, and then records the pairs on the session. A denial, or a module that still needs input the call did not carry, ends the session `FAILED` with `runner failed: <reason>` before any manifest, secret or commit is written. Iteration calls and `apply` are authorized synchronously from the recorded pairs. See [Authorization sidecar API](../authz/).

## Manifest

Prefix `/v1/manifest`. One route, requiring operation role `developer`.

`POST /api/v1/manifest/probe` tells a client what a root module needs before a session can run on it. The body is `{"repo_uri": "<uri>", "root_module_path": "<path>"}` (the path is optional and defaults to the repository root; the same URI and path rules as on `generate` apply). The core clones the repository’s default branch, inspects the module and compares it with its committed `kumoss.yaml`. It reads only, and never returns variable values.

```
{
  "status": "not_found",
  "needs_input": true,
  "missing_variables": [
    {"name": "db_password", "type": "string", "description": "",
     "required": true, "sensitive": true}
  ],
  "selectable_var_files": [
    {"path": "envs/dev.tfvars", "selected": false, "sets": ["region"]}
  ],
  "missing_var_files": [],
  "missing_scopes": [{"provider": "azurerm", "source": "hashicorp/azurerm"}],
  "provider_changes": []
}
```

`status` is `not_found` (no manifest yet), `up_to_date`, or `drifted` (the module changed since the manifest was written). When `needs_input` is true, the first `generate`, `drift` or `import` call must carry the answers in `manifest`; when it is false the session sets the manifest up on its own. A repository that is unreachable or a path that is not a directory in it is `400`, an unreadable configuration or manifest is `422`, and a failed clone is `502`. The whole model is in [Root module manifest](../../root-module-manifest/).

## Events

Prefix `/v1/events`. One route.

`GET /api/v1/events/subscribe/{session_id}` streams a session’s progress as Server-Sent Events. It requires a signed-in caller with read access to the session — the owner, or any user with a panel role.

The response is `text/event-stream` with `Cache-Control: no-cache`, `Connection: keep-alive`, and `X-Accel-Buffering: no`, the last of which stops the reverse proxy from buffering the stream. The first line is a `: keepalive` comment; every subsequent event is one JSON object:

```
data: {"status_msg": "GENERATING", "detail": {"message": "..."}}
```

`status_msg` is the session’s current status name. The message is sanitized by removing double quotes before it is embedded. The server polls the session’s status every five seconds and closes the stream when the status becomes `COMPLETED`, `UNCOMPLETED` (a rejected round), or `FAILED`, or when the configured iteration ceiling (`orchestration.max_session_events_iteration`) is reached. Reaching the ceiling closes the connection but preserves the session, so a client may reconnect.

Both the token and session access are checked once, at connect time. An unknown session is `404`; no read access is `403`.

The web application consumes this with `fetch` and a `ReadableStream` rather than `EventSource`, because `EventSource` cannot send an `Authorization` header. See [Follow a session](../../../guides/follow-a-session/).

## Repository operations

Prefix `/v1/repository`. Three routes, all requiring operation role `developer`.

`PUT /api/v1/repository/pr` creates a pull request from the session’s working branch. The body is `{"session_id": "<uuid>"}`. The caller must own the session. On success the answer is `201` with the pull request:

```
{"id": 42, "url": "https://.../pull/42", "status": "active"}
```

`PUT /api/v1/repository/pr/merge` merges the session’s **most recently opened** pull request into the default branch at the git provider. The body is the same `{"session_id": "<uuid>"}`. The caller must own the session. Success is `204` with no content. A locked session is `409 Session <id> is blocked; PR merge is not allowed.`, an unknown session or a session with no pull requests is `404`.

`POST /api/v1/repository/parse` resolves a repository through the [mapping sidecar](../mapping/), clones it, and returns the resolved clone URL with the Terraform root-module directories it found, as POSIX paths relative to the repository root. The body is `{"repo_uri": "<input>"}`, where the input is a full `https://` URI or an identifier the mapper accepts — with the bundled mapper, a bare repository name such as `my-iac`. This route takes no session, so there is no ownership check — the wizard calls it as soon as the repository is entered.

```
{
  "repo_url": "https://github.com/MySuperOrg/my-iac.git",
  "project_identifier": "my-iac",
  "roots": [".", "environments/dev", "environments/prod"]
}
```

`project_identifier` is the input, trimmed and echoed. Later calls (`manifest/probe`, `generate`, `drift`, `import`) must send the returned `repo_url` as `repo_uri`: they accept `https://` URIs only and do not resolve names. The session’s first call may also send `project_identifier` back, so the session and the module’s manifest record what the user named the repository; the wizard does. While `services.mapping` is disabled the input is used as is, so it must already be a URI.

An input the mapper cannot resolve is `404` with the mapper’s own explanation; a mapper that times out is `504`, and one that fails or answers off-contract is `502`. An empty input, or one that is (or resolves to) a URI that is not `https://` or embeds a password or token, is `422`. A repository `git ls-remote` cannot reach is `400`, and a failed clone or scan is `502`. The `400` and the clone `502` carry the fixed detail "Repository is not reachable or access was denied."; git’s own output is only logged. The detection rules behind the answer are in [Repository layout](../../repository-layout/).

## Authentication

Prefix `/v1/auth`. One route.

`GET /api/v1/auth/config` is **the only public route under `/v1`**, deliberately so: the single-page application has to read it before it can log in at all. Outside `/v1`, the framework’s interactive documentation — `/api/docs`, `/api/redoc`, and `/api/openapi.json` — is served without authentication as well. It returns the four non-secret OIDC settings, taken straight from `config.yaml`:

```
{
  "issuer_url": "",
  "client_id": "",
  "audience": "",
  "scope": "openid profile email",
  "artifact_metadata_header_prefix": "x-amz-meta-"
}
```

A blank `issuer_url` tells the browser that authentication is disabled and it should use the local development identity. See [Enable authentication](../../../guides/enable-authentication/).

`artifact_metadata_header_prefix` is not configurable. It is derived from `storage.provider` — `x-amz-meta-` for S3 and RustFS, `x-ms-meta-` for an Azure storage account — and is how the browser knows which header names carry an artifact’s metadata when it reads one from a pre-signed URL. The core never reads that metadata itself, so this is the only way the client can learn it. See [Networking and TLS](../../../guides/production/networking-and-tls/) for the CORS rules that must expose those headers.

The authorization sidecar is not reached through a route of its own: the core consults it from the IaC routes, once per provider scope of the session’s root module. See [Authorization sidecar API](../authz/).

## Users

Prefix `/v1/users`. One route.

`GET /api/v1/users/me` returns the authenticated caller’s identity and roles, and is what the browser calls to learn what to render:

```
{
  "id": 1,
  "email": "dev@kumoss.local",
  "display_name": "Local Developer",
  "operation_role": "devops",
  "panel_role": "admin"
}
```

`id` is the database primary key, not the token subject. `email` and `display_name` may be null. `panel_role` is null for a user with no admin-panel access.

## Sessions

Prefix `/v1/sessions`. Two routes, both open to any signed-in user.

`GET /api/v1/sessions/list` returns a page of session summaries. The list is **always** scoped to the caller’s own sessions — there is no parameter that widens it.

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `page` | `1` | One-based page number, minimum 1. |
| `page_size` | `20` | Items per page, 1 to 100. |
| `operation` | none | Filter by operation type. |
| `status` | none | Filter by the session’s **most recent** status. |
| `search` | none | Partial match on the first query, the workspace URI, or the session id. Up to 200 characters. |

The envelope carries `items`, `total`, `page`, `page_size`, and `total_pages`. Each item resolves server-side everything the list view renders: `uuid`, `username`, `operation`, `providers`, `first_query`, `workspace` (URI, branch, root path), `current_status`, the `in_flight` and `is_blocked` flags, and the timestamps. `username` is the owning user’s e-mail, or `user-<id>` when the user has none; the name is historical, and it is a response field only — there is no `username` query parameter. `providers` lists the Terraform providers of the session’s root module as `[{"name": "azurerm", "scope_id": "<subscription id>"}]`, with a null `scope_id` for providers that have no scope; it is empty until the session’s first call has set the manifest up. It replaces the former `provider` and `scope_id` fields.

`GET /api/v1/sessions?id={session_id}` returns the full session aggregate: the summary fields and one entry in `rounds` per generation round. Each round carries its own statuses, its `reports`, `compliance_checks`, `plans`, and `code_changes` artifacts as client-fetchable URLs, oldest first, and its `pull_requests`. Each `compliance_checks` entry also carries the check’s `passed` verdict; the list is empty when the round was not checked.

Pass `include_chat_history=true` to also populate `chat_history` with the session’s conversation: one `{"user": …, "assistant": …}` turn per finished round, oldest first. The `user` side is the query as the caller typed it; the `assistant` side states how that round turned out and what the caller can do next. A round whose reply could not be produced contributes no turn, so the list can be shorter than `rounds`. That variant always reads fresh from the database, so status polling should stay on the default. The caller must be the owner or hold a panel role; an unknown session is `404`.

This route never returns the internal conversation the backend feeds to the LLM. That record is admin-only — see below.

## Admin

Prefix `/v1/admin`. Five routes. The whole router requires a panel role, so `viewer` is the floor for every route in it; three routes raise the floor further.

| Route | Panel role | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/v1/admin/sessions/list` | `viewer` | A page of session summaries across all users. |
| `GET /api/v1/admin/sessions?id={session_id}` | `viewer` | Any session’s full aggregate. |
| `PATCH /api/v1/admin/sessions/{session_id}/toggle_lock` | `editor` | The session’s new lock state. |
| `GET /api/v1/admin/users` | `admin` | A page of users with their roles. |
| `PUT /api/v1/admin/users/{user_id}/roles` | `admin` | The updated user. |

`GET /api/v1/admin/sessions/list` takes the same `page`, `page_size`, `operation`, `status`, and `search` parameters as the caller-scoped list, plus `user_email`, which partial-matches the owning user’s e-mail and accepts up to 254 characters. The response envelope is identical.

`GET /api/v1/admin/sessions?id={session_id}` is the unrestricted counterpart of the session detail route: same response and the same `include_chat_history` parameter, but no ownership check beyond the panel role. An unknown session is `404`.

It adds one parameter of its own. `include_history=true` populates `history` with the internal conversation the backend feeds to the LLM. That record carries no contract: its shape follows whatever the prompting strategy needs, and it may contain raw tool output, validation notes, and status text. Treat it as debugging material, never as the caller’s conversation. Either history parameter reads fresh from the database.

`PATCH /api/v1/admin/sessions/{session_id}/toggle_lock` takes `{"locked": true}` or `{"locked": false}` and answers with the resulting state. `true` blocks both apply and pull-request merge on that session; `false` releases them. An unknown session is `404`.

```
{"uuid": "917d0485-a0a2-4c34-8f33-a89d28aba9b0", "is_blocked": true}
```

`GET /api/v1/admin/users` takes `page`, `page_size`, and a `search` that partial-matches e-mail or display name, up to 254 characters. Each item extends the `/users/me` shape with the `issuer`, the `subject`, and `created_at`.

`PUT /api/v1/admin/users/{user_id}/roles` is a **full-state** assignment, not a patch: the body is `{"operation_role": "devops", "panel_role": "editor"}` and whatever it omits is cleared. `panel_role` is optional and setting it to null removes all admin-panel access. `user_id` is the database primary key. An unknown user is `404`. One case is refused outright: a panel admin removing their own `admin` role is `409 A panel admin cannot remove their own admin role.`

Note what is **not** here. There is no route to delete a user or a session, and a panel role never grants the right to act on another user’s session — continuing it, opening or merging its pull request, and applying it all remain owner-only.

## Notifications

Prefix `/v1/notifications`. One route, open to any signed-in user.

`POST /api/v1/notifications` submits a user-originated notification — today, the support request typed into the web application’s header — and the core relays it to the notifications sidecar. The body mirrors the sidecar contract’s `NotificationRequest` with one deliberate difference: it has **no** `audience` field. The core derives the audience server-side from the caller and the users store, so the browser cannot choose recipients. Unknown fields are rejected.

| Field | Required | Constraint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kind` | yes | Event category, dotted lowercase, for example `support.user_question`. 1 to 128 characters. |
| `severity` | yes | One of `info`, `warning`, `error`, `critical`. |
| `subject` | yes | 1 to 256 characters. |
| `body` | yes | 1 to 16384 characters. |
| `links` | no | Up to 32 objects, each `{"label": …​, "url": …​}` with a label of 1 to 128 characters and an absolute HTTP URL of up to 2048 characters. |
| `context` | no | Free-form object. |

Success is `202` with the sidecar’s delivery id:

```
{"delivery_id": "3f2504e0-4f89-11d3-9a0c-0305e82c3301"}
```

Unlike the pipeline’s own best-effort notifications, this route tells the caller when nothing was delivered: `502 Notification was not delivered.` if the sidecar did not accept it, and `503 Notifications are disabled.` if the sidecar is switched off in the configuration.

- [HTTP APIs](../) for the sidecar contracts the core calls.
- [Make a request](../../../guides/make-a-request/) for the same flow from the web application.

# Upgrade notes

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/prerelease/main/guides/upgrade-notes/

This page lists the changes that need action from an operator, an integrator or a custom sidecar implementation when upgrading. Read it before rolling out a new core image.

## Intent check replaces the LLM compliance audit

The LLM half of the compliance check is now the **intent check**: it judges only whether the plan does what the session’s requests ask (`scope_exceeded`, `scope_incomplete`, same ids and severities). It no longer receives or audits the conventions — the Terraform guidelines, the providers' `resource_creation`, `networking` and `permissions` guidelines, and the resource prompts. Those still guide generation, but after generation only the compliance policies enforce rules. The `orchestration.enable_compliance_checker` switch is unchanged and still gates both halves; see [How compliance works](../../architecture/compliance/). What changes:

- **Prompt moved.** The rules prompt is now `general/intent/rules`, seeded on the next boot from `core/prompts/seed/general/intent/rules.yaml`. `general/compliance/report` is no longer read and can be deleted from Langfuse; `general/compliance/impact` is unchanged. If you customized `general/compliance/report`, port your changes to a new version of `general/intent/rules` and move the environment label to it; see [Change a prompt](../customize-prompts/#change-a-prompt). Rules about conventions rather than intent belong in a [compliance policy](../../reference/compliance-policy/) now.
- **Tool and trace names.** The agent’s sentinel tool is `report_intent_findings` (was `report_compliance_findings`), without a `passed` argument: the verdict is computed from the severities. Its Langfuse observation is `Chain - INTENT_CHECKER` (was `Chain - COMPLIANCE_CHECKER`).
- **Finding source.** Findings of the intent check carry `source: "intent"` (was `"llm"`). Stored reports keep loading: `"llm"` is read as `"intent"`. The web UI marks them with an **intent** badge, next to the **policy** badge of policy findings.
- **New warning.** The general policy gains `provider_version_pin`, a `warn` for every root module provider with no version constraint or one not of the form `~> X.Y`, such as an exact pin. It never locks a session, but workspaces with missing or exact provider pins start reporting it. A general policy you customized does not get it; see [The shipped rules](../../reference/compliance-policy/#shipped-rules).

## Project identifier; IaC contract 2.1.0

A repository can be named by a **project identifier**, such as `sistemas-kumoss-rsg-esc1-dev`, that the mapping sidecar resolves to its URL. A session now keeps that name and sends it to the IaC sidecar, so an IaC service implementation can pick the credentials a command runs with by it. Nothing is required of an operator; what changes:

- **Database.** Migration `0003` adds the nullable `workspaces.project_identifier` column. The core applies it at startup, like the others; existing sessions get null. See [Database schema](../../reference/database-schema/).
- **Core API.** `POST /api/v1/repository/parse` also answers `project_identifier`, the input echoed. The first `generate`, `drift` or `import` call may send it back as `project_identifier`, as the web application does; the core then checks through the mapping sidecar that it resolves to `repo_uri` and answers `422` otherwise, before any session is created. It is optional: clients that do not send it behave as before. See [Core API](../../reference/api/core/#infrastructure-as-code).
- **Manifest.** `kumoss.yaml` gains an optional top-level `project_identifier`, written only when the session has one. It never makes the manifest drift, but a first call saves the manifest when only the identifier changed. The layout version stays `"1"`; earlier cores ignore the key when reading and drop it when they save. See [Root module manifest](../../reference/root-module-manifest/#project-identifier).
- **IaC contract 2.1.0 (additive).** Every IaC call of such a session carries the optional `Kumoss-Project` header. An implementation may ignore it, as the bundled one does, so 2.0.0 implementations keep working unchanged. See [IaC sidecar API](../../reference/api/iac/#project).
- **Session cache.** The cached session context moved to a new key version; entries in the old shape are rebuilt from the database on first use. Nothing to flush.

## Compliance policy with OPA; `forbidden_actions` removed

With `orchestration.enable_compliance_checker` on, generate rounds now also evaluate Rego policies with OPA against the final plan, before the LLM audit, and all results go into one compliance report. The policies are the Langfuse text prompts `general/policies/compliance`, evaluated on every round, and `<provider>/policies/compliance`, evaluated when the root module declares that provider (skipped for a provider without one), all seeded on the next boot. See [Compliance policy](../../reference/compliance-policy/).

What that changes:

- **`forbidden_actions` is gone.** The six `<provider>/guidelines/forbidden_actions` seeds are deleted and no agent reads that prompt any more: not the request filter, not the IaC generator, not the compliance checker. The request filter no longer declines requests as prohibited. Versions already in Langfuse (including those the Phoenix migration script imported) stay there, unused; the seeder never deletes. **This removes guardrails**: an install that relied on those lists and writes no policy has no replacement for them beyond the shipped policies. Those deny standalone deletions, removed customer-managed keys and command execution (general policy) and, per provider, three of the most critical prohibitions the lists held that can be decided from the plan alone, such as security groups open to the internet or `cluster-admin` bound to a ServiceAccount. Rules that allowed an exception on an explicit user request were not translated. Write the other prohibitions you need as Rego rules in `<provider>/policies/compliance` or `general/policies/compliance`.
- **`critical_deletion` moved to the policy.** The seed of `general/compliance/report` no longer defines it; the policy does, deterministically. If you customized that prompt, your version keeps its `critical_deletion` section and standalone deletions are reported twice, once by each source. Delete the section from your version.
- **Three more general rules.** The general policy also denies `customer_managed_key_removed` (a resource the plan updates or replaces losing its customer-managed encryption key) and `command_execution` (a `null_resource` or a provisioner on a resource the plan creates or updates, or any `data "external"` in the configuration, repository code included), and warns with `unprotected_credential_output` (a root module output named like a credential and not marked `sensitive = true`). A round that updates a repository resource carrying a provisioner, or whose configuration holds a `data "external"`, is now locked. The OCI policy’s `oci_public_ingress` now also checks `oci_core_default_security_list`. See [Compliance policy](../../reference/compliance-policy/).
- **Bans removed from the prompts.** What a policy enforces is no longer restated in the guideline and resource prompts, which feed both the IaC generator and the LLM audit. The seeds lost the "No arbitrary command execution" section of `general/guidelines/terraform`, the "guest configuration only through user data or cloud-init" bullets of the compute resource prompts and `vsphere/guidelines/resource_creation`, the bans on internet-open ingress (security groups, NSGs, firewalls, OCI security lists, the OCI default security list, bastions), on basic roles and service account keys (`google`), `cluster-admin` (`kubernetes`), `Allow any-user` (`oci`) and Owner and similar assignments (`azurerm`), the `vsphere` provider-block and TLS bullets, and the deletion safeguards bullet of `oci/guidelines/resource_creation`. Bullets were removed whole, so the generator is no longer told to avoid these patterns: a round that generates one is locked by the policy instead of being written correctly. The parts of those bullets no policy checks (no secrets in user data, Owner or User Access Administrator at narrower scopes, the alternatives to service account keys, locking down the OCI default security list, OCI delete-protection defaults…​) are now checked by nothing; restore them in your own prompts if you need them. Prompts you customized keep your text, bans included. See [Customize prompts](../customize-prompts/#compliance-policy).
- **The core image ships `opa`** (OPA 1.22.4). A custom core image must provide it on the `PATH`.
- **Startup check.** With the checker on, the core evaluates the general policy and the policy of every provider that ships a seed (`aws`, `azurerm`, `google`, `kubernetes`, `oci`, `vsphere`) against an empty plan after seeding, and refuses to start if that fails: no `opa` binary, a broken policy, or Langfuse unreachable. A provider policy missing from Langfuse is skipped.
- **Fail closed.** A policy that cannot be evaluated during a round adds a blocking `policy_unavailable` finding, so the session is locked and the compliance failure notification is sent.
- **Compliance reports.** Each violation has `source` (`llm` or `opa`; absent on older reports, meaning `llm`) and the report has `policy_revisions`, the Langfuse prompt versions of the policies that ran, each as `"<prompt name>@<version>"`, the general policy first, for example `["general/policies/compliance@3", "aws/policies/compliance@1"]` (empty when no policy ran). It replaces the single `policy_revision` string of earlier builds; reports stored with `policy_revision` are still read, into the list. Consumers of the report JSON must read the new field.

## Langfuse replaces Phoenix

Traces and prompts moved from Arize Phoenix to a self-hosted Langfuse v4. See [Monitor with Langfuse](../monitor-with-langfuse/) and [Customize prompts](../customize-prompts/).

What changes:

**Stack.** `phoenix` and `phoenix-db` are gone. Langfuse brings `langfuse-web`, `langfuse-worker`, `langfuse-db` (PostgreSQL), `langfuse-clickhouse`, `langfuse-redis` and a `langfuse` bucket on the object storage. Plan for the extra memory, mostly ClickHouse’s.

**UI address.** Langfuse is served on its own port, `3000` (`http://localhost:3000` in Compose), not under `/monitoring/`: the stock image cannot be served under a path. It has a login: the stack provisions `admin@example.com` / `kumoss-admin-1` (Compose) or a generated password (Helm, see [Deploy with Helm](../deploy-with-helm/)). The admin panel’s link now reads **Langfuse**; it goes to `/langfuse` on the proxy, which redirects to the UI.

**Configuration.** `telemetry.collector_url` is replaced by `telemetry.langfuse_url`, and the core authenticates with a project key pair from `LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY` / `LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY`. A `config.yaml` still carrying `collector_url` is refused at boot. See [the `telemetry` section](../../reference/configuration/#telemetry).

**Projects.** The nine Phoenix projects (`dev-terraform-day2`, `pro-terraform-drift`, …​) become one Langfuse project. The environment is Langfuse’s environment field, and the operation and providers are trace tags.

**Prompt tags are labels.** The seeder labels versions instead of tagging them, with the same names (`development`, `staging`, `production`, `seed`).

**Prompt names are folders.** `aws-guidelines-networking` is now `aws/guidelines/networking`, which Langfuse shows as an `aws` folder holding a `guidelines` one. The migration script below renames your prompts accordingly.

**Helm.** phoenix. and `postgres.phoenix` are replaced by `langfuse.`
and `postgres.langfuse`; `secrets.phoenixDbPassword` by the
`secrets.langfuse*` values. A Secret given as `secrets.existingSecret`
must hold the new keys (see the Helm guide). The proxy gets a
`langfuse` port (3000) and the Ingress an optional
`ingress.langfuseHost`. `charts/kind-up.sh` maps Langfuse to host
port 3000; delete and recreate an existing kind cluster to get the
mapping.

**Local Compose overrides.** A `docker-compose.override.yml` that still configures `phoenix` or `phoenix-db` makes Compose refuse the project; remove those entries.

### Moving your prompts

Traces are not migrated: Phoenix keeps them until you delete its volume. Prompts are moved with `core/scripts/migrate_phoenix_prompts.py`, which needs only Python 3.10 or later and runs in two steps, so the two stacks never have to run together:

1. **Before upgrading**, with Phoenix still running, export every prompt version and its tags: ``` python3 core/scripts/migrate_phoenix_prompts.py export \ --phoenix-url http://localhost/monitoring/ --out phoenix-prompts.json ```
2. Upgrade, and start Langfuse alone (in Compose, `docker compose up -d langfuse-web langfuse-worker`; starting the whole stack is fine too).
3. Import the file. The key pair is the one the core uses (`pk-lf-kumoss-dev` / `sk-lf-kumoss-dev` in the Compose stack): ``` LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY=pk-lf-kumoss-dev LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY=sk-lf-kumoss-dev \ python3 core/scripts/migrate_phoenix_prompts.py import \ --langfuse-url http://localhost:3000/ --in phoenix-prompts.json ``` Each Phoenix version becomes a Langfuse version, oldest first, carrying its tags as labels, so every label ends up on the version its tag was on. A prompt with no `seed` tag (Phoenix installs older than that tag) gets `seed` on its oldest version, the one the seeder created, so the next core start never moves labels off your own versions. Versions that are not a single text are listed and skipped: the core cannot read them. `--dry-run` shows what would be created; running the import again skips what it already imported.
4. Start (or restart) the core. The seeder finds the `seed` label where Phoenix had the `seed` tag and carries on as before: a seed changed since reaches only the environments still on the seed.

If the core started before the import, it seeded the shipped prompts first; the import then adds your versions on top and moves the labels to them, and the next core start brings the seeds up to date as above.

When the prompts are in Langfuse, remove the old Phoenix volume (`docker volume rm kumoss_phoenix_db_data` for a Compose project named `kumoss`; with Helm, the PersistentVolumeClaim `data-<fullname>-phoenix-db-0`, `data-kumoss-phoenix-db-0` for a release named `kumoss`).

## Database migrations with Alembic

The core no longer builds its tables with `create_all`. It runs Alembic migrations at startup instead, in one transaction and under a PostgreSQL advisory lock.

- **Existing databases.** The first start adopts them: it applies the provider rename below if still pending, records the baseline revision in a new `alembic_version` table, and runs the later revisions. The first of those adds `histories.user_queries`. Nothing to do by hand, but back the database up first.
- **Pre-authentication volumes.** A database with sessions but no `users` table is refused at startup; migrate it by hand or recreate it.
- **Schema changes in forks.** Change the models and add a revision; see [Changing the schema](../../reference/database-schema/#changing-the-schema).

## Providers come from the root module

Sessions no longer take a provider and a scope from the user. The core reads the providers from the root module’s `required_providers` and keeps the scopes, variable answers and picked var files in a `kumoss.yaml` manifest committed in the module. See [Root module manifest](../../reference/root-module-manifest/).

What that changes:

- **Web application.** The wizard asks for the request, the repository URL and the root module, then shows an inputs form only when the module needs something. The provider and scope questions, the permissions step and the call to the mapping service are gone.
- **First session on each module.** The first session after the upgrade sets the module’s manifest up: the user answers its scopes (and any required variable without a value) once, and the session commits `kumoss.yaml` to its branch. Merge that pull request so later sessions find the manifest on the default branch.
- **Core API.** `generate`, `drift` and `import` no longer take `terraform_providers` or `scope_id`. Unknown fields are ignored, so an old client is not rejected, but what it sends has no effect. Probe the module with `POST /api/v1/manifest/probe` and send the answers in `manifest` on the first call. See [Core API](../../reference/api/core/).
- **Session read models.** Session summaries and details expose `providers: [{name, scope_id}]` instead of `provider` and `scope_id`.
- **Tracing.** The span `metadata` carries `providers` (a list of provider type names) instead of `cloud`.

## Provider names are Terraform provider types

Providers are named everywhere by their Terraform provider type, the last segment of the source address:

| Before | Now |
| --- | --- |
| `azure` | `azurerm` |
| `gcp` | `google` |
| `aws` | `aws` |
| `oci` | `oci` |
| `kubernetes` | `kubernetes` |
| `vmware` | `vsphere` |

Any other provider a module uses (`random`, `helm`…​) is a session provider too, under its own type name.

**Database.** The `terraform_providers` table is migrated at startup: the `provider` column becomes `varchar(64)` with the new names, `scope_id` becomes nullable, and the old enum type is dropped. Nothing to do by hand. See [Database schema](../../reference/database-schema/).

**Prompts.** Phoenix prompt names follow the provider type:
azure-guidelines- is now `azurerm-guidelines-`, gcp- is
`google-` and vmware- is `vsphere-`, and the seed folders under
`core/prompts/seed/` were renamed to match. The seeder creates the new
names on the next boot, with the shipped content. Versions you
curated under the old names are not moved and no longer read: copy
them to the new names in Phoenix and move the environment tag. See
[Customize prompts](../customize-prompts/).

**Prompt selection.** A session uses the prompts of every provider of its module that has them. A provider without prompts no longer aborts a session with `Prompt not found`; it gets the `general-*` prompts only.

## Sidecar contracts 2.0.0

The IaC, authorization and mapping contracts moved to 2.0.0 together. A custom implementation of any of them must be upgraded with the core.

| Contract | Breaking change |
| --- | --- |
| IaC (`iac.v1.yaml`) | The request is a plain CLI invocation. `init`, `plan`, `apply` and `import` drop the required `scope_id` + `terraform_provider` pair, and `plan` and `import` drop `variables`. Every engine command takes an optional `env` (environment variables it may add but never replace), and `plan` and `import` an optional `vars` (input variable values, passed as the last `-var-file`); `var_files` stays, with any path shape inside the workspace. The service knows no provider: the core sends each scope as `env` or `vars`, so a deployment must leave `ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID` and `GOOGLE_PROJECT` unset on the service. The bundled service no longer checks the AWS account with STS before each command: existing AWS modules that do not pass `var.aws_account_id` to the provider’s `allowed_account_ids` run in whatever account the service’s credentials belong to. `/v1/import/scope-resource-ids` takes `provider` (`azurerm`, `google` or `aws`) instead of `terraform_provider`, and rejects any other provider with `422` instead of answering exit code `2`. See [IaC sidecar API](../../reference/api/iac/#versioning). |
| Authorization (`authz.v1.yaml`) | `resource.properties.provider` is any Terraform provider type name instead of an enum of the former names. The core sends one evaluation per provider scope of the session’s root module, or one module-level evaluation with an empty `resource.id` and no provider when the module has no scoped provider. First calls are evaluated inside the session, after the `202`. Update PDP policies that match `azure`, `gcp` or `vmware`. See [Authorization sidecar API](../../reference/api/authz/). |
| Mapping (`mapping.v1.yaml`) | The request takes `identifier` only and the response answers `repo_url` and `identifier` only: `terraform_provider`, `scope_id` and the `TerraformProvider` enum are gone, and a request that still sends `terraform_provider` is `422`. The core’s `POST /api/v1/mapping/resolve` passthrough was removed; the core now calls the service from `POST /api/v1/repository/parse` instead (see below). A `404’s `detail` is shown to the user. See [Mapping sidecar API](../../reference/api/mapping/). |

## The mapping sidecar is bundled and on by default

The wizard’s repository step now resolves what the user types through the mapping sidecar, so a bare repository name works as well as a URL. Kumoss bundles a mapping service (`services/mapping`, image `kumoss-mapping`) that appends a name to `MAPPING_PREFIX_IDENTIFIER` with a `.git` suffix, and the shipped `config.yaml` enables it (`services.mapping.enabled: true`, `endpoint: "http://mapping:8081"`).

What that changes:

- **Core boot.** With mapping enabled, the core refuses to boot without `KUMOSS_MAPPING_TOKEN`. Add it to `core/.env` (and the same value to `services/mapping/.env`), or set `services.mapping.enabled: false`. The Helm chart generates the token itself; a `secrets.existingSecret` must now also hold `KUMOSS_MAPPING_TOKEN`.
- **Compose.** Copy `services/mapping/env.sample` to `services/mapping/.env` and set `MAPPING_PREFIX_IDENTIFIER` to your organization’s base URL (e.g. `https://github.com/my-org/`). Left empty, only full `https://` URLs resolve, as before.
- **Your own mapping implementation.** Keep your `services.mapping.endpoint` and remove the bundled `mapping` service from your deployment (Helm: `mapping.enabled: false` disables both; set `config.services.mapping` back on with your endpoint).
- **Core API.** `POST /api/v1/repository/parse` accepts a repository name as `repo_uri` and answers `repo_url` next to `roots`; send that `repo_url` on later calls. It can now also answer `404` (name not resolvable) and `504` (mapper timeout). See [Core API](../../reference/api/core/).

## Kumoss-managed state keys changed

With [Kumoss-managed state](../state-backends/kumoss-managed/) the state key is now the SHA-256 of the repository and the root module path only; earlier releases also hashed the cloud scope. **State written under the old keys is not migrated.** Left as is, the first session on each project plans against empty state and proposes creating resources that already exist.

Before running sessions on an existing project, copy its state object in the state bucket from `<old_state_id>/terraform.tfstate` to `<state_id>/terraform.tfstate`. The old key appears in the `Terraform state: …​ key=` log lines of the previous release; the new one in the same line the upgraded core logs on the project’s first `init`. Do not apply a plan made before the copy. See [State keys](../state-backends/kumoss-managed/#state-keys).

Projects whose repository declares its own backend, or whose backend comes from the IaC sidecar, are not affected.

# Authorization sidecar API

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/prerelease/main/reference/api/authz/

The authorization service answers **may this user perform this action on this scope?** — asked before every IaC generation, drift detection, import, apply, PR creation, and PR merge.

Contract: `contracts/openapi/authz.v1.yaml` (version 2.0.0), implementing the OpenID AuthZEN 1.0 Access Evaluation API (§5). Kumoss bundles no PDP implementation: authorization is an optional extension point you deploy yourself and point `services.authz.endpoint` at. Bearer token: the value of the variable named by `services.authz.token_env`, `KUMOSS_AUTHZ_TOKEN` by default. The service is **optional** and ships disabled (`services.authz.enabled: false`, `endpoint: ""`).

> **Important**
> **Kumoss’s own roles do not live here.** The operation roles (`developer` < `devops`) and panel roles (`viewer` < `editor` < `admin`) that decide what a signed-in user can do are rows in the core database, managed from the admin panel. The AuthZEN PDP is an **organizational** gate — it lets you enforce policies like "only the platform team may generate infrastructure in the production subscription." See [Roles and permissions](../../roles-and-permissions/).

## Endpoints

The contract exposes two endpoints:

| Endpoint | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /access/v1/evaluation` | Evaluates whether a subject is permitted to perform an action on a resource, per AuthZEN §5. **Called on every write route.** |
| `GET /healthz` | Liveness probe, answers `\\{"status":"ok"}`. |

## Enforcement

The core calls the PDP on every route that mutates infrastructure or repository state. The `action.name` value maps to the operation:

| Core route | action.name | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /v1/iac/generate` | `generate` | First call and iterations |
| `POST /v1/iac/drift` | `drift` | First call and iterations |
| `POST /v1/iac/import` | `import` | First call and iterations |
| `POST /v1/iac/apply` | `apply` | Apply trigger |

### One evaluation per provider scope

A session’s root module may use several providers, so the core asks the PDP once per provider **scope** of the module, and every evaluation must allow:

- For each provider with a scope — `azurerm` (subscription), `google` (project), `aws` (account), `oci` (compartment) — one request with `resource.id` set to that scope and `properties.provider` set to the provider’s Terraform type name.
- A module with no scoped provider (only `kubernetes`, `vsphere`, `random`…​) gets a single module-level request instead, with an empty `resource.id` and no `properties.provider`; `repo_uri` and `root_module_path` still identify the module.

The pairs come from the module’s [manifest](../../root-module-manifest/), so **when** the check runs differs by call:

- **First call** (`generate`, `drift`, `import` with `repo_uri`) — the route answers `202` first, and the session evaluates the pairs right after it has resolved the manifest and before it saves anything (manifest, secrets, commit). A denial ends the session `FAILED` with the PDP’s reason, rather than a synchronous `403`.
- **Iteration calls and `apply`** — evaluated synchronously on the route, from the pairs recorded on the session at its first call; a denial is a `403`.

> **Note**
> PR routes (`PUT /repository/pr` and `PUT /repository/pr/merge`) are
> governed by Kumoss’s own operation roles, not by the authz PDP. See
> [Roles and permissions](../../roles-and-permissions/).

When `services.authz.enabled` is `false` (the default), the core does not call out at all and treats every operation as authorized. When enabled, the core **never** fails open:

| Situation | What the core answers |
| --- | --- |
| PDP unreachable, or the call times out | `504` (gateway timeout) |
| PDP returns a network-level error | `502` (bad gateway) |
| PDP returns `decision: false` | `403` with the PDP’s `reason_user` context (on a first call, the session ends `FAILED` with it instead) |
| PDP returns `decision: true` | The request proceeds |

## POST /access/v1/evaluation

### Request

```
{
  "subject": {
    "type": "user",
    "id": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/.../v2.0",
    "properties": {
      "issuer": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/.../v2.0",
      "email": "someone@example.com",
      "groups": ["platform-team", "devops"]
    }
  },
  "action": {
    "name": "generate"
  },
  "resource": {
    "type": "scope",
    "id": "my-subscription-id",
    "properties": {
      "provider": "azurerm",
      "repo_uri": "https://dev.azure.com/org/project/_git/infra",
      "root_module_path": "environments/dev"
    }
  }
}
```

#### Subject

| Field | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | Yes | Always `user`. |
| `id` | Yes | The OIDC `iss` (issuer) claim from the user’s token. |
| `properties.issuer` | No | The OIDC `iss` claim (universal default). |
| `properties.email` | No | Present only when the token’s `email_verified` is true (universal default). |
| `properties.*` | No | Any additional claims configured via `oidc.claims` in `config.yaml`. For example, `groups`, `identifier`, `tenant_id`. See [OIDC configuration](../../configuration/#config-oidc). |

#### Action

| Field | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | Yes | One of: `generate`, `drift`, `import`, `apply`, `pr.create`, `pr.merge`. The core currently sends the first four; a PDP must still accept the `pr.*` names. |
| `properties` | No | Free-form object; the core does not send it. |

#### Resource

| Field | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | Yes | Always `scope`. |
| `id` | Yes | The scope identifier (subscription, project, account, compartment). Empty in the module-level evaluation of a module with no scoped provider. |
| `properties.provider` | No | Terraform provider type name the scope belongs to (`azurerm`, `google`, `aws`, `oci`); any string matching `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,63}$` is valid on the contract. Omitted in the module-level evaluation. Contract 2.0.0 changed this from an enum of the core’s former names (`azure`, `gcp`, `aws`, `oci`, `kubernetes`, `vmware`), so a PDP policy matching those values must be updated. |
| `properties.repo_uri` | No | The git repository URL. |
| `properties.root_module_path` | No | The root module path within the repository. Omitted when empty. |

`additionalProperties` is `false` on the request envelope, subject, action, and resource objects. It is `true` on all `properties` objects, so PDPs may read custom fields.

### Response

```
{
  "decision": true,
  "context": {
    "reason_user": {
      "en": "Authorized by platform policy."
    },
    "reason_admin": {
      "en": "Policy platform-team-azure matched."
    }
  }
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `decision` | Required boolean. `true` to allow, `false` to deny. |
| `context.reason_user` | Optional. Human-readable explanation shown to the end user on denial. |
| `context.reason_admin` | Optional. Detailed explanation logged at WARNING for operators. |

A denial is still `200`: the decision was computed, and it was "no." The error statuses are for cases where no decision could be reached.

### Error responses

Error bodies use `application/problem+json` per RFC 9457.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `200` | A decision was computed, granted or denied. |
| `400` | Malformed request (bad JSON, non-UTF-8). |
| `401` | Missing or invalid bearer token. Carries a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` challenge. |
| `422` | Well-formed JSON that failed schema validation. |
| `502` | Downstream backend error inside the PDP. |

## Stub PDP

A minimal always-allow (or always-deny) stub is included for testing the conformance suite and local development:

```
cd contracts/conformance/authz
uv sync
STUB_DECISION=true uv run uvicorn stub:app --port 8083
```

Set `STUB_TOKEN=mysecret` to require bearer auth on the stub. Set `STUB_DECISION=false` to make it deny everything.

## Conformance

The implementation-agnostic Schemathesis suite at `contracts/conformance/authz/` runs against any implementation of this contract:

```
cd contracts/conformance/authz
uv sync
uv run pytest \
  --service-url=https://authz.your.example \
  --service-token=$YOUR_TOKEN
```

`--service-token` is needed only if the implementation enforces authentication.

The suite checks schema conformance of the responses — that valid requests produce documented status codes with documented shapes. It cannot check that the decisions are **correct**: a PDP that grants everything passes it. Correctness of the policy is your own test suite’s job.

- [Roles and permissions](../../roles-and-permissions/) for the roles that gate Kumoss itself.
- [the `services` section](../../configuration/#config-services) of the configuration reference for enabling the sidecar and configuring `oidc.claims`.
