## Continuous operations

Keep the infrastructure and its code in agreement without anyone having to check by hand.

### Scheduled drift detection and import

Drift detection and import will run on a recurring schedule through a managed queue, in addition to running on demand from a session. Teams will learn that live infrastructure has diverged from its code, or that unmanaged resources have appeared, as soon as the next run completes.

Today both operations run on demand; see [Remediate drift](../guides/remediate-drift/) and [Import infrastructure](../guides/import-infrastructure/).

## Cloud and code lifecycle

Cover the whole path between running infrastructure and the code that describes it, in both directions.

### From cloud to code

Kumoss will bring existing cloud infrastructure under management from scratch: it will discover the resources in a scope, generate the compliant Infrastructure as Code that describes them, and create the repository that holds it. Infrastructure built outside code will get a governed, version-controlled starting point in one step.

### From code to cloud

Starting from an application repository, Kumoss will analyze the application to identify the infrastructure it needs, then generate that infrastructure together with its state configuration. An application and the platform it runs on will move to a running deployment along one reviewed path.

### Infrastructure diagrams and change previews

Kumoss will render a diagram of the infrastructure a project manages and highlight how a request changes it before the change is merged. Reviewers will see the impact of a plan visually, alongside the code diff.

## Operations at scale

Let platform teams act on many resources and many projects with a single request, instead of repeating the same request one project at a time.

### Bulk operations

Any request will be able to run against all projects or a selection of them, instead of one project at a time. A platform team will be able to ask, for example, to update the tags of all storage accounts, or to apply a new security baseline, and Kumoss will run the request in every targeted project. Each project goes through the usual generation, validation, and reporting phases, and the outcome reaches reviewers as one pull request per project with a summary of what changes where, so the team can approve, adjust, or reject the change project by project.

### Multiproject requests

A single request will be able to target several projects at once. A team will be able to ask, for example, to add a new database to a list of projects, and Kumoss will run the generation, validation, and reporting phases for each project, tailoring the code to the conventions and compliance policies of each one. Progress and results will be tracked per project, so a failure in one project does not block the others.

Today a session works on a single project; see [Follow a session](../guides/follow-a-session/).

## Quality and governance

Make the quality of generated code and the reliability of every compliance verdict measurable, verifiable, and enforceable.

### Evaluation harness and automated testing

An evaluation harness will score generated code, plan outcomes, and the accuracy of compliance verdicts against a versioned set of reference scenarios for each operation and cloud. Together with automated tests that run on every change, it will catch regressions in prompts, orchestration, and services before they reach a release.

### Model benchmarking

Kumoss will publish benchmark results showing how supported language models perform on its own tasks, measuring the quality of generated code, compliance accuracy, cost, and latency. Operators will choose the models in their configuration based on evidence; see [LLM providers and models](../reference/llm-providers/) for the models Kumoss supports today.

### Policy as code with Open Policy Agent

Kumoss evaluates the final plan of every generate round against a deterministic policy written in Rego with [Open Policy Agent](https://www.openpolicyagent.org), alongside the language-model intent check. The policies are stored in Langfuse: a general one, which ships with three deny rules (standalone deletions, removed customer-managed keys, command execution) and two warnings (credential outputs not marked sensitive, provider versions not pinned as `~> X.Y`), and one per provider, evaluated when a module declares that provider and shipped for AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, OCI and vSphere with three rules each. A deny, or a policy that cannot be evaluated, locks the session; see [Compliance policy](../reference/compliance-policy/) and [Resolve a locked session](../guides/resolve-a-locked-session/).

### Policy bundles and self-repair

Kumoss will load the policy bundles an organization already maintains outside Kumoss, and feed policy denies back into the generate-and-validate loop, so the model can repair the code before the round is locked.

### Multicloud governance overview

A governance overview will give administrators a single view of the resources and projects across every connected cloud, showing which are managed as code and how many comply with or violate the active policies. Platform and security teams will see their compliance posture at a glance and move from a finding straight to the session that fixes it.

## Cost management (FinOps)

Make the cost of infrastructure visible before and after every change, and connect Kumoss to the tools that FinOps teams already use.

### Accurate cost estimates and cost guardrails

Cost estimates for each plan will come from cloud pricing data instead of a language-model approximation, and will cover usage-based resources where pricing allows. Teams will set cost thresholds per project or environment that send a change for review before it is applied when the threshold is exceeded.

Today the estimate is an approximation for comparison; see [Follow a session](../guides/follow-a-session/).

### Cost overview by resource and project

A cost overview will show what each resource, project, and cloud costs, combining billing data with the infrastructure Kumoss manages. Administrators will spot idle or oversized resources and turn them into a request that fixes them, in the same view as the [governance overview](#governance-overview).

### Integration with FinOps tools and assistants

Kumoss will exchange cost data with external FinOps platforms and AI-based FinOps assistants through an open contract, using the [FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS)](https://focus.finops.org) where possible. FinOps tools will be able to ask Kumoss for a cost-saving change as a reviewed pull request, and Kumoss will use their recommendations as context when it generates code.

## Agent interoperability

Let assistants and other AI agents work with Kumoss through open protocols, under the same guardrails as any other request.

### Model Context Protocol (MCP) support

Kumoss will expose its capabilities through the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io), so that MCP-compatible assistants and IDEs can request compliant infrastructure directly. The same guardrails and review flow will apply to every request, whichever client sends it.

### Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol support

Support for the [Agent2Agent protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org) will let other AI agents discover Kumoss and delegate infrastructure tasks to it. Kumoss will then act as a specialized agent within larger multi-agent workflows.

## Deployment and adoption

Shorten the path from download to a working, production-grade deployment.

### Helm chart for Kubernetes

An official Helm chart deploys Kumoss and its sidecars on Kubernetes, with production-oriented defaults for configuration, secrets, and scaling. A first version lives in `charts/kumoss`, published with each release to `oci://ghcr.io/inditextech/charts/kumoss` ([Deploy with Helm](../guides/deploy-with-helm/)): it runs the Compose topology, takes external databases, Redis, and object storage, and binds cloud credentials through workload identity. It complements the Docker Compose stack, which remains the quickest way to evaluate Kumoss.

### Installation wizard

A guided installation wizard will walk operators through the first setup of models, identity provider, Git, cloud credentials, and storage, validating each step as it goes. Operators will reach a working deployment without editing configuration files by hand.

## Shape the roadmap

The roadmap evolves with the community. To propose an initiative, comment on a planned one, or offer to help build it, open or join a discussion on the [issue tracker](https://github.com/InditexTech/kumoss/issues). For contribution guidance, including the requirement to open an issue before substantial work, see [Contributing](../contributing/).

---

# Glossary

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/glossary/

This glossary lists the terms, abbreviations, and phrases used across the Kumoss documentation, together with their definitions. Use this terminology for clarity and consistency when discussing Kumoss.

## Compliance check

The check of a generated plan after a generate round: the compliance policies, Rego policies evaluated by OPA (a general one and one per provider of the module), then the intent check, an independent, second LLM agent that judges only whether the plan does what the session’s requests ask. Failing findings of either, or a policy that cannot be evaluated — and, optionally, a high-impact verdict — lock the session until a panel editor unlocks it or a later generate round passes clean.

See [How compliance works](../architecture/compliance/) and [Resolve a locked session](../guides/resolve-a-locked-session/).

## Compliance policy

The deterministic part of the compliance check: Rego policies, stored as the Langfuse prompts `general/policies/compliance` and `<provider>/policies/compliance`, that Open Policy Agent evaluates against the plan of every generate round, the general policy always and a provider’s when the root module declares that provider. The same plan always gets the same verdict, and a `deny` finding locks the session.

See [Write a policy rule](../guides/write-a-policy-rule/) and [Compliance policy](../reference/compliance-policy/).

## Drift

Infrastructure changes made outside Terraform — for example a console edit or a hotfix — that no longer match the code. Kumoss can detect drift and generate code that reconciles it.

See [Remediate drift](../guides/remediate-drift/).

## Filter

The phase where a small-model agent classifies a request: a change request proceeds, a question is answered in the conversation, and an out-of-scope or ambiguous request is declined with an explanation.

See [Make a request](../guides/make-a-request/).

## Generation

The phase where the main-model agent edits Terraform files through tools to satisfy the request, committing and pushing the result to the session branch.

See [Follow a session](../guides/follow-a-session/).

## IaC engine

The command-line tool — OpenTofu by default, or HashiCorp Terraform — that the `iac` sidecar runs to initialize, validate, plan, and apply infrastructure code.

See [Deployment view](../architecture/deployment-view/).

## Intent check

The LLM half of the compliance check: an independent agent that reads the session’s requests and the plan and reports only `scope_exceeded` (a change nobody asked for) and `scope_incomplete` (a part of a request left out), with the rules in the `general/intent/rules` prompt. It does not check the organization’s conventions.

See [How compliance works](../architecture/compliance/) and [Resolve a locked session](../guides/resolve-a-locked-session/#intent-check).

## Langfuse

The self-hosted service where Kumoss keeps its prompts and sends its traces. The core reads every prompt from Langfuse at request time, from the version that carries the deployment’s `environment` label.

See [Monitor with Langfuse](../guides/monitor-with-langfuse/) and [Customize prompts](../guides/customize-prompts/).

## Manifest

The `kumoss.yaml` file a session commits in a Terraform root module: the module’s providers, the scope of each provider that has one, the optional var files picked, and the values of its input variables (sensitive ones by name only, their values kept in Kumoss’s object storage). Answered once per root module and reused by every later session on it.

See [Root module manifest](../reference/root-module-manifest/).

## Mode

The operating mode chosen in the web application header: Generate Infrastructure, Partial Drift Remediation, Full Drift Remediation, Partial Import, or Full Import. The drift and import modes require the `devops` operation role.

See [Operating modes](../reference/operating-modes/).

## OpenTofu

The bundled, verified default IaC engine (MPL-2.0). HashiCorp Terraform (BUSL-1.1) is also bundled and selectable with `IAC_BINARY`.

See [Deployment view](../architecture/deployment-view/).

## Operation role

`developer` or `devops`, assigned per user and checked by the API on every IaC route; `devops` is above `developer` and is required for drift remediation.

See [Roles and permissions](../reference/roles-and-permissions/).

## Panel role

An optional, hierarchical role — `viewer`, `editor`, or `admin` — that gates the admin panel: `viewer` reads cross-user sessions, `editor` also toggles a session lock, and `admin` also manages users and roles.

See [Roles and permissions](../reference/roles-and-permissions/).

## Pinned plan

The plan file and validated workspace that a successful generate round renames into the session’s `pinned` directory, replacing any earlier pin, and that `POST /api/v1/iac/apply` executes without re-planning. Only generate rounds pin — drift rounds never do — and apply consumes and discards it whatever the outcome.

See [Merge and apply](../guides/merge-and-apply/).

## Project identifier

What the user named a repository by when it is not its URL, such as `sistemas-kumoss-rsg-esc1-dev`, which the mapping sidecar resolves to the repository. Checked against the repository when a session starts, recorded on the session and in the root module’s manifest, and sent to the IaC sidecar with each command, so an IaC service implementation can pick the credentials the command runs with. Never a credential itself.

See [Root module manifest](../reference/root-module-manifest/#project-identifier).

## Prompt

A text in Langfuse that gives Kumoss’s agents your organization’s standards: conventions, intent rules, impact criteria, exception lists, and the compliance policy. Named `<scope>/<type>/<name>` and seeded from `core/prompts/seed/` on a fresh deployment.

See [Customize prompts](../guides/customize-prompts/) and [Prompt registry](../reference/prompt-registry/).

## Report

Kumoss’s readable summary of the plan: what is created, updated, deleted, or recreated, the potential impact, and an estimated cost.

See [Follow a session](../guides/follow-a-session/).

## Request

The natural-language text a user submits describing the infrastructure change, the drift to reconcile, or the question to ask. Each request within a session opens a round.

See [Make a request](../guides/make-a-request/).

## Round

One request-and-response cycle inside a session, with its own statuses, report, plan, code changes, and pull requests. The first API call creates round 1 with status `started` and the handler immediately opens round 2 for the actual work; the API exposes both a round’s database id and its per-session number, and the web application labels rounds by number.

See [Follow a session](../guides/follow-a-session/).

## Scope

Where a provider’s resources live: the subscription of `azurerm`, the project of `google`, the account of `aws`, or the compartment of `oci`. Kept in the root module’s manifest, sent to the IaC sidecar with each command, and evaluated by the authorization sidecar. Other providers have no scope.

See [Root module manifest](../reference/root-module-manifest/#scopes).

## Session

One conversation with Kumoss about one repository. A session owns a Git branch named `Kumoss/YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS` (UTC) and a directory on the shared volume, and each user request within it opens a round.

See [Follow a session](../guides/follow-a-session/).

## Session lock

A flag on the session that blocks apply and pull-request merge. It is set automatically at the end of a generate round when the compliance policy denies the plan (or cannot be evaluated), when the intent check finds an `error` or `critical` violation such as `scope_exceeded`, or, where the deployment enables it, when the impact is High, and cleared either by an admin-panel editor or by a later generate round whose compliance check passes without a high-impact verdict. Some internal material calls this a plan lock.

See [How compliance works](../architecture/compliance/), [Resolve a locked session](../guides/resolve-a-locked-session/), and [Session locks](../guides/administer-users-and-locks/#session-locks).

## Sidecar

An integration point between Kumoss and an organization’s systems, implementing an OpenAPI contract. Kumoss bundles the `iac`, `notifications`, and `mapping` sidecars; for `authz`, provide your own implementation. Any implementation of a contract is used by pointing `services.<name>.endpoint` in `config.yaml` at it.

See [HTTP APIs](../reference/api/).

## Validation

The phase where the `iac` sidecar runs `init`, `validate`, and `plan` against the shared workspace to check that the generated code is sound and preview its effect.

See [Follow a session](../guides/follow-a-session/).

## Workspace

The per-run directory, shared with the `iac` sidecar, where Kumoss clones the repository and the IaC engine runs its commands. Each run gets its own directory under the session’s path; only the `pinned` plan is per session.

See [Deployment view](../architecture/deployment-view/).

---

# Deployment view

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/architecture/deployment-view/

This page describes how Kumoss’s containers are deployed on one Docker Compose stack, the operational notes that follow from that topology, and the architectural characteristics that result from the decisions described across this section.

## Infrastructure diagram

The block diagram below shows the deployment topology: every container in the Compose project, the host ports published by the proxy, and the calls between them. The user’s browser sits outside the bridge network on purpose.

![Kumoss Compose deployment topology: the stack’s containers on one bridge network, with only the proxy publishing host ports and the user’s browser outside the network](../../_images/deployment-topology.png)

Pan, zoom, search, trace a relationship, switch themes. [Open in a new tab](../../_attachments/deployment-topology.html)

/* Progressive enhancement for the block above. Guarded so that a page holding
   several diagrams runs this once, and deferred to DOMContentLoaded because a
   parse-time script cannot yet see the diagrams below it. */
(function () {
  if (window.__archifyEmbed) return
  window.__archifyEmbed = true

  /* The viewer's own interactive chrome. Its toolbar and zoom bar are
     position:fixed, so they always reach the bottom of whatever viewport the
     iframe gives them -- measuring them would make the height measurement
     below a fixpoint that can never shrink. Same selector list as
     docs/diagrams/capture-png.mjs, which hides them instead; here they stay
     visible and are only excluded from the measurement. */
  var CHROME = '.toolbar, .diagram-nav, .focus-chip, .guided-views, .archify-toast, .no-print'

  var style = document.createElement('style')
  style.textContent = [
    '.archify-actions{display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:.35rem .9rem;align-items:baseline;',
    'margin-block:-.65rem 1.5rem;font-size:.875rem;line-height:1.5}',
    '.archify-hint{opacity:.72}',
    '.archify-frame{width:100%;border:0;display:block}',
    /* A viewer is ~800KB and takes real time to arrive, so it loads out of
       the way while the still stays on screen, and is only swapped in once
       it has something to show. Off-screen rather than display:none: a
       display:none iframe has no viewport, so the application inside would
       not lay out, and revealing it would show an empty frame anyway --
       which is the whole failure this avoids. */
    '.archify-frame[data-archify-loading]{position:absolute;left:-99999px;top:0}',
    /* Only while the viewer is live. The still image is centred by the theme
       inside the narrower .imageblock; the frame is centred by this margin
       inside the wider one. */
    '.imageblock.archify-live{margin-inline:auto}',
    /* The theme insets an image block's contents by 40px, which puts the
       diagram 40px right of every heading and paragraph on the page. Those
       do line up with each other: a heading's box starts 64px further left
       than its text, because the theme carves that gutter with a negative
       margin and an equal padding to hold the hover anchor. So the column
       edge is where the text sits, and the diagram was the one thing off it.
       Dropped on both forms, so activating a block does not shift it. */
    '.imageblock.archify-block > .content{padding-inline:0}',
  ].join('')
  document.head.appendChild(style)

  /* The .imageblock wrapper is what escapes the 820px .sectionbody cap
     (`width: min(calc(var(--content-max-width)*1.25), var(--doc-inset-cap))`),
     so the viewer is swapped in inside it rather than in place of it. */
  function blockFor (actions) {
    var el = actions.previousElementSibling
    while (el && !el.classList.contains('imageblock')) el = el.previousElementSibling
    return el
  }

  /* Width is the only lever on how large the viewer draws: its SVG comes out
     at roughly 0.9x the viewport width it is given, and viewport height barely
     moves it. But --doc-inset-cap holds .imageblock at 1025px however wide the
     window gets, which on a large display leaves the whole right half of the
     article column unused. Track the column instead, so a 2560px screen gets
     a 1490px frame rather than the still's 945px. */
  function columnWidth (block) {
    var column = block.closest('.doc')
    return column ? column.clientWidth : 0
  }

  function widen (block) {
    var width = columnWidth(block)
    if (width) block.style.width = width + 'px'
  }

  /* Height of the real content, which is not the same as the document height:
     the viewer is a full-viewport application, so both scrollHeight and body
     height just echo back the height we set. Measure the lowest visible
     content edge instead, ignoring the fixed chrome. */
  function contentHeight (frame) {
    var doc = frame.contentDocument
    if (!doc) return 0
    var view = doc.defaultView
    var root = doc.querySelector('.container') || doc.body
    var nodes = root.querySelectorAll('*')
    var bottom = 0
    for (var i = 0; i < nodes.length; i++) {
      var node = nodes[i]
      var computed = view.getComputedStyle(node)
      if (computed.display === 'none' || computed.visibility === 'hidden' || computed.opacity === '0') continue
      if (computed.position === 'fixed' || node.closest(CHROME)) continue
      var rect = node.getBoundingClientRect()
      if (!rect.width || !rect.height) continue
      bottom = Math.max(bottom, rect.bottom)
    }
    return bottom ? Math.ceil(bottom + 24) : 0
  }

  /* A wider frame makes the viewer draw a larger diagram, which makes it
     taller, which is the measurement that sized the frame. Settle it over a
     few bounded passes instead of assuming one is enough, and stop once the
     change is not worth another reflow.

     A measurement of zero means the viewer has not laid itself out yet, not
     that it never will: each one is a whole application, and end-to-end-flow
     loads five of them at once over a cold cache. Keep waiting, because
     giving up here strands the frame at its seeded height for good. */
  function fit (frame, pass, waits) {
    var height = contentHeight(frame)
    if (!height) {
      if ((waits || 0) < 60) setTimeout(function () { fit(frame, pass, (waits || 0) + 1) }, 250)
      return
    }
    var current = parseInt(frame.style.height, 10) || 0
    if (Math.abs(height - current) < 8) return
    frame.style.height = height + 'px'
    if ((pass || 0) < 3) setTimeout(function () { fit(frame, (pass || 0) + 1, 0) }, 250)
  }

  /* Replaces one still with its viewer, then calls `done` to free the slot for
     the next one -- on load, or on the breaker below, whichever comes first.

     The still stays on screen for the whole download. An earlier version put
     the frame in place the moment it was created, which left a blank grey
     panel where the diagram had been until ~800KB arrived: on a fast static
     server that is a flicker, on anything slower it is the whole reading
     experience. So the frame loads off-screen, at the size it is about to
     occupy, and the swap happens in one synchronous block. */
  function activate (actions, done) {
    var block = blockFor(actions)
    if (!block || block.classList.contains('archify-live')) return done()
    var content = block.firstElementChild || block
    var still = content.querySelector('img')

    var frame = document.createElement('iframe')
    frame.className = 'archify-frame'
    frame.title = actions.dataset.archifyTitle || 'Interactive diagram'
    /* Load it at the size it will be revealed at, so the viewer lays out for
       the real column and appearing costs no second reflow. Antora writes no
       width/height on the still, so one that has not decoded yet measures
       zero: fall back to a nominal height rather than a collapsed frame. */
    var seed = still ? Math.round(still.getBoundingClientRect().height) : 0
    frame.style.height = (seed > 120 ? seed : 620) + 'px'
    frame.style.width = (columnWidth(block) || block.clientWidth || 900) + 'px'
    frame.setAttribute('data-archify-loading', '')

    /* Everything that makes the frame visible, in one go, so no intermediate
       state is ever painted. The frame is never moved in the DOM --
       re-inserting an iframe reloads it, which would throw away the wait --
       so the still is removed around it instead. */
    function reveal () {
      frame.removeAttribute('data-archify-loading')
      frame.style.width = ''
      /* .imageblock is display:flex and .content is a shrink-wrapping flex
         item: the image sized it by its own intrinsic width, but an iframe
         has none, so .content would collapse to the UA's 300px iframe default
         and the frame's width:100% would resolve against an indefinite
         container. Pin .content to the flex container's width so the
         percentage has something definite to resolve against. */
      content.style.width = '100%'
      block.classList.add('archify-live')
      widen(block)
      for (var i = content.children.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        if (content.children[i] !== frame) content.children[i].remove()
      }
    }

    /* One viewer loads at a time, so a frame that never fires load would hold
       the queue for good and strand every diagram below it as a still.
       Release the slot after a generous wait; this frame still reveals itself
       if it turns up late. */
    var settled = false
    function settle () {
      if (settled) return
      settled = true
      done()
    }
    setTimeout(settle, 15000)

    frame.addEventListener('load', function () {
      /* The viewer repeats its own title as an <h1> above the diagram, and
         every page that embeds one already carries that line as the section
         heading right above the frame. Two of the same sentence is one too
         many, and at column width the repeat wraps onto a second line and
         runs into the viewer's own toolbar. Hidden here rather than removed
         from the specification: a title is required there, and the "Open in a
         new tab" page has no surrounding heading to make it redundant. Same
         document, same origin, so this is a stylesheet and not a message. */
      var inner = frame.contentDocument
      if (inner) {
        var hide = inner.createElement('style')
        hide.textContent = '.container > .header{display:none}'
        inner.head.appendChild(hide)
      }

      /* `load` means the viewer's assets arrived and its scripts ran, not that
         it has drawn: the SVG appears in a later layout pass. Revealing on
         load alone shows the viewer's own empty panel for a frame or two, so
         wait for the drawing to exist -- briefly, and then reveal anyway,
         because a viewer that never draws must not keep the still forever. */
      var tries = 0
      ;(function ready () {
        var drawn = false
        try { drawn = !!(inner && inner.querySelector('svg')) } catch (e) { drawn = true }
        if (!drawn && ++tries <= 20) return void setTimeout(ready, 100)

        reveal()
        settle()

        /* Only now is the frame in the flow at its final width, so this is
           where the height measurement belongs. */
        setTimeout(function () { fit(frame, 0) }, 400)
        var width = 0
        new ResizeObserver(function () {
          /* Width only: observing our own height would loop against fit(). */
          var next = Math.round(frame.getBoundingClientRect().width)
          if (next === width) return
          width = next
          fit(frame, 0)
        }).observe(frame)
      })()
    })

    content.appendChild(frame)
    frame.src = actions.dataset.archifySrc
  }

  /* A page can hold five of these and each is a whole application of roughly
     800KB, so they are loaded strictly one at a time.

     Serial, not merely staggered. An earlier version started one every 900ms,
     which on a slow origin simply put all five in flight together: a browser
     opens about six connections per origin, five long downloads take nearly
     all of them, and the next click on the navigation sidebar gets no socket
     at all. That is not a slow page, it is a page that has stopped answering
     -- the network panel shows the navigation cancelled with zero bytes
     transferred. One viewer at a time bounds the cost to a single connection
     however slow the origin is, and the reader keeps a still until its
     replacement is ready, so nothing is lost by waiting.

     Proximity decides the order and never whether. Two earlier versions let it
     decide whether, and both stranded the lower diagrams as stills for good:
     the reader saw a tiny illegible image where a viewer should be. The cause
     outlives either mechanism. Antora writes no width or height on a still, so
     every image reflows everything below it as it decodes -- which means a
     block can be carried into range with no event to announce it. An
     IntersectionObserver's one-shot entry arrives against a position the block
     no longer holds; a rect read on scroll is never stale, but nothing reads it
     once the reader stops scrolling. Working through the whole queue removes
     that class of failure instead of widening the window it hides in: being
     near a diagram only brings it forward. */
  function enhance () {
    var pending = []
    var actions = document.querySelectorAll('.archify-actions[data-archify-src]')
    for (var i = 0; i < actions.length; i++) {
      var block = blockFor(actions[i])
      if (!block) continue
      /* Marks the blocks this script owns, so the stylesheet above can reach
         them while they are still stills. */
      block.classList.add('archify-block')
      pending.push(actions[i])
    }
    if (!pending.length) return

    var queued = false
    var running = false

    function stop () {
      window.removeEventListener('scroll', schedule)
      window.removeEventListener('resize', schedule)
    }

    /* Leaving the page ends the queue. Without this, a click on the navigation
       sidebar races a pump that is about to start another ~800KB viewer: the
       browser asks for the next document while this page opens one more
       connection for a viewer nobody will ever see, and on a slow origin the
       navigation is what waits. The reader reads that as a page that has
       stopped answering. Nothing below needs the queue once the document is
       on its way out. */
    window.addEventListener('pagehide', function () {
      pending.length = 0
      stop()
    })

    /* One observer for the whole column, not one per diagram. Every live block
       tracks the same element, so five separate observers on it did the same
       work five times over on every resize. */
    var column = document.querySelector('.doc')
    if (column) {
      new ResizeObserver(function () {
        var live = document.querySelectorAll('.imageblock.archify-live')
        for (var i = 0; i < live.length; i++) widen(live[i])
      }).observe(column)
    }

    /* The one place a viewer is ever started. Nothing else calls activate, so
       there is exactly one download in flight no matter what triggers a
       pump -- scroll, resize, or the previous one finishing. */
    function pump () {
      if (running || !pending.length) return
      running = true
      activate(pending.shift(), function () {
        running = false
        if (pending.length) setTimeout(pump, 250)
        else stop()
      })
    }

    /* Reorders what is left so anything the reader can nearly see goes next,
       and never activates anything itself. A diagram already passed keeps its
       place in the queue: the saving worth having is not loading five viewers
       at once, not reclaiming one that has scrolled off the top. */
    function promote () {
      queued = false
      var visible = []
      var rest = []
      for (var i = 0; i < pending.length; i++) {
        var block = blockFor(pending[i])
        var close = block && block.getBoundingClientRect().top <= window.innerHeight + 400
        ;(close ? visible : rest).push(pending[i])
      }
      pending = visible.concat(rest)
      pump()
    }

    function schedule () {
      if (queued) return
      queued = true
      requestAnimationFrame(promote)
    }

    window.addEventListener('scroll', schedule, { passive: true })
    window.addEventListener('resize', schedule)
    promote()
  }

  if (document.readyState === 'loading') document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', enhance)
  else enhance()
})()

Named volumes are written into each container’s subtitle instead of being drawn as separate nodes (`core_db_data`, `object_storage_data`, `workspaces`, and the `langfuse_*` volumes), and Langfuse’s six containers — `langfuse-web`, `langfuse-worker`, `langfuse-db`, `langfuse-clickhouse`, `langfuse-redis`, and the one-shot `langfuse-bucket` — are folded into one langfuse node. Two edges are left out because the [system architecture diagram](../) already carries them — the core’s OTLP traces and prompt calls to Langfuse, and the proxy’s port 9000 path to object storage — and the connections that leave the stack (LLM and git provider APIs from the core, the Slack webhook from notifications) appear in the notes beside the diagram rather than as external nodes.

Only the proxy publishes host ports; all other containers are reachable solely on the internal network. The `workspaces` volume is the one mount shared by two containers (core and iac), which is what lets the iac service run the IaC engine against the core’s git clones. Both containers run as the same unprivileged user (`kumoss`, uid/gid 10001, fixed by the `KUMOSS_UID`/`KUMOSS_GID` build args) so files either one creates are writable by the other. Additional Compose hardening for the iac container (dropping all capabilities, `no-new-privileges`, a read-only root filesystem, and CPU/memory/pid limits) was prototyped but is not present in the checked-in `docker-compose.yml`; it remains a recommended deployment hardening because the container executes provider code from generated HCL.

## Operational notes

The Compose stack described here is the **local/non-production** deployment model and the reference topology for production. The Helm chart in `charts/kumoss` maps the same topology onto Kubernetes; see [Deploy with Helm](../../guides/deploy-with-helm/).

### Topology

- All the containers share one Docker bridge network. Only `proxy` publishes host ports: 80 (SPA, API, SSE), 9000 (presigned object-storage access) and 3000 (the Langfuse UI, on a port of its own because the stock Langfuse image cannot be served under a path); every other service is internal-only via `expose`.
- Compose `depends_on` orders start-up: core waits for core-db, notifications, mapping, iac, Redis, and object storage to start, and for `langfuse-web` to be **healthy** (a cold Langfuse migrates its databases first); the proxy waits for core, `langfuse-web`, and object storage. Langfuse’s web and worker wait for healthy langfuse-db, ClickHouse and Redis and for `langfuse-bucket` to have created their bucket, and the worker also for a healthy web. SearXNG has no dependency ordering — the core calls it per request, so a missing or slow engine surfaces only as the `web_search` tool’s "unavailable" result. The prompt seeder still retries, for platforms without that ordering.
- Named volumes persist state: `core_db_data`, `object_storage_data`, `workspaces`, and Langfuse’s `langfuse_db_data`, `langfuse_clickhouse_data`, `langfuse_clickhouse_logs` and `langfuse_redis_data`.

### Core start-up

The FastAPI lifespan enforces a strict order: database, then Redis, then object-storage bucket creation, then Langfuse prompt seeding. Failure of any step aborts boot. Git credential configuration follows and is best-effort.

Configuration comes from a single `config.yaml`, read once at startup from `/etc/kumoss/config.yaml` (or the path in `KUMOSS_CONFIG`). The core Dockerfile bakes the repository’s copy into the image, and the checked-in Compose file bind-mounts it over that path, so a change needs a core restart; without a mount, it needs an image rebuild.

Secrets never appear in the file: *env fields name environment
variables (database URL, service bearer tokens, storage keys, git
personal access token), and the core validates at boot that every
enabled service’s token and every referenced LLM credential resolves.
Each `KUMOSS<SERVICE>_TOKEN` must match between the core’s outbound
client and the sidecar’s inbound validation.

Authentication needs no secret: the `oidc` block and `admin.default_root_email` are plain configuration that Pydantic validates at load, so an `issuer_url` without a `client_id` fails the boot; discovery and JWKS are fetched lazily on the first request, so a wrong or unreachable issuer surfaces as a `401` at first login, not at boot. Operationally, what matters here is that enabling or changing OIDC means `docker compose restart core`, and that the IdP must have `<origin>/auth/callback` registered as the SPA redirect URI.

## Operational limits and single-instance assumptions

The stack is designed as one core process. These are the consequences to plan for before running more than one:

- **Runs are in-process background tasks.** A core crash or restart mid-run leaves `sessions.in_flight = true` with no lease and no expiry, and the compare-and-set will refuse the session for ever; recovery is a manual `UPDATE sessions SET in_flight = false`.
- **The `workspaces` volume must be shared and persistent across replicas.** A pinned plan lives on disk at `/workspaces/<session>/pinned`, so an apply routed to a replica that did not run the generate round finds no pinned plan and fails the session.
- **Only the PostgreSQL compare-and-set is replica-safe.** Redis holds no locks; its single-flight registry is an in-process `asyncio.Lock` per key, so it de-duplicates cache misses within one process only.
- **Static storage credentials are rendered in plaintext** into `backend_override.tf` on the shared volume when Kumoss-managed state is used with access/secret keys or an Azure account key. Prefer credential chains or workload identity where the provider allows it.
- **One Git identity for every user.** All pushes and pull requests use the single PAT in `GIT_TOKEN`, and commits are authored, by default, as `Kumoss <kumoss@noreply.invalid>` (`git.author_name` / `git.author_email`), so repository history attributes nothing to the requesting user — the session record in core-db is the audit trail.
- **The artifact proxy on port 9000 answers** `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. Presigned URLs are the only access control on that port.

## Architectural characteristics

- **Ports and adapters.** Domain services depend on interfaces, infrastructure adapters implement them, and a per-run factory wires the object graph explicitly, so LLM providers, git hosts, Terraform execution, and storage backends are replaceable through configuration alone.
- **Contract-first sidecars.** OpenAPI specifications are the authoritative boundary, with generated clients on one side and, on the other, intentionally minimal bundled implementations for IaC, notifications and mapping, inviting substitution in enterprise deployments; the authorization contract ships without an implementation, as an optional extension point you implement yourself.
- **Deliberately direct execution.** Pipelines run as in-process background tasks with a database compare-and-set as the only concurrency control; sidecar calls are synchronous HTTP with job polling rather than event-driven messaging; SSE progress derives from status polling. These are visible trade-offs, not accidents.
- **Deep, centralized telemetry.** Model calls, tool executions, and engine runs are traced to Langfuse, which doubles as the runtime prompt registry, making prompt management an operational concern rather than a code change. No tracing decorator exports anything when the wrapped call raises: most of them build the span only **after** the call returns, and the chain decorator, which does create its span first, never ends it on an exception. Failures are therefore visible in the logs and the session status, not as error spans, and the sidecars are not instrumented at all.
- **LLM checks LLM, code decides.** The intent check is a separate agent loop with no repository access at all — its only tool is the sentinel `report_intent_findings`, and it judges only whether the plan does what the session’s requests ask; the pass/fail verdict is computed deterministically from the structured violations it reports, and the resulting database lock is what actually stops a non-compliant plan from being applied. The compliance policy, evaluated by OPA before the intent check, adds findings that do not depend on a model at all.
- **Stateless, local identity.** The core trusts only a signed JWT from the single configured issuer, validates it on every request without an introspection round-trip, and keeps users, roles, and session ownership in its own database, so federation, MFA, and session policy stay the identity provider’s concern.

# How compliance works

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/architecture/compliance/

Kumoss lets a change be merged and applied only after it has been checked against your organization’s rules. This page explains the mechanism as a whole: when the checks run, what each one is, how their results become a session lock, and how a lock is cleared. The pages it links to cover each part in detail.

## When the checks run

The checks run at the end of every **generate** round, after the plan has been validated and the report written, and before the plan is pinned for apply. Drift and import rounds are never checked and never lock a session: drift remediation ends at the merge, and an import changes no infrastructure.

Two switches in `config.yaml` decide which checks run; both default to `false` in code, and the shipped `config.yaml` turns both on:

- `orchestration.enable_compliance_checker` runs the compliance policy and the intent check.
- `orchestration.block_on_high_impact` lets a high-impact verdict lock the session.

See [Configuration](../../reference/configuration/).

## The three checks

| Check | Deterministic | What it does | Defined in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Compliance policy** | Yes | Open Policy Agent evaluates Rego policies against the plan’s JSON: the general policy, and the policy of each provider the root module declares. Fails closed: a policy that cannot be evaluated locks the round too. | Prompts `general/policies/compliance` and `<provider>/policies/compliance` |
| **Intent check** | No | A language model judges only whether the plan does what every request of the session asks: `scope_exceeded` (a change nobody asked for) and `scope_incomplete` (a part of a request left out), both of severity `error`. It does not judge safety, conventions, deletions, or versions, and a change the user asked for is never a violation. | Prompt `general/intent/rules` |
| **High impact** | No | The report model rates the change `low`, `medium`, or `high` from written criteria. | Prompt `general/compliance/impact` |

Only the policy check is deterministic: it reads attributes of the plan, so the same plan always gets the same verdict. The intent check and the impact rating depend on what the request means and on what a change implies, which only a model can judge, so their verdicts can vary between runs. Rules that can be stated as a condition on the plan therefore belong in the policies. Your conventions (the guideline and resource prompts) only guide generation: no check reviews a plan against them afterwards except what a policy enforces. For what each check looks for, why, and where to adapt it, see [Why a session is locked](../../guides/resolve-a-locked-session/#why).

## From findings to a lock

1. The core evaluates the policies, then runs the intent check, and merges both into one **compliance report** for the round; only this merge produces a verdict. Each finding carries its source (`opa` for the policies, `intent` for the intent check), a rule id, a severity, and, when it concerns one, the resource.
2. The report fails when either source has a finding of severity `error` or `critical`. Findings of severity `warning` are reported only.
3. The core sets the session’s lock from that round alone: locked when the report failed, or when the impact is `high` and `block_on_high_impact` is on; unlocked otherwise. A later clean round therefore clears an earlier lock.
4. When the report failed, or a high impact locked the session, the notifications sidecar, if enabled, alerts the session owner and every user with the panel role `editor` or higher.

The compliance report is stored as the round’s **Compliance Check** artifact, and the lock as the session’s `is_blocked` flag in core-db; see [Data and state](../data-and-state/).

## What a lock does

While a session is locked, its owner can still read everything, continue the conversation, and create the pull request, but merging the pull request and applying the plan are refused with `409`. The web application shows the **Deployment Blocked** screen with the findings that caused the lock, each badged **policy** or **intent** by its source.

A lock is cleared in one of two ways:

- The owner sends a follow-up request whose round passes every check.
- A reviewer with the panel role `editor` or `admin` unlocks the session from the admin panel. That unlock lasts until the owner’s next generate round, which sets the lock again from its own results.

See [Session locks](../../guides/administer-users-and-locks/#session-locks).

## Where to go next

| If you are | Read |
| --- | --- |
| A user whose session is locked | [Resolve a locked session](../../guides/resolve-a-locked-session/) |
| A reviewer deciding whether to unlock | [Lock or unlock the apply of a session](../../guides/administer-users-and-locks/#unlock-a-session) |
| Adapting the rules to your organization | [Compliance prompts](../../guides/customize-prompts/#compliance-prompts) and [Write a policy rule](../../guides/write-a-policy-rule/) |
| Looking for the exact policy contract | [Compliance policy](../../reference/compliance-policy/) |

# Data and state

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/architecture/data-and-state/

This page describes what each of Kumoss’s data stores holds: core-db, Langfuse’s stores, Redis, object storage, and the `workspaces` volume on the filesystem shared between the core and the iac sidecar.

## core-db

**core-db (PostgreSQL 17)** is the system of record for the application domain. Thirteen tables: `users` (unique on `(issuer, subject)`, with `email`, `display_name`, `operation_role`, nullable `panel_role`), `sessions` (owned by a `user_id`, including the `in_flight` concurrency flag and the `is_blocked` compliance lock that gates apply), `workspaces`, `terraform_providers`, `pull_requests`, `histories`, `statuses`, `rounds`, and the artifact-metadata tables `artifacts`, `terraform_plans`, `reports`, `compliance_checks` (the compliance verdict plus its stored findings), and `code_changes`. Roles are managed from the admin panel or, for the first administrator on IdPs that emit no `email_verified` claim, by a one-off SQL update (see [Grant the first administrator access](../../guides/enable-authentication/#bootstrap-admin)). The schema is versioned with Alembic and migrated by the core at startup (see [Changing the schema](../../reference/database-schema/#changing-the-schema)). A `core_db_data` volume from a pre-auth stack (sessions keyed by a `username` column, no `users` table) is too old to migrate: the core refuses to start on it, so migrate it by hand or recreate it.

For the table-by-table breakdown, the enumerated columns, and how deletion cascades, see [Database schema](../../reference/database-schema/).

## Langfuse’s stores

Langfuse owns its stores exclusively; they hold operational/LLM telemetry and prompts, fully separate from Kumoss’s domain data. **langfuse-db (PostgreSQL 17)** stores prompt versions and their labels, plus Langfuse’s users, project and API keys. **langfuse-clickhouse** stores the traces. **langfuse-redis** is Langfuse’s job queue (run with `noeviction`, unlike the core’s cache), and the `langfuse` bucket on the object-storage service keeps the raw ingested events.

## Redis

**Redis 8** is a cache, not a store: read-through/write-through for session facts, last statuses, and finished-session aggregates, with 2-second timeouts so a slow Redis fails open to PostgreSQL. It holds no locks and no pub/sub channels.

## Object storage

### Artifacts

Object storage holds generated artifacts under `sessions/<session id>/rounds/<round primary key>/`, as `reports/<report type>-<token>.json`, `compliance/check-<token>.json`, `plans/{plan|drift}-<token>.txt`, or `changes/<token>-<sanitized file name>`. RustFS is the **default and bundled** implementation: the Compose stack starts it as the `object-storage` container, and because it is open source (Apache-2.0) the default stack needs no proprietary or source-available storage component. It is not the only option. `storage.provider` selects one of three adapters, never more than one at a time:

| `storage.provider` | Backend | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RUSTFS` (default) | The bundled RustFS, or **any S3-compatible object store** reached through a custom `endpoint_url` (path-style addressing, static access and secret keys) | Presigned URLs are signed against `public_endpoint_url`, the address browsers reach |
| `S3` | **AWS S3** on its regional endpoint | Credentials from static keys or the AWS SDK default chain (instance role, workload identity) |
| `STORAGE_ACCOUNT` | **Azure Blob Storage** in a storage account | Shared-key authentication, SAS-token presigning; the account name is derived from `endpoint_url` and the container from `bucket` |

There is no dedicated Google Cloud Storage adapter; a GCS bucket could only be reached through its S3-compatible interoperability endpoint with the `RUSTFS` provider, which the repository does not test. For **state**, a first-class `gcs` backend remains available by letting the repository declare it — see [below](#terraform-state). Presign expiry is 48 hours by default, floored at 30 hours so links outlive cached session aggregates.

### Root module secrets

The artifacts bucket also holds the values of the **sensitive** input variables users answered for a root module, one JSON object per module at `manifests/<sha256 of repository and module path>/secrets.json`. The module’s committed `kumoss.yaml` names those variables but never holds their values; plain values, picked var files, provider scopes and the project identifier, when there is one, live in that file, in the repository. Back the bucket up and restrict it accordingly. See [Root module manifest](../../reference/root-module-manifest/).

### Terraform and OpenTofu state

Object storage for Terraform/OpenTofu state is on by default as
shipped. A remote backend, however, is not optional regardless of that
setting: workspaces are ephemeral and the `.gitignore` the core seeds
excludes **.tfstate, so local state would be lost after the run. Because `storage.terraform_state_bucket` ships set to `kumoss-terraform-state`, the default is that *Kumoss manages state itself**, in a second bucket in the same store kept separate from the
artifacts bucket. A deployment can instead set the value to `""` so
that **each repository declares its own remote backend** — `azurerm`,
`s3`, `gcs`, or anything else the engine supports — authenticated with
the cloud credentials given to the IaC sidecar, or hand the sidecar a
backend configuration file through `IAC_BACKEND_CONFIG` instead.

As shipped, the core creates that second bucket at boot and renders its backend into a `backend_override.tf` in the workspace before every `init` — so a repository’s own backend block is overridden without editing its committed HCL, and the iac sidecar is the container that must reach the store. Setting the value to `""` turns all of that off: no bucket is created, no override is written, and the workspace falls back to whatever backend the repository’s own Terraform files declare. A bare `terraform_state_bucket:` key with no value is **not** the same as `""` — it parses as YAML null and fails boot with a Pydantic validation error — and **deleting** the key entirely also leaves managed state on, since the configuration default is the same `kumoss-terraform-state` value.

See [Configure state backends](../../guides/configure-state-backends/) for the full decision between the three ownership models and how core and sidecar configuration interact.

## Workspaces volume

The `workspaces` volume is per-run: each run clones the repository into a unique directory shared with the iac container, and the runner removes it in a `finally` block. A **successful generate round** is the exception — it renames its directory to `/workspaces/<session>/pinned` before the cleanup runs, so that directory survives on the volume until apply’s `discard_pinned` or the next generate round replaces it. That pinned directory keeps the initialized backend and the plan file, which is why apply executes the reviewed plan without re-running `init`. Durable outputs otherwise leave via git pushes and artifact uploads, not the volume.

# Roles and permissions

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/reference/roles-and-permissions/

Every user record in Kumoss’s database carries two roles from two independent groups: an **operation role**, which decides which Infrastructure as Code (IaC) actions the user may run on their own sessions, and an **admin-panel role**, which decides what the user may do in the admin panel. See [Glossary](../../glossary/) for the short definitions of both terms; this page is the complete reference: every grant each level carries, the permission matrix the API enforces, and who receives which role by default.

Roles live in the core database, not in the authorization sidecar. The AuthZEN PDP is consulted on every write route via `POST /access/v1/evaluation` to decide whether the caller may perform an action on each provider scope of the session’s root module — a check that is disabled by default (`services.authz.enabled: false`) and has no bearing on operation or panel roles. See [Deploy to production](../../guides/deploy-to-production/) for when to enable it.

## Two independent role groups

The two groups solve different problems and do not affect each other. A panel `admin` with operation role `developer` cannot run drift remediation, and cannot apply or merge a pull request on somebody else’s session — acting on a session belongs to its owner only, whatever the panel role. Conversely, a `devops` user with no panel role sees only their own sessions.

### Operation roles

Operation roles are hierarchical, and every user has one.

| Operation role | Grants |
| --- | --- |
| `developer` | Generate Infrastructure, create and merge pull requests, and apply a pinned plan on sessions they own. |
| `devops` | Everything `developer` can do, plus Partial and Full Drift Remediation. The web application also reserves the Partial Import and Full Import modes for `devops`. |

### Admin-panel roles

Admin-panel roles are hierarchical too, and optional: most users have no panel role and see only their own sessions.

| Panel role | Grants |
| --- | --- |
| none | Own sessions only. |
| `viewer` | Read-only view of every user’s sessions in the admin panel. |
| `editor` | `viewer`, plus lock and unlock apply and pull-request merge on any session (see [Session locks](../../guides/administer-users-and-locks/#session-locks)). |
| `admin` | `editor`, plus user and role management. |

### Session access rules

The API enforces these rules regardless of role:

- The **owner** can always read a session and is the only one who can act on it (continue it, create or merge its pull request, apply).
- A user with **any panel role** can read any session, both through the admin routes and through the regular session routes, including its live event stream.
- Everyone else receives `403 Not the session owner`.

## Roles at a glance

| Route | Minimum operation role | Extra condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /api/v1/iac/generate` | `developer` | Owner only when continuing an existing session |
| `POST /api/v1/iac/drift` | `devops` | Owner only when continuing an existing session |
| `POST /api/v1/iac/import` | `developer` | Owner only when continuing an existing session. The web application offers the import modes only to `devops`. |
| `POST /api/v1/iac/apply` | `developer` | Owner only; session not locked (`409`). A pinned plan must exist, otherwise the round the `202` opened fails and the session ends `failed`. |
| `POST /api/v1/repository/parse` (list Terraform roots in a repository) | `developer` | None; the wizard calls it on every new session, immediately after the repository URL is entered |
| `POST /api/v1/manifest/probe` (what a root module needs) | `developer` | None; the wizard calls it once the root module is chosen. It reads only and never returns variable values |
| `PUT /api/v1/repository/pr` (create pull request) | `developer` | Owner only |
| `PUT /api/v1/repository/pr/merge` | `developer` | Owner only; session not locked |

The web application is stricter than the API in one place: it disables Partial Drift Remediation, Full Drift Remediation, Partial Import, and Full Import for users below `devops`, showing the hint "Requires the devops operation role." The API itself accepts an import from any `developer`. With authentication disabled (blank `oidc.issuer_url`), the local development identity holds `devops` and sees every mode.

## Permission matrix

The matrix reflects what the backend enforces. The web application hides or disables controls accordingly.

| Capability | No panel role | `viewer` | `editor` | `admin` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sign in, run sessions allowed by the operation role | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| View own sessions, details, artifacts, lock state; reopen own sessions | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Open the admin panel | no | yes | yes | yes |
| List sessions across all users, paginated | no | yes | yes | yes |
| Filter by type and status; search by user e-mail, project, query text, or session id | no | yes | yes | yes |
| Open any user’s session detail, including conversation history | no | yes | yes | yes |
| View any session’s statuses, reports, plans, code-change artifacts, repository link, pull-request links, lock state | no | yes | yes | yes |
| Open Langfuse from the admin sessions tab | no | yes | yes | yes |
| Receive support requests sent from the web application’s header | no | no | yes | yes |
| Lock or unlock apply and pull-request merge on a session | no | no | yes | yes |
| List and search users | no | no | no | yes |
| Assign operation roles | no | no | no | yes |
| Assign or remove panel roles | no | no | no | yes |
| Remove one’s own panel `admin` role | no | no | no | **no** (`409`) |
| Act on another user’s session (continue, create or merge a pull request, apply) | no | no | no | no (owner only) |
| Delete a user or a session | not implemented | not implemented | not implemented | not implemented |

Backend routes behind the matrix:

| Route | Who |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/v1/sessions/list`, `GET /api/v1/sessions?id={session_id}` | Any signed-in user; the list is always scoped to the caller, the detail is owner or any panel role |
| `GET /api/v1/events/subscribe/{session_id}` | Owner or any panel role |
| `GET /api/v1/admin/sessions/list`, `GET /api/v1/admin/sessions?id={session_id}` | panel `viewer` or higher |
| `PATCH /api/v1/admin/sessions/{session_id}/toggle_lock` | panel `editor` or higher |
| `GET /api/v1/admin/users`, `PUT /api/v1/admin/users/{user_id}/roles` | panel `admin` |

Missing or invalid credentials yield `401`; an insufficient panel role yields `403 Requires admin-panel role '<role>' or higher`.

## Who gets which roles

**With authentication disabled** (blank `oidc.issuer_url`, the checked-in default), every request runs as the built-in local development identity, which holds `devops` and panel `admin`. Anyone who can reach the stack has full access to both views; use this only on an isolated workstation.

**With OIDC enabled**, a new user is created on first login with operation role `developer` and no panel role: they can generate infrastructure and see their own sessions, nothing more. The first administrator comes from one of two places:

- `admin.default_root_email` in `config.yaml`: the user whose token carries that e-mail with `email_verified: true` is elevated to `devops` and panel `admin` at login. The elevation is one-way and is re-checked on every request. Only identity providers that emit `email_verified` in access tokens (Keycloak, for instance) can use this path.
- A one-off database grant for providers that never emit `email_verified` (Entra ID, Auth0, Okta). See [Grant the first administrator access](../../guides/enable-authentication/#bootstrap-admin).

After that, the administrator manages everyone else from the Users tab. The bootstrap elevation is re-applied on every request of the root user, so demoting that user from the Users tab is undone the next time they call the API; clear `admin.default_root_email` and restart the core first if a real demotion is needed.

With authentication disabled there is no identity provider to sign out of, but the "Log out" action still works locally: it clears the user in the browser and shows the login screen. Pressing **Sign In** re-fetches `GET /api/v1/users/me` and puts the browser straight back in as the dev identity.

Do not confuse this with the authorization sidecar. The AuthZEN PDP is an organizational gate consulted on every write route, and only when `services.authz.enabled` is `true`. The core never reads any user or role store from the PDP.

## Next steps

- [Administer users and locks](../../guides/administer-users-and-locks/) to perform the tasks this reference describes.
- [Enable authentication](../../guides/enable-authentication/) to configure OIDC and the first administrator.

# Repository layout

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/reference/repository-layout/

When a repository URL is entered, Kumoss looks inside it for the directories that hold Terraform-compatible code and offers them as the session’s **root module path**. This page is the complete reference for that detection.

## How Kumoss finds Terraform roots

After the repository URL is entered, the wizard calls `POST /api/v1/repository/parse`. The core accepts only `https://` URLs, validates the URL with `git ls-remote`, clones only the repository metadata (`--filter=blob:none --no-checkout`, 60-second limit), lists every file committed on the **default branch** with `git ls-tree -r HEAD --name-only`, and applies these rules to the directory paths. File contents are never read, and the temporary clone is deleted afterwards.

1. A directory is a **candidate** when it contains at least one `.tf` file.
2. A candidate is **dropped** when any segment of its path is `modules`, `examples`, `example`, or `.terraform`.
3. A candidate is a **root** when it contains a marker file — `main.tf`, `provider.tf`, `providers.tf`, `backend.tf`, `terraform.tf`, `versions.tf` — or any `.tfvars` / `.tfvars.json` file.
4. A candidate without a marker is still a root when it is the deepest `.tf` directory on its branch of the tree and does not sit under a directory that already qualified. Directories nested under a qualifying root are absorbed into it and are not offered separately.
5. The result is the sorted list of repository-relative paths. `.tf` files at the repository top level make the repository root itself a root, offered as `.`. The repository root absorbs nothing, though: the nesting test compares path prefixes, and no path begins with `./`, so a repository with top-level `.tf` files **and** a qualifying `envs/dev/main.tf` offers both `.` and `envs/dev`.

With no result the wizard shows "No root modules found in this repository."; with exactly one it skips the "Which root module?" step; with several it asks the user to pick. The chosen path becomes the session’s root module path: it is fixed on the first request, the engine runs `init`, `validate`, `plan`, and `apply` inside that directory, and it is one of the three inputs that identify the project’s state when Kumoss manages state (see [State keys](../../guides/state-backends/kumoss-managed/#state-keys)). The web application offers only detected paths; API callers may pass any repository-relative `root_module_path` that contains no `..` segment and resolves, symlinks included, to an existing directory inside the repository; an omitted `root_module_path` means the repository root. The agents' file tools are confined to that directory (see [Agent tool loop](../../architecture/end-to-end-flow/#agent-tool-loop)).

| Repository files (default branch) | Offered root module paths | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `envs/dev/main.tf`, `envs/prod/main.tf`, `modules/network/vpc.tf`, `modules/network/examples/basic/main.tf` | `envs/dev`, `envs/prod` | Both `envs/*` directories have a marker; everything under `modules/` is skipped as shared module code. |
| `platform/main.tf`, `platform/network/subnets.tf`, `platform/storage/buckets.tf` | `platform` | `platform` has a marker, so its two subdirectories are absorbed. The wizard skips the path step. |
| `lib/iam/policies.tf`, `lib/iam/roles.tf`, `README.md` | `lib/iam` | No marker, but it is the deepest `.tf` directory and nothing above it qualifies. |
| `main.tf`, `variables.tf`, `modules/net/vpc.tf` | `.` | Top-level `.tf` files make the repository root the only root. |
| `main.tf`, `envs/dev/main.tf` | `.`, `envs/dev` | The repository root is a root, but it absorbs no subdirectory, so `envs/dev` is offered as well and the wizard asks the user to pick. |

If a directory is missing from the offered list, check that its `.tf` files are committed on the default branch and that no parent directory is named `modules`, `examples`, `example`, or `.terraform`. The rules live in `core/src/infrastructure/filesystem/root_module_detector.py`.

## Next steps

- [Make a request](../../guides/make-a-request/) to see this detection from the wizard’s side.
- [Root module manifest](../root-module-manifest/) for what Kumoss reads from the chosen root module and the `kumoss.yaml` it commits there.
- [Guides](../../guides-overview/) for the rest of the session inputs.
