# Prompt registry

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/reference/prompt-registry/

Kumoss’s agents read their conventions, intent rules, impact criteria, and exception lists from prompts stored in the prompt management of [Langfuse](https://langfuse.com/docs/prompt-management). This page is the reference for how that registry works: where prompts live, the seed file conventions, how seeding and runtime lookup work, which agent reads which prompt, and the shipped inventory. To change a prompt, see [Customize prompts](../../guides/customize-prompts/).

## Where prompts live

| Layer | Where | Who changes it | When it takes effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Runtime prompts** | Langfuse prompt management (**Prompts** in the Langfuse UI, on port 3000 in the default stack; persisted in `langfuse-db`) | Prompt maintainers, in the Langfuse UI or API | Immediately on the next request; the core caches nothing |
| **Seed files** | `core/prompts/seed/<scope>/<type>/<name>.yaml` (`.rego` for policies) in the repository, copied into the core image | Contributors, and operators preparing a new deployment | At core startup: missing prompts are created, and a changed seed is published to the environments still on the previous seed (see [How seeding works](#how-seeding-works)) |

The seed files are the initial content of the registry, nothing more. The core always reads Langfuse; it never falls back to a seed file at runtime.

## Seed file conventions

### Path

```
core/prompts/seed/<scope>/<type>/<name>.yaml
core/prompts/seed/<scope>/policies/<name>.rego
```

- `<scope>` is `general` or a Terraform provider type name, the last segment of the provider’s source address, such as `azurerm` for `hashicorp/azurerm`. It must match `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,63}$`. The shipped seeds use `general`, `aws`, `azurerm`, `google`, `oci`, `kubernetes`, and `vsphere`; any other provider (`helm`, `datadog`…​) can be given prompts by adding a folder with its type name.
- `<type>` is one of `guidelines`, `resources`, `compliance`, `intent`, or `policies`. Seeds of type `policies` are `.rego` files; every other type is a `.yaml` file.
- `<name>` must match `^[a-z0-9_]+$` (lowercase letters, digits, and underscores).

The loader rejects any other depth, scope, type, or name at startup
with a `PromptSeedLoadError`, for example `Invalid prompt name
'Bad-Name' in …​; must match ^[a-z0-9_]+$`. A `.rego` file under a type
other than `policies`, or a `.yaml` file under `policies`, is rejected
too. The loader only globs .yaml and `.rego`, so a `.yml` file, or
any other extension, is skipped without an error: a typo in the
extension produces a missing prompt, not a failed boot.

### Qualified name

The Langfuse prompt name is derived from the path, never declared inside the file, so a misfiled prompt cannot misreport its identity:

```
<scope>/<type>/<name>
```

Langfuse shows each `/` as a folder, so its **Prompts** view is laid out like `core/prompts/seed/`: a folder per scope, and in it one per type. A prompt you create by hand must carry the full name, slashes included, to be found.

| File | Langfuse prompt name |
| --- | --- |
| `aws/guidelines/networking.yaml` | `aws/guidelines/networking` |
| `aws/guidelines/resources_list.yaml` | `aws/guidelines/resources_list` |
| `aws/resources/s3_bucket.yaml` | `aws/resources/s3_bucket` |
| `azurerm/resources/storage_account.yaml` | `azurerm/resources/storage_account` |
| `general/guidelines/terraform.yaml` | `general/guidelines/terraform` |
| `general/intent/rules.yaml` | `general/intent/rules` |
| `general/policies/compliance.rego` | `general/policies/compliance` |
| `aws/policies/compliance.rego` | `aws/policies/compliance` |

Two files that would produce the same qualified name abort the boot with `Duplicate qualified name …​`.

### Content

| Key | Required | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `body` | Yes | Non-empty string | The prompt text, usually Markdown. Stored as a Langfuse **text** prompt. |
| `description` | No | String | The commit message of each version the seeder creates, shown in the Langfuse version history. |

Every shipped seed provides both keys and starts with the repository’s SPDX comment header. The loader reads `body` and `description` and ignores every other key.

A `.rego` seed has no keys: the whole file, comments included, is the body, so `opa fmt` and `opa test` run on the very file that is seeded. It must not be empty. The commit message of its versions is generated (`Rego policy evaluated by OPA (<name>).`).

## How seeding works

A Langfuse prompt has numbered versions, and **labels** that each point at one version at a time: setting a label on a version takes it off any other. Langfuse keeps the `latest` label on the newest version itself. Kumoss uses one label per `environment` value and one of its own, `seed`.

At every core startup, after the database, Redis, and object storage have been initialized, the seeder:

1. Loads every seed file, sorted and validated as above.
2. Makes an authenticated read against Langfuse at `telemetry.langfuse_url`, retrying for about 90 seconds while Langfuse does not answer. If it stays unreachable, the boot fails with `Langfuse unreachable after 15 attempts`; if it rejects the key pair, with `Langfuse refused the API key pair (401)`. Langfuse must therefore be available whenever the core starts.
3. For each seed, reads the prompt’s version labeled `seed`, the one the seeder last pushed. A prompt without that label gets it on its latest version first.
4. If the prompt does not exist, creates it as a text prompt whose first version carries every `environment` value as a label (`development`, `staging`, and `production`) plus `seed`.
5. If the text of the `seed` version differs from the seed file, creates a new version with the seed’s text and moves to it, in one request, every environment label that is still on the `seed` version, together with `seed`. A label on any other version, or a label you removed, is left alone. If the latest version already holds the seed’s text because you saved it by hand, the labels move to it instead of to a copy.
6. Logs `Prompt seeding complete: N created, M updated, K unchanged`.

Only the text counts: the seeder compares the `seed` version’s text with the seed file and ignores its config and commit message.

What this means in practice:

- **Seeding never moves a label off your versions.** A seed changed by a release reaches every environment label that is still on the `seed` version. Once you move a label to your own version, that label keeps it on every later boot, and seed changes for it are yours to merge by hand. Do not move `seed` onto your own version, and do not remove it: without it, the seeder takes the latest version as its own, which may be yours.
- **New seed files are pushed too.** Adding a seed file and restarting the core creates the new prompt, even on an existing deployment.
- **A write fails whole.** A version is created together with its labels, and labels move in one request, so a failed write leaves the prompt as it was. The boot fails with an error naming the prompt (and, for a label move, the version and labels), and the next boot tries again.
- **The environment label matters.** Seeded versions carry all three environment labels, so changing `environment` keeps working for them. It does not for prompts you created by hand, or for labels you removed: the seeder never adds a label it did not find on its `seed` version.

## Runtime lookup

Each time an agent runs, the core fetches the prompts it needs from Langfuse by `<scope>/<type>/<name>` and the `environment` label, and reads the version’s text: the text of a text prompt, or the content of a chat prompt holding a single message. Any other shape is an error. The text is used as it is: Langfuse’s `{{variable}}` placeholders are not filled in. There is no cache: every session sees the version the label is on now, so a change in Langfuse takes effect on the next run without rebuilding or restarting the core.

Which provider prompts a session uses depends on its root module: the core asks for the `<provider>/*` prompts of every provider the module’s `required_providers` declares.

- A missing **provider** prompt is skipped. A provider without prompts, such as `random`, `helm`, or a module that declares no provider yet, gets the `general/*` prompts only.
- A missing **general** prompt, or one without a version carrying the environment label, stops the run with `prompt_name=<name>. No version labeled '<environment>'`. The session does not fail visibly; see [A session stops without an error](../../guides/customize-prompts/#session-stops).
- When several providers of a module have the same guideline, for example `azurerm` and `kubernetes` both have `permissions`, the agent receives all of them, each as a section headed by its provider name.
- A resource prompt the compositor picks is taken from the first provider that has it.

## Which agent reads which prompt

For a generate or drift round, the core builds the round’s conventions in two model passes and then gives each agent its prompts:

1. **First compositor pass.** The prompt compositor receives the `resources_list` and `abbreviations` of every provider of the root module that has them. The small model reads the request and calls the `construct_information` tool with the resource names and abbreviations it considers relevant. Names must match the `resources_list` entries exactly.
2. **Second compositor pass.** The compositor runs again with the full text of the resource prompts selected in the first pass, looks for dependencies (a subnet needs a network, a function needs a storage account), and returns more resources and abbreviations. Both passes are merged into the round’s conventions.
3. **Prompts for each agent**, as in the table below.

| Agent | Prompts it receives |
| --- | --- |
| Prompt compositor (every generate and drift round) | `<provider>/guidelines/abbreviations`, `<provider>/guidelines/resources_list`, and the selected `<provider>/resources/*` |
| IaC generator | `general/guidelines/terraform`; each provider’s `resource_creation`, `networking`, and `permissions`; the selected `<provider>/resources/*` and abbreviations |
| Intent checker (generate rounds, when `orchestration.enable_compliance_checker` is `true`) | `general/intent/rules` only; none of the conventions, which guide generation and are not checked by any agent |
| Compliance policies (same condition; evaluated by OPA, not a model) | `general/policies/compliance`, and `<provider>/policies/compliance` for each provider the root module declares that has one |
| Report generator (generate reports) | `general/compliance/impact` |
| Request filter | `general/guidelines/requests` |
| Drift target generator (partial drift rounds) | `general/guidelines/targeting_policies` |
| Drift exception filter (every drift round and every generate round’s drift pre-check) | Each provider’s `drift_exceptions` |
| Import scope diff (import rounds that find unmanaged resources; parsed by the core, not a model) | Each provider’s `import_exceptions` |

### Discovery depends on `resources_list`

Nothing enumerates the `<provider>/resources/*` prompts that exist in Langfuse. The compositor can only pick names that appear in `resources_list`:

- A name listed in `resources_list` without a matching resource prompt is logged as a warning, and its conventions are missing from the round.
- A resource prompt that exists but is not named in its provider’s `resources_list` is never selected. The loader does not cross-check the seed files against `resources_list` at startup.

Every shipped `resources_list` names all of its provider’s resource seeds. The name only needs to appear in the body: the AWS, Azure, GCP, OCI, and vSphere lists name entries in backticks with a description, while the Kubernetes list uses plain bullets (`- namespace`). Follow the style of the file you edit.

## Shipped seed inventory

The `aws`, `azurerm`, `google`, and `oci` scopes ship the same seven guideline prompts; `kubernetes` and `vsphere` ship six, without `import_exceptions`. The resource prompts differ per provider. Every scope, `general` included, also ships one policy, `policies/compliance.rego`.

| Scope | `guidelines` | `resources` | `compliance` | `intent` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `general` | `requests`, `targeting_policies`, `terraform` | None | `impact` | `rules` |
| `aws` | `abbreviations`, `drift_exceptions`, `import_exceptions`, `networking`, `permissions`, `resource_creation`, `resources_list` | `aurora`, `auto_scaling_group`, `bedrock`, `cloudwatch`, `dynamodb`, `ebs_volume`, `ec2`, `ecr_repository`, `ecs_fargate_service`, `efs`, `eks_cluster`, `elasticache_redis`, `iam_role`, `internet_gateway`, `kms_key`, `lambda`, `launch_template`, `load_balancer`, `nat_gateway`, `rds`, `redshift`, `route53`, `route_table`, `s3_bucket`, `sagemaker`, `secrets_manager`, `security_group`, `sns_topic`, `sqs_queue`, `subnet`, `vpc`, `vpc_endpoint`, `waf_web_acl` | None | None |
| `azurerm` | `abbreviations`, `drift_exceptions`, `import_exceptions`, `networking`, `permissions`, `resource_creation`, `resources_list` | `aks_cluster`, `application_gateway`, `application_insights`, `azure_openai`, `bastion`, `container_app`, `container_registry`, `cosmosdb`, `diagnostic_setting`, `function`, `key_vault`, `load_balancer`, `log_analytics_workspace`, `managed_disk`, `nat_gateway`, `network_security_group`, `postgres_flexible_server`, `private_dns_zone`, `private_endpoint`, `public_ip`, `redis_managed`, `resource_group`, `role_assignment`, `service_bus`, `storage_account`, `subnet`, `user_assigned_identity`, `virtual_machine`, `virtual_network`, `vm_scale_set`, `webapp` | None | None |

The `oci` import exception list ships but is not read: only Azure, GCP, and AWS scopes can be listed for import.

## Seed file examples

A provider guideline, `core/prompts/seed/aws/guidelines/networking.yaml` (shipped; body shortened), producing `aws/guidelines/networking`:

```
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 INDUSTRIA DE DISEÑO TEXTIL S.A. (INDITEX S.A.)
#
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0

description: AWS networking conventions (VPCs, subnets, gateways, security groups).
body: |
  # AWS Networking Guidelines

  ## Topology
  - Default to a multi-AZ VPC with public and private subnets per
    availability zone.

  ## Address space
  - Use RFC1918 ranges. Avoid overlapping with on-premises CIDRs
    or other VPCs that will be peered.
  - Allocate `/16` per VPC by default; carve `/24` subnets within.
```

A resource prompt, `core/prompts/seed/aws/resources/s3_bucket.yaml` (shipped; body shortened), producing `aws/resources/s3_bucket`:

```
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 INDUSTRIA DE DISEÑO TEXTIL S.A. (INDITEX S.A.)
#
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0

description: AWS S3 Bucket default configuration (encryption, versioning, public access, lifecycle, logging).
body: |
  # AWS S3 Bucket

  For an S3 Bucket, unless explicitly requested otherwise, use the
  following default configuration:

  - Naming convention: `<project>-<purpose>-<environment>`. Bucket
    names are globally unique, lowercase, 3-63 characters.
  - Versioning must be enabled.
  - Server-side encryption must use aws:kms with bucket key enabled.
```

# Import infrastructure

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/guides/import-infrastructure/

The Kumoss web application offers two import modes: Partial Import, for the unmanaged resources your request names, and Full Import, for every unmanaged resource in the session’s scopes. Both find the resources the cloud holds but the Terraform state does not, write a resource block for each, run `terraform import` on them, and reconcile the imported configuration with the real resources. They differ only in how the resources are selected. This guide covers both.

## Prerequisites

- The `devops` operation role to select either mode in the web application; below `devops` both are shown disabled with the hint "Requires the devops operation role." The API itself, `POST /api/v1/iac/import`, requires only `developer`, plus ownership when it continues an existing session. See [Roles and permissions](../../reference/roles-and-permissions/) for the complete role matrix.
- A repository URL and, the first time, the root module’s scopes, as covered in [Make a request](../make-a-request/). The scopes are what discovery lists: the subscription of an `azurerm` provider, the project of a `google` provider and the account of an `aws` provider, all of them when the module uses several. `oci`, `kubernetes` and `vsphere` have no scope listing, so an import round on a module that uses none of the three finds nothing to import (see [Limitations](#limitations)).
- The IaC sidecar’s credentials must be able to read the cloud inventory for the scope: Azure Resource Graph, GCP Cloud Asset Inventory, or an AWS Resource Explorer aggregator index. See [Terraform providers](../../reference/terraform-providers/).

## Partial import

**Use case.** Some resources were created by hand, or by another tool, and you want only some of them managed from the repository: "import the key vault and its private endpoint".

**Required inputs.** Repository URL and a **non-empty** request naming what to import. The API rejects a partial import with an empty text.

**Workflow.**

1. **Filtering.** The request filter runs in import mode and declines requests that are not about importing. A declined request ends the round `uncompleted` with the filter’s rationale.
2. **Prompt composition**, as in generate.
3. **Discovery.** The core lists what the Terraform state tracks (`/v1/import/state-resource-ids`) and what each listable scope of the root module holds (`/v1/import/scope-resource-ids`, once per scope), and keeps the resource IDs the state does not track, merged across scopes. A scope that cannot be listed is reported without hiding the others. Azure IDs are compared case-insensitively; every other provider compares them exactly. The IaC sidecar already leaves out resources another control plane owns, such as AKS-managed resource groups or GKE nodes.
4. **Import exception list.** IDs on the `<provider>/guidelines/import_exceptions` lists of the module’s providers are withheld from the rest of the round, whatever the request says. See [Import exception list](../customize-prompts/#import-exception-list).
5. **Selection.** The `import_filter` agent narrows the remaining unmanaged IDs to the ones your request names.
6. **Generate, validate and import loop**, up to `orchestration.max_import_iteration` attempts (5 by default). Each attempt: 1. generates or corrects the resource blocks for the selected IDs, without modifying configuration that was already there, and commits and pushes them to the session branch; 2. runs `init`, `validate` and `plan` on the session’s targets; 3. has an agent read the branch diff and pair each generated block’s Terraform address with its listed cloud resource ID, then build the import ID in the format the "Import" section of the provider’s documentation gives for that resource type and provider version (the full ID, a name, a short ID or a composite, depending on the type), read once per resource type from the Terraform Registry with `terraform_docs`, falling back to `web_search` when the registry cannot answer; 4. runs `terraform import` for each pair, one address at a time, through the IaC sidecar’s `/v1/import`. If the plan fails, its error is fed back to the generator as the next attempt’s request. If any import is rejected, the generator is given every rejected address with the engine’s error, plus the addresses already imported, which it must leave unchanged. The next attempt corrects the blocks and retries only the resources that are still not imported; resources imported by an earlier attempt stay in the state. A failed plan and a rejected import each count as one attempt.
7. **Convergence.** When at least one resource was imported, the round runs the drift loop of [Remediate drift](../remediate-drift/) over the plan’s targets, up to `orchestration.max_drift_reports` iterations, so the generated configuration matches what was imported. Its final plan is what the report judges state alignment from.
8. **Report.** An `import` JSON report: the selected, imported and failed counts, an outcome, an execution summary, one entry per resource with its address, ID, status and error, the resources the exception list withheld, the state alignment, and recommendations. The outcome is `Succeeded` when every selected resource was imported, `Partial` when some failed, and `Failed` when none was imported. Withheld resources are not failures and do not lower the outcome.

**When there is nothing to import.** The round still completes with an `import` report that says why: the scope could not be listed (with the IaC sidecar’s diagnostics), the scope holds no importable resource, every resource in it is already managed, every unmanaged resource is on the import exception list, or no unmanaged resource matched the request.

**When the attempts run out.** If the last attempt’s plan passed, the round goes on with what did import: convergence runs for the imported resources, and the report lists the ones that still failed, with the engine’s error for each, and reports `Partial` or `Failed`. If the last plan itself failed, the round fails and the session ends `failed`.

**Inspects existing IaC and state.** Yes: the state inventory, the cloud scope inventory, and the configuration the plan runs on.

**Targets.** Generated from the session’s changes, so the plan covers the imported resources.

**Artifacts and reports.** Plans per attempt, code-change files, drift reports from convergence, an `import` JSON report, a pushed branch.

**State.** Changed **during the round**. `terraform import` writes to the state as soon as each import succeeds, before any pull request exists; a resource imported in a round stays in the state even if the round later fails.

**Plan pinned, apply, pull requests, compliance, locks.** No plan is pinned and no apply follows. You can create a pull request from the branch; in the web application the merge button is labeled for merging only, and merging ends the session with "Pull Request merged. The imported resources are now managed from your repository." Import rounds run no compliance check and never set the lock.

**Example.** "Import the storage account `stappdev001` and the key vault `kv-app-dev`." Kumoss finds both among the unmanaged resources in the subscription, writes an `azurerm_storage_account` and an `azurerm_key_vault` block, and imports them. The storage account imports; the key vault is rejected because its import ID was built in a form the provider does not parse. The engine’s error goes back to the generator, which leaves the storage account’s block untouched, the address agent rebuilds the key vault’s import ID from its listed ID, and the next attempt imports only the key vault. The report shows both resources imported and `Succeeded`.

## Full import

**Use case.** Adopt everything in a scope that Terraform does not yet manage, for example when bringing an existing subscription into a repository.

**Required inputs.** Repository URL. The web application asks for no request text and sends the fixed request "Import all the infrastructure".

**Workflow.** Identical to [partial import](#partial-import) except that the request filter and the `import_filter` selection are skipped: every unmanaged resource in the scope that is not on the import exception list is selected.

**Inspects existing IaC and state, targets, artifacts, state, apply, compliance, locks.** As for partial import.

**Example.** "Import all the infrastructure" on a GCP project with a bucket, a service account and one IAM binding that Terraform does not track. Kumoss selects all three, generates the blocks, imports them, and reports `Succeeded`.

## Limitations

- Scope discovery exists only for `azurerm`, `google` and `aws` scopes. A root module that uses none of them (only `oci`, `kubernetes`, `vsphere`…​) has nothing to list, and the round ends with a report that says so and imports nothing. In a module that mixes providers, only the resources of its listable scopes are found.
- The import exception list is matched against the exact IDs the scope listing returns (case-insensitively on Azure), so an entry must be spelled the way discovery spells it.
- Imports are bounded by `orchestration.max_import_iteration`. Resources still rejected when the attempts run out stay out of the state; their resource blocks stay on the branch, so review them before merging.
- A resource the address agent cannot pair with a generated block is not imported and is not fed back to the generator.
- Import rounds run no compliance check, show no impact banner, and pin no plan.

## Next steps

- [Merge and apply](../merge-and-apply/) to open and merge the pull request; an import session ends there.
- [Import exception list](../customize-prompts/#import-exception-list) to keep resources out of every import round.

# Compliance policy

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/reference/compliance-policy/

The compliance policies are the deterministic part of Kumoss’s compliance check: [Rego](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/policy-language) modules that [Open Policy Agent](https://www.openpolicyagent.org) (OPA) evaluates against the plan of every generate round. No language model is involved, so the same plan always gets the same verdict. A `deny` finding locks the session.

Two kinds of policy run together:

| Prompt | Package | Evaluated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `general/policies/compliance` | `kumoss.compliance` | On every generate round. It must exist. |
| `<provider>/policies/compliance` | `kumoss.providers.<provider>` | On the rounds whose root module declares that provider. A provider without one is skipped. |

`<provider>` is the Terraform provider type name, as in the other provider prompts: `aws`, `azurerm`, `google`, `kubernetes`, `oci`, `vsphere`. A type name containing `-` is not a valid Rego identifier, so its package uses the bracket form, for example `package kumoss.providers["google-beta"]`. Every policy gets the same [input](#input) and returns the same [decision](#decision).

This page is the contract a policy follows. To add a rule step by step, see [Write a policy rule](../../guides/write-a-policy-rule/). For how the policies relate to the other checks that can lock a session, see [How compliance works](../../architecture/compliance/).

## How the policies run

At the end of every generate round, when `orchestration.enable_compliance_checker` is `true`:

1. The core fetches the general policy and the policy of every provider the root module declares in `required_providers` (the session’s providers), each from the version that carries your environment’s label in Langfuse. A provider whose policy prompt does not exist, or has no version with that label, is left out: a module declaring `random` gets no `random` policy, and no error. Nothing is cached, so a label moved in Langfuse applies to the next round.
2. It builds the [input document](#input) from the round’s final plan and the root module’s providers, and runs all the fetched policies in one `opa` process (OPA 1.22.4, shipped in the core image) that queries `data.kumoss`, so the general package and every provider package are read from a single result: ``` opa eval --stdin-input --strict-builtin-errors --format json \ --data general.rego --data aws.rego ... data.kumoss ```
3. It reads each policy’s [decision](#decision): blocking `deny` findings, non-blocking `warn` findings, and the list of rules checked.
4. The intent check, the language-model half, runs next, and both results are merged into one compliance report for the round; see [How findings appear in the report](#report).
5. If either part has an `error` or `critical` finding, the session is locked and the compliance failure notification is sent.

Errors name the prompt and the line they come from, for example `aws/policies/compliance:12: …​`.

Every policy sees the whole plan, not only its provider’s resources: a module may use several providers. A provider policy’s rules therefore match on their own resource `type`s.

Drift and import rounds are never checked.

## Where the policies live

Each policy is a Langfuse text prompt, seeded from `core/prompts/seed/<scope>/policies/compliance.rego`: the general policy from `general/`, and one policy each for `aws`, `azurerm`, `google`, `kubernetes`, `oci`, and `vsphere`. To give another provider a policy, create its `<provider>/policies/compliance` prompt in Langfuse. The core uses the raw text of the version: Langfuse’s `{{variable}}` templating is not applied, so the braces of Rego are safe. A version you customized is never overwritten by a Kumoss upgrade. How versions, labels, and seeding work is in [How seeding works](../prompt-registry/#how-seeding-works).

## Input

The document every policy receives as `input`:

```
{
  "plan": { ... },
  "kumoss": {
    "schema": "kumoss.compliance.input/v1",
    "providers": ["azurerm", "kubernetes"]
  }
}
```

| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `input.plan` | The final plan’s `terraform show -json` or `tofu show -json` document, unchanged. Rules usually walk `input.plan.resource_changes`. |
| `input.kumoss.schema` | `kumoss.compliance.input/v1`. Changes if the shape of `input` ever does. |
| `input.kumoss.providers` | The provider type names of the root module’s `required_providers` (`azurerm` for `hashicorp/azurerm`): the providers whose policies are evaluated. The general policy can use it to scope a rule to the providers a module actually uses; see [Root module manifest](../root-module-manifest/). |

Three properties of the plan limit what a rule can check:

- It is a `-target` plan: it holds the session’s targets only, so a rule cannot see resources outside them.
- Values known only after apply are absent from `after` and listed in `after_unknown`.
- It carries sensitive values unmasked. Never put a value that can hold a secret (passwords, keys, tokens, connection strings, user data, policy or script bodies) in a finding’s `message`, which ends up in the compliance report, the session’s artifacts, and the notification; name the resource address and the attribute instead. Addresses, CIDR blocks, ports, protocols, and paths, which the shipped rules quote, are fine.

## Decision

Each policy’s package, `data.kumoss.compliance` or `data.kumoss.providers.<provider>`, is read with the same contract, so the general module must declare `package kumoss.compliance` and a provider’s `package kumoss.providers.<provider>`. All keys are optional; a missing one counts as empty, and keys outside these three are ignored.

| Key | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `deny` | set of `{rule_id, message, resource?, severity?}` | Blocking findings. `severity` is `error` (the default) or `critical`. |
| `warn` | set of `{rule_id, message, resource?}` | Non-blocking findings, reported with severity `warning`. |
| `rules` | set of strings | Every rule id the policy evaluates, so the report lists the rules that passed too. Rule ids of findings are added to it anyway. |

`rule_id` and `message` are non-empty strings; `resource`, when present, is a string, usually the resource address.

## How findings appear in the report

The policies' decisions and the intent check’s findings are merged into one compliance report per round; only this merge produces the verdict:

- Each policy violation carries `source: "opa"`; findings of the intent check carry `"intent"`. Reports stored with the former value `"llm"`, or before the policy existed with no `source`, load as intent findings. The web application marks policy findings with a **policy** badge and intent check findings with an **intent** badge, in the **Compliance Check** artifact and in the **Why** list of the **Deployment Blocked** screen.
- The policies' findings come first.
- `policy_revisions` lists the versions that ran, each as `"<prompt name>@<version>"`, the general policy first, for example `["general/policies/compliance@3", "aws/policies/compliance@1"]`, or is empty when no policy ran. Reports stored when there was only the general policy carry a single `policy_revision` string; they are read into the list.
- `passed` is `false` when either source has an `error` or `critical` finding, and the session is then locked as for any failed compliance check. When the policies are what blocks, the summary starts with `Blocked by the compliance policy: N finding(s) (<rule ids>).`

## When a policy cannot be evaluated

The policies fail closed. If one cannot be evaluated, the round gets a blocking `policy_unavailable` finding (severity `error`) whose message gives the reason, so the session is locked and the compliance failure notification is sent. The intent check still runs, and its findings are in the same report.

Since all the policies run in one evaluation, one broken provider policy blocks every round of a module that declares that provider, and a broken general policy blocks every round.

### Problems in a policy

Fix these in a new version of the policy:

- A syntax or compile error in any of the policies.
- A fetched policy does not define its package (`package kumoss.compliance` for the general policy, `package kumoss.providers.<provider>` for a provider’s), or the package is not an object.
- `deny`, `warn`, or `rules` is not a set; a finding is not an object or lacks `rule_id` or `message`; or a `deny` severity is neither `error` nor `critical`.
- A builtin error. The policies run with `--strict-builtin-errors`, so `to_number("x")` fails rather than being undefined.
- The evaluation did not finish within 30 seconds.

### Problems around the policy

These need your operator:

- A policy could not be fetched from Langfuse: Langfuse is unreachable, the version carrying the environment label is not a single text prompt, or, for the general policy only, the prompt or such a version does not exist.
- The plan JSON could not be read.
- `opa` could not be run.

### Startup check

When `enable_compliance_checker` is `true`, the core, after seeding the prompts, evaluates the general policy and the policy of every provider that ships a seed (`aws`, `azurerm`, `google`, `kubernetes`, `oci`, `vsphere`) against an empty plan, and refuses to start if that fails: a missing `opa` binary, a broken policy, or Langfuse unreachable. A provider policy missing from Langfuse is skipped there too. A broken version that gets the environment label while the core is running is caught only when it is evaluated, and then blocks every round it applies to.

## The shipped rules

### General policy

The general seed defines five rules that apply whatever the provider. `critical_deletion` looks at every managed resource and `provider_version_pin` at the root module’s provider configuration; the other three look only at what the plan creates or updates (a replacement included), so a resource the round leaves alone is not judged.

| Rule id | Decision | Finds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `critical_deletion` | `deny`, `critical` | A managed resource whose plan actions are exactly `["delete"]`, even when the user requested the deletion. A replacement (`["delete", "create"]` or `["create", "delete"]`), a `forget` (a `removed` block with `destroy = false`) and data sources are allowed. |
| `customer_managed_key_removed` | `deny`, `error` | A resource the plan updates or replaces that loses its customer-managed encryption key: an attribute named `kms_key_id`, `kms_key_arn`, `kms_master_key_id`, `kms_key_name`, `kms_key_self_link`, `default_kms_key_name`, `customer_managed_key`, `disk_encryption_set_id` or `key_vault_key_id`, at any nesting depth, is set before the change and empty or absent after it. Switching to another key is allowed, and a key whose new value is only known at apply time is not judged. |
| `command_execution` | `deny`, `error` | Terraform running commands: a `null_resource`, or a provisioner of any kind (`local-exec`, `remote-exec`, `file`) on a resource the plan creates or updates, child modules included; and any `data "external"` data source anywhere in the configuration, changed or not, since it runs its program on every plan. A resource with a provisioner that the round leaves untouched is not flagged. |
| `unprotected_credential_output` | `warn` | A root module output the plan creates or updates whose name contains, case-insensitively, `password`, `passwd`, `secret`, `token`, `private_key`, `api_key`, `access_key`, `credential` or `connection_string`, and that is not marked `sensitive = true`. The name is only a hint, hence a warning; the message carries the output’s name, never its value. |
| `provider_version_pin` | `warn` | A root module provider (an entry of the plan’s `configuration.provider_config` without `module_address`; the built-in `terraform.io/builtin/*` providers are skipped) with no version constraint, or one that is not of the form `~> X.Y`: an exact pin such as `= 4.63.0` (which the plan shows as `4.63.0`), an open range such as `>= 5.0`, or `~> 6.1.0`. The finding has no `resource`; the message carries the provider’s full name. A warning, since an existing pin is never changed as a side effect and a workspace may keep one on purpose; child modules pin for themselves. |

`critical_deletion`, the rule a custom policy most often starts from:

```
package kumoss.compliance

rules contains "critical_deletion"

deny contains finding if {
	some change in input.plan.resource_changes
	change.mode == "managed"
	change.change.actions == ["delete"]
	finding := {
		"rule_id": "critical_deletion",
		"severity": "critical",
		"resource": change.address,
		"message": sprintf(
			"%s is destroyed without being recreated; standalone deletions are never allowed, even when requested.",
			[change.address],
		),
	}
}
```

The seed declares its five ids in one `rules contains rule if some rule in {…​}` statement; the excerpt above declares only its own. The code is explained line by line in [How a rule works](../../guides/write-a-policy-rule/#how-a-rule-works).

`data "external"` runs its program while the plan is made, so by the time `command_execution` locks the round the program has already run in the IaC sidecar; the rule keeps the code from being applied and merged. Provisioners and `null_resource` commands run at apply and are stopped before they run.

Some safeguards of the former prompts are not in the general policy. Removing `lifecycle.prevent_destroy` cannot be detected: the plan JSON does not contain `lifecycle` blocks. Turning off deletion protection and replacing a stateful resource are visible in the plan, but the prompts allowed them on an explicit request, so they were not translated (see below).

### Provider policies

No prompt lists forbidden actions any more. The provider seeds translate the most critical rules of the removed `forbidden_actions` prompts that can be decided from the plan alone. Each has three rules, all `deny` with the default severity `error`, with ids prefixed by the provider (`k8s_` for Kubernetes). They check only resources the plan creates or updates, and only values known at plan time; `vsphere_unverified_ssl` reads the plan’s provider configuration instead.

Provider
Rule id
Denies

`aws`

`aws_public_ingress`

Security group ingress (inline, `aws_security_group_rule` or `aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule`) from `0.0.0.0/0` or `::/0` on anything but TCP 80 or 443. ICMP is exempt.

`aws_iam_wildcard_admin`

An IAM policy statement allowing `Action` "" on `Resource` `""`,
including the inline policies of a role.

`aws_s3_public_access`

A `public-read` or `public-read-write` bucket ACL, or any S3 Block Public Access flag set to `false`, at bucket or account level.

`azurerm`

`azurerm_public_inbound`

A network security group inbound `Allow` rule from `*`, `Internet`, `0.0.0.0/0` or `::/0` on anything but TCP 80 or 443. ICMP is exempt.

`azurerm_subscription_owner`

Owner or Contributor assigned at subscription, management group or root scope.

`azurerm_host_command`

The CustomScript extension on a virtual machine or scale set, or an `azurerm_virtual_machine_run_command`.

`google`

`google_public_ingress`

An ingress firewall rule or firewall policy rule from `0.0.0.0/0` or `::/0` on anything but TCP 80 or 443; a rule without ports opens every port. ICMP is exempt.

`google_sa_key`

A `google_service_account_key`.

`google_basic_role_to_sa`

`roles/owner`, `roles/editor` or `roles/viewer` granted to a
`serviceAccount:` member through any google_*iam_member or
`google*_iam_binding`.

`kubernetes`

`k8s_privilege_escalation`

`allow_privilege_escalation = true` in any security context.

`k8s_runtime_socket`

A `hostPath` volume on the container runtime socket or a directory exposing it: `/`, `/run`, `/var/run`, and the Docker, containerd and CRI-O sockets and directories.

`k8s_cluster_admin_sa`

`cluster-admin` bound to a ServiceAccount.

`oci`

`oci_public_ingress`

Ingress from `0.0.0.0/0` or `::/0` on anything but TCP 80 or 443, in a security list (`oci_core_security_list`), a VCN’s default security list (`oci_core_default_security_list`) or a network security group rule. ICMP is exempt.

`oci_bastion_open`

A bastion whose `client_cidr_block_allow_list` contains `0.0.0.0/0` or `::/0`.

`oci_any_user_no_condition`

An `Allow any-user` policy statement without a `request.principal` condition.

`vsphere`

`vsphere_host_management`

Host-level resources: `vsphere_host*`, `vsphere_vnic`, `vsphere_license`.

`vsphere_unverified_ssl`

A `vsphere` provider block with `allow_unverified_ssl = true` written as a literal.

`vsphere_snapshot`

A `vsphere_virtual_machine_snapshot`.

Rules of the removed prompts that allowed an exception on an explicit user request were not translated: a policy sees the plan, not the request. Write such rules as `warn` rules, so a reviewer sees them without the session being locked, or leave them to review.

## Write your own rules

Further prohibitions (no public storage, no owner role assignments, allowed regions, mandatory tags…​) are written as rules in the policy of the provider they concern, or in the general policy when they span providers, each adding its id to `rules`. To give a provider without a seed a policy, create its `<provider>/policies/compliance` prompt in Langfuse with `package kumoss.providers.<provider>`. See [Write a policy rule](../../guides/write-a-policy-rule/).

## Testing commands

All commands use the OPA image at the version the core ships. With OPA 1.22.4 installed locally, run `opa` with the same arguments instead.

Run the shipped rules' tests, from the `core` directory (the shell expands the glob, so run it there):

```
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/core:ro" -w /core \
  openpolicyagent/opa:1.22.4-static \
  test prompts/seed/*/policies tests/policies
```

The tests are in `core/tests/policies`, one `<scope>_test.rego` per policy. The general policy’s fixtures are real Terraform 1.16 and OpenTofu 1.13 plans, `fixtures/<engine>/data.json`, and a Terraform plan exercising its command and output rules, `fixtures/general/data.json`; the AWS, Google, and Kubernetes rules are tested against real `terraform plan` output, `fixtures/<provider>/data.json`. `opa test` loads each as `data.fixtures.<directory>`.

Check that policies compile, from the folder that holds them, passing the general policy together with the provider policies a round would run:

```
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/w:ro" -w /w \
  openpolicyagent/opa:1.22.4-static check general.rego aws.rego
```

Evaluate the policies against an input document, as the core does:

```
docker run --rm -i -v "$PWD:/w:ro" -w /w openpolicyagent/opa:1.22.4-static \
  eval --stdin-input --strict-builtin-errors --format pretty \
  -d general.rego -d aws.rego data.kumoss < input.json
```

How to build `input.json` from a plan is shown in [Write a policy rule](../../guides/write-a-policy-rule/#steps).

- [Write a policy rule](../../guides/write-a-policy-rule/) to add a rule, test it, and publish it.
- [Prompt registry](../prompt-registry/) for how the policies are seeded, versioned, and labeled in Langfuse.
- [Resolve a locked session](../../guides/resolve-a-locked-session/) for what users see when a policy denies a plan.

# Configure state backends

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/guides/configure-state-backends/

Kumoss’s workspaces are **ephemeral by design**: every call clones the repository into a fresh directory on the shared `workspaces` volume and deletes it afterwards. A local `terraform.tfstate` dies with that directory, and the next session plans against empty state, proposing to create infrastructure that already exists. Every project therefore needs a **remote backend**, and this page helps you decide who provides it.

The seeded `.gitignore` excludes .tfstate, `.tfstate.*`, and
`*_override.tf`, so state and the generated backend file never reach a
commit or a pull request.

## Choose a model

Exactly one party decides where state goes. Answer these questions in order and stop at the first **yes**:

1. **Does every repository already declare a backend that must keep working** (shared with CI or with engineers' laptops)? Use [Repository-declared backend](../state-backends/repository-declared/).
2. **Must one central backend, defined by the platform team, serve every repository?** Use [Sidecar-supplied backend](../state-backends/sidecar-supplied/).
3. **Otherwise**, keep the shipped default, [Kumoss-managed state](../state-backends/kumoss-managed/): the repositories need no backend block at all.

Two settings select the model, one on the core and one on the IaC sidecar:

| `storage.terraform_state_bucket` *(core `config.yaml`)* | `IAC_BACKEND_CONFIG` *(`services/iac/.env`)* | Effective model | Who decides where state goes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a bucket name *(shipped)* | unset *(shipped)* | **Kumoss-managed** | The core, from `storage.*` |
| `""` | unset | **Repository-declared** | Each repository’s own `backend` block |
| `""` | a file path | **Sidecar-supplied** | The deployment, through a mounted file |
| a bucket name | a file path | **Mixed — a misconfiguration** | Nobody fully; see [Which value wins](#precedence) |

[Kumoss-managed state](../state-backends/kumoss-managed/)

The shipped default: the core creates the bucket and writes the backend for you.

[Repository-declared backend](../state-backends/repository-declared/)

Blank the state bucket and let each repository’s own backend block own state.

[Sidecar-supplied backend](../state-backends/sidecar-supplied/)

Mount a backend configuration file on the IaC sidecar and own the decision centrally.

## Turn managed state off

Kumoss-managed state is **on as shipped**, so the two other models start by turning it off. **Only an explicit empty string does that:**

```
storage:
  terraform_state_bucket: ""    # "" or whitespace-only: managed state off
```

The other spellings do not behave the same way:

| What you write | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `terraform_state_bucket: ""` | Managed state off. |
| The key deleted | The field default `kumoss-terraform-state` applies: managed state **stays on**. |
| `terraform_state_bucket:` with nothing after it | YAML null: the core fails at boot with `storage.terraform_state_bucket / Input should be a valid string`. |

The core reads `config.yaml` only at startup, so restart it after the change (`docker compose restart core`). Outside Compose, mount the file and point `KUMOSS_CONFIG` at it, as described in [Images and configuration delivery](../production/networking-and-tls/#images-and-config-delivery).

## Which value wins

When several layers configure the backend, the engine **merges them key by key**. Highest priority first:

1. **`IAC_BACKEND_CONFIG`**: the file the sidecar passes to `init` as `-backend-config=<file>`.
2. **`backend_override.tf`**: written by the core when managed state is on.
3. **The repository’s own `terraform { backend }` block.**

A key that a higher layer does not set falls through to the next one. The backend *type* (`azurerm`, `s3`, …​) always comes from the workspace, either from the repository or from the override.

**Example.** A repository declares a backend, managed state is left on, and the sidecar also mounts a file:

```
# 3. The repository's main.tf
terraform {
  backend "azurerm" {
    storage_account_name = "acmetfstate"
    container_name       = "tfstates"
    key                  = "platform.tfstate"
  }
}

# 2. backend_override.tf, written by the core (managed state on)
terraform {
  backend "azurerm" {
    storage_account_name = "acmekumoss"
    container_name       = "kumoss-terraform-state"
    key                  = "<state_id>/terraform.tfstate"
    access_key           = "..."
  }
}

# 1. The file IAC_BACKEND_CONFIG points at
key = "central.tfstate"
```

What `init` binds:

| Key | Effective value | Taken from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | `central.tfstate` | The sidecar file |
| `storage_account_name` | `acmekumoss` | The core’s override |
| `container_name` | `kumoss-terraform-state` | The core’s override |
| `access_key` | the core’s key | The core’s override |

Two lessons follow:

- **A repository backend is ignored whenever managed state is on.** None of the repository’s values survive, and Kumoss logs no warning about it. The plan runs against whatever the managed key holds, usually nothing. Turn managed state off to keep a repository’s backend.
- **Never combine managed state with `IAC_BACKEND_CONFIG`.** The result is a backend that neither side fully describes. A file that supplies a single `key` also removes Kumoss’s per-project key, so every project shares one state object.

The order was verified empirically by running `tofu init` and `terraform init` against a local backend with the same key set in all three layers.

## Change models safely

**Switching models moves no state.** Turning managed state on does not import the state your repositories' backends hold; turning it off leaves what Kumoss stored in its bucket where those backends do not look.

`init` **always** runs with `-reconfigure` (`tofu init -no-color -input=false -reconfigure`), because `-input=false` cannot answer the *"Backend configuration changed"* prompt. As a result:

- **State already in the new backend is adopted.** Re-pointing a project at a backend that already holds its state is safe.
- **State under the previous backend is not migrated.** Kumoss never copies state between backends.
- **A project starts from empty state** after any change to its backend or its key: switching `storage.provider`, renaming `terraform_state_bucket`, or moving the root module. (Upgrading from a release that put the cloud scope in the managed state key counts too; see [Upgrade notes](../upgrade-notes/).) The next plan proposes creating resources that already exist.

Migrate before the next session runs, with the engine itself:

```
tofu state pull > project.tfstate           # against the old backend
tofu init -reconfigure -backend-config=...  # point at the new backend
tofu state push project.tfstate
```

`tofu init -migrate-state`, run by hand in an equivalent workspace, works too. Keep the pulled file as a backup, and verify with a plan that shows no changes before letting Kumoss run again.

## What Kumoss does not do

State ownership stops at "write the backend and key". Everything below is yours:

- **No state migration**, between any two backends (see above).
- **No versioning, backups, or retention.** Kumoss does not enable versioning, object lock, soft delete, or point-in-time restore, and it never deletes a state object.
- **No DynamoDB lock table.** Locking uses the S3-native lockfile or the Azure blob lease; there is nothing to provision.
- **No `gcs` backend adapter.** `storage.provider` has three members (`RUSTFS`, `S3`, `STORAGE_ACCOUNT`). For a `gcs` backend, use the repository-declared or sidecar-supplied model and let the repository’s block, or a mounted file, declare `gcs`.
- **No state encryption beyond the store’s own.** State can contain secrets; rely on encryption at rest and restrict access accordingly.
- **Import writes to state during the round.** The import modes run `terraform import` before any pull request is reviewed. See [Import infrastructure](../import-infrastructure/).

## Troubleshooting

### Find the active state

Start here whenever you are unsure which state file a project uses. The answer depends on three layers (see [Which value wins](#precedence)), so check all three, highest priority first. The commands read the **running** containers, not your local files, so they show what is actually deployed.

1. **Sidecar layer.** Check whether the IaC sidecar overrides the backend: ``` docker compose exec iac sh -c 'echo "IAC_BACKEND_CONFIG=${IAC_BACKEND_CONFIG:-<unset>}"; [ -n "$IAC_BACKEND_CONFIG" ] && cat "$IAC_BACKEND_CONFIG"' ``` ``` IAC_BACKEND_CONFIG=<unset> ``` A path that does not start with `/` is relative to each cloned workspace, so `cat` fails here even when `init` finds the file. Read that file in the repository instead.
2. **Core layer.** Check whether Kumoss-managed state is on in the image that is running: ``` docker compose exec core python -c " from src.shared.config import system_config as c s = c.storage print('managed state :', 'ON' if s.state_bucket else 'OFF') print('provider :', s.provider.name) print('bucket :', s.state_bucket or '-') print('endpoint :', s.endpoint_url) " ``` ``` managed state : ON provider : RUSTFS bucket : kumoss-terraform-state endpoint : http://object-storage:9000 ```
3. **Repository layer.** When managed state is `OFF`, read the backend block the repository commits: ``` git -C _REPOSITORY_PATH_ grep -n -A8 'backend "' ``` ``` main.tf:2: backend "azurerm" { main.tf-3- resource_group_name = "tfstate-rg" main.tf-4- storage_account_name = "acmetfstate" main.tf-5- container_name = "tfstates" main.tf-6- key = "platform.tfstate" ```

Read the results together:

| Sidecar layer | Core layer | The active state is… |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<unset>` | `ON` | `<bucket>/<state_id>/terraform.tfstate` in the store at `endpoint`. Get the `state_id` from the core log (see below). |
| `<unset>` | `OFF` | Wherever the repository’s backend block points. In the example above: container `tfstates`, blob `platform.tfstate` in account `acmetfstate`. |
| a path | `OFF` | The repository’s backend block, with every key the file sets replacing the repository’s value. |
| a path | `ON` | Mixed: a misconfiguration. Fix it before trusting any state (see [Which value wins](#precedence)). |

**Get the `state_id` under managed state.** The core logs the bucket and key each time it writes the override, before every `init`:

```
docker compose logs core | grep "Terraform state:"
```

```
Terraform state: rustfs bucket=kumoss-terraform-state key=3f9a…c41e/terraform.tfstate
```

Use this line to **find the key**, not to decide which model is active. It is written by the core, so:

- It appears **only** when managed state is on. No line does not tell you where state is, only that the repository or the sidecar decides.
- It does **not** include `IAC_BACKEND_CONFIG` overrides, which the core never sees.
- It prints no account or endpoint; those come from `storage.endpoint_url`.
- It appears only after a session has run `init` since the container was last created, and an apply logs nothing new: it reuses the workspace the plan initialized, so it writes to the same state.

**Confirm the object exists and is the one being written.** After an apply, the state object’s modification time must change:

- Azure
- AWS
- RustFS (bundled)

```
az storage blob show --auth-mode login \
  --account-name acmetfstate --container-name tfstates \
  --name platform.tfstate \
  --query "{size: properties.contentLength, modified: properties.lastModified}"
```

```
aws s3api head-object --bucket acme-team-tfstate \
  --key envs/prod/terraform.tfstate \
  --query "{size: ContentLength, modified: LastModified}"
```

```
# One-off: the backend uses path-style addressing, so the client must too.
aws configure set default.s3.addressing_style path

AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=rustfsadmin AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=rustfsadmin \
AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 \
  aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 \
  s3 ls s3://kumoss-terraform-state/ --recursive
```

### Plans against empty state

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
| --- | --- |
| The repository declares a backend, yet every plan proposes creating resources that already exist | **Managed state is on and its override replaces the repository’s backend** (see [Which value wins](#precedence)). The log line above appears. Set `storage.terraform_state_bucket: ""` and restart the core. |
| Every session plans against empty state, and nothing is ever recorded | Managed state is off, but the repository declares no backend: `init` succeeds against the *local* backend, and the state dies with the clone. Add a `terraform { backend …​ }` block, or turn managed state back on. |
| Plans propose recreating everything after a configuration change | The project’s state key or backend changed and the state was not migrated. Compare the logged `key=` with the bucket contents, then migrate (see [Change models safely](#changing-backend-configuration)). |
| Two repositories collide on one state file | An `IAC_BACKEND_CONFIG` file supplies a single `key` for every repository. Declare distinct keys per repository, or use managed state alone. |

### Boot and `init` failures

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
| --- | --- |
| Core fails at boot: `Failed to initialize object storage` | Managed state is on and the state bucket cannot be created or reached (credentials, `CreateBucket` permission, endpoint). The artifact and state buckets are checked together; verify both, or pre-create them. |
| `init` fails with a credentials or `AccessDenied` error | The **IaC sidecar** lacks credentials for the state store, or its identity has no access to it. The core’s credentials do not count. See [the two credential grants](../state-backends/repository-declared/#two-credential-grants) and [Credentials required](../state-backends/kumoss-managed/#credentials-required). |
| `init` on `azurerm` cannot find the storage account | `init` runs with `ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID` set from the root module’s `azurerm` scope. Pin `subscription_id` in the backend block when the state account lives in another subscription. |
| `init` fails with `InvalidAccessKeyId` after switching to `provider: S3` | `RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY` / `RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY` are still `rustfsadmin` in `core/.env` and were embedded in the override. Blank both and recreate the core (`docker compose up -d core`). |
| `init` fails to dial the endpoint (`connection refused`, DNS failure) | The sidecar cannot reach the state store. Put it on the same network (`bridge-network` in Compose) or allow that egress. |
| `init` fails on the backend configuration file | `IAC_BACKEND_CONFIG` is not checked at startup: the path is wrong, the file is not mounted, or uid `10001` cannot read it. The error is in the failing job’s stderr. |
| `Error acquiring the state lock` | Another run holds the lock, or a crashed run left it stale. If stale, run `tofu force-unlock LOCK_ID` in an equivalent workspace, or remove the `.tflock` object or break the blob lease. |
| Session fails with a Terraform backend error before `init` runs | The core could not write `backend_override.tf`. The `workspaces` volume must be writable by uid/gid `10001` (`chown -R 10001:10001` on a volume from a root-running stack). |

### The override file in a pull request

If a `backend_override.tf` shows up in a pull request, the workspace `.gitignore` write failed: the core logs `terraform gitignore couldn’t be created`, carries on, and `git add -A` picks the file up. Check that the `workspaces` volume is writable by uid/gid `10001`, remove the file from the branch, and re-run the round.

A repository without a `.gitignore` is not the cause: the seeded file is honored for the working tree even though it is never committed. A repository that already tracks a `.gitignore` gets Kumoss’s template appended, and that change is committed to the session branch.

# Follow a session

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/guides/follow-a-session/

After you submit a request, Kumoss takes you to the progress screen and, when the round finishes, to the results. This guide shows what each stage means, how to read the results, and how to return to a session.

## Prerequisites

- A session opened by following [Make a request](../make-a-request/).

## Watch the progress

The progress screen shows an assistant animation, a progress bar, and one short status sentence at a time, such as what is being generated or which validation error is being fixed. A round moves through these stages:

| Stage | What Kumoss is doing | Typical duration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Filtering | Reading and classifying your request. | Seconds |
| Generating | Writing or editing Terraform files and pushing them to the session branch. | Minutes |
| Validating | Running `init`, `validate`, and `plan` in the engine, and feeding any errors back to the generator. A drift check on the touched resources runs here too, which can cycle through Generating and Validating again. | Minutes; longer for large roots |
| Report | Writing the report and, when enabled, running the compliance check. | Minutes |

You can close the tab: the session continues on the server, and you can reopen it later as described in [Return to a session later](#return). To be told when a round ends, turn on browser notifications from the **Configuration** icon in the header.

> **Note**
> The number of generate-and-validate attempts is limited by
> `orchestration.max_validation_iteration`, five in the shipped
> `config.yaml`. See [Configuration](../../reference/configuration/).

## Read the results

The results screen has the chat on the left and three tabs on the right: **Plan**, **Code**, and **Report**. It opens on **Report**.

A reading order that works: the impact level first, then the **Deleted** and **Recreated** filters of the changes table, then the plan for anything you do not expect, and the cost last.

### Report tab

Kumoss’s summary of the plan, in four parts:

- **Execution Summary**: a paragraph describing the change.
- **Potential Impact**: **Low Impact**, **Medium Impact**, or **High Impact**, with a description. Choose the card for the status, the description, and detail bullets. With the default criteria, high means destructive actions, restarts, downtime, or critical networking changes; medium means configuration updates that change behavior without guaranteed downtime; low means isolated new resources or non-disruptive updates such as tags or locks. Depending on your deployment, a high impact locks the session; see [High impact](../resolve-a-locked-session/#high-impact).
- **Estimated Cost**: a monthly figure, and the derived hourly one, for resources with a fixed price. Usage-based and free resources appear in the breakdown as "Usage-based" or "Free" and are left out of the total. Treat the figure as an approximation for comparison, not as a quote.
- **Changes table**: filter by **All**, **Created**, **Updated**, **Deleted**, or **Recreated**. Each row names a resource with a short note; choose it for the description and the raw plan detail.

[![Report tab with the Execution Summary](../../_images/session-report.png)](../../_images/session-report.png)

Figure 1. The Report tab of a generate round that adds a private storage account: a medium impact, an estimated fixed cost of $7.30 a month, three created resources, and one updated subnet

Drift and import rounds produce a different report; see [Read the drift report](../remediate-drift/#drift-report) and [Import infrastructure](../import-infrastructure/).

### Plan tab

The plan text exactly as the engine produced it. This is the authoritative description of what would change: when the report and the plan disagree, the plan is right.

### Code tab

Every file the session has created or modified so far, across rounds, as diffs.

### Compliance findings

When the compliance check runs, its findings are stored as the round’s **Compliance Check** artifact in the session details: a summary, each violation with its severity, rule id, and resource, and the rules that passed. Findings from the compliance policy carry a **policy** badge, findings from the intent check an **intent** badge. When a finding locks the session, the same findings appear under **Why** on the **Deployment Blocked** screen; see [Resolve a locked session](../resolve-a-locked-session/).

## Return to a session later

You can reopen a session from three places:

- **Footer**: on the start screen, the **Sessions** panel lists your most recent sessions with date, request, and project. **View all** opens the full list.
- **User page**: the user icon in the header shows your profile, your **Session History** with **View all sessions**, and, for reviewers, the **Admin Panel**.
- **Your sessions list**: search by project, request text, or session id, and filter by type and status.

Open a row in the sessions list for the session’s details: the timeline of rounds and statuses, the artifacts (report, plan, compliance check, and changed files, viewed inline), the session id, path, providers and their scopes, and the repository and pull request links.

To continue, choose **Reload Session**. It reopens the session in the wizard, where you can create the pull request, apply, or send a follow-up request. Failed sessions cannot be reloaded.

Only you and reviewers with a panel role can see your sessions, and nobody else can act on them.

## If something goes wrong

### The request is declined or answered

You are taken to the results screen, and the filter’s explanation, or the answer to your question, is the last message in the chat. Nothing was changed and nothing was pushed for that round. To continue in the same session, type a new request in "Ask a follow-up question…​"; earlier rounds' results stay visible on the right.

### The session fails

The round is marked failed with a reason. The most common is "runner failed: Validation loop exceeded.": the engine kept rejecting the code after the last attempt. Other reasons name an engine or repository error. A failed session cannot be resumed ("This session failed and can’t be resumed"); start a new one, usually with a more specific request.

### The connection times out

After long inactivity you see "Connection timed out — no response from server". Reload the page and reopen the session from the footer.

### Your login expires

You see "Your session has expired. Please sign in again." Your Kumoss session keeps running on the server; sign in and reopen it.

## Next steps

- [Merge and apply](../merge-and-apply/) once you are ready to act on the results.
- [Resolve a locked session](../resolve-a-locked-session/) if the round locked the session.
- [Make a request](../make-a-request/) to phrase a follow-up request that the filter accepts.

# Make a request

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/guides/make-a-request/

This guide walks through opening a session in the Kumoss web application: choosing a mode, pointing Kumoss at a repository, and phrasing the request so the filter accepts it as a change.

## Prerequisites

- **An account.** Your administrator gives you access through your organization’s identity provider. On first login you have the `developer` role, which lets you generate infrastructure, open and merge pull requests, and apply your own sessions. Drift remediation needs the `devops` role; ask your administrator (see [Administer users and locks](../administer-users-and-locks/)).
- **A repository URL** that holds Terraform-compatible code and that Kumoss’s service account can clone and push to. Enter the plain `https://` URL; SSH, `file://` and other non-HTTPS URLs, and URLs with a password or token embedded, are rejected.
- **The scope of each cloud provider the root module uses**, the first time anyone works on that module: the Azure subscription ID for `azurerm`, the GCP project ID for `google`, the AWS account ID for `aws`, the OCI compartment OCID for `oci`. You do not pick a provider: Kumoss reads them from the module’s `required_providers`. Other providers (`kubernetes`, `vsphere`, `random`…​) need no scope.
- **Values for the module’s required input variables** that nothing else sets, again only the first time. See [Root module manifest](../../reference/root-module-manifest/).

Kumoss never asks you for cloud or Git credentials. It uses the identity your platform team configured.

## Steps

1. **Choose the mode** in the header drop-down. Most work uses **Generate Infrastructure**. The drift and import modes are shown grayed out with the hint "Requires the devops operation role." if you do not hold that role.
2. **"What do you need?"** Type your request (up to 500 characters) and press Enter. The rotating hints under the field show the expected level of detail, for example "Deploy a PostgreSQL database on Azure" or "Create a virtual network with three subnets".
3. **"What is the repository URL?"** Paste the repository URL, or a name your deployment’s mapping service resolves, such as a project identifier; the session keeps that name and passes it to the IaC service, which may run commands with that project’s credentials. Kumoss clones only its metadata and looks for Terraform roots among the files committed on the default branch: directories that hold `.tf` files, skipping `modules`, `examples`, and `.terraform` folders, and keeping those with a `main.tf`-style marker or a `.tfvars` file (the exact rules and examples are in [Repository layout](../../reference/repository-layout/#terraform-roots)). This is the step that takes a few seconds ("Scanning repository…​").
4. **"Which root module?"** If the repository has more than one Terraform root, pick the directory to work in. With exactly one root this step is skipped. If none is found you see "No root modules found in this repository. Please check the repository and try again." — usually because the `.tf` files are not committed on the default branch or live under a `modules` or `examples` directory. Top-level `.tf` files are offered as the path `.`.
5. **Inputs.** Kumoss checks what the root module needs ("Checking what the root module needs…​"). When it already has everything — the module was set up by an earlier session, or needs nothing — the session starts straight away. Otherwise the form "This root module needs a few values" asks only for what is missing: - **Scopes**: one field per cloud provider of the module that has no scope yet — Subscription ID, Project ID, Account ID, or Compartment OCID. - **Values**: one field per required variable nothing sets, typed after its declaration (JSON for lists and maps). Tick **Secret** to keep a value out of the repository; a variable the code declares sensitive is always a secret. - **Variable files**: the module’s optional `.tfvars` files, if it has any. Picked files apply in the order you pick them (a later file wins), and a variable a picked file sets can be left empty; a value you type wins over the files. The answers are asked once per root module. Plain values and scopes are saved in a `kumoss.yaml` file the session commits next to the module; secrets are kept by Kumoss and only their names are committed. Once the session’s pull request is merged, later sessions on the module ask nothing. If the module changes later (a new required variable, a new cloud provider), only what the change needs is asked.

The session then starts and you are taken to the progress screen.

**Errors at this stage.** The wizard shows "Could not scan repository for root modules. Please try again." when the repository cannot be scanned, whatever the underlying cause, and "Could not read the root module’s inputs. Please try again." when the inputs check fails. Both happen before the session is created. The API response’s `detail` is just as generic — "Repository is not reachable or access was denied." for a missing repository, a refused credential, an unknown host or a timeout alike — so a request cannot be used to probe what sits behind a URL; the Git client’s own text is written only to the core log, where an operator can read it. Check that the URL is reachable and that Kumoss’s service account has access.

Some failures only show once the session has started, and end it `failed` with the reason: a repository that became unreachable, a module that still needs input, or your organization’s authorization service refusing one of the module’s scopes. The authorization check runs once the module’s scopes are known, before anything is saved or committed; in a deployment that has not connected such a service, which is the shipped default, it always passes.

## Writing a request that gets accepted

Every request is first read by a filter that decides whether it is an infrastructure change Kumoss can make. The rules are set by your organization in the prompt registry; the defaults are these.

**Accepted: change requests.** Creating, modifying, or deleting cloud infrastructure managed with Terraform, and questions that resolve directly into such a change. Missing parameters never block a request: naming conventions supply names, resource templates supply settings, and the existing workspace supplies placement (resource group, region, environment). "Create a new storage account", with nothing else, is accepted, and the response states the defaults and assumptions applied.

**Answered, not executed: informational questions.** "Which resources exist in this repository?", "How could this be improved?", "What is the impact of changing X?". Kumoss answers in the chat and the round ends without changes. You can follow up with a change request in the same session.

**Declined**, with the reason shown to you:

| Reason | Example | How to fix it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Out of scope | "Restart the web server", "What’s the difference between blob and file storage?" | Ask for a Terraform-managed change, or accept that it is a question. |
| Ambiguous target | "Rename the subnet" when the workspace has five subnets | Name the resource: "rename subnet `app-subnet-01` to `app-subnet-web`". |
| Missing referent | "Add a rule to the web firewall" when no firewall exists in the workspace | Create it first, or point at the right repository or path. |

Practical rules:

- **One intent per request.** "Add a private storage account for application logs" is better than a list of six unrelated changes. Use follow-ups for the next step.
- **Name existing resources exactly** when you modify or delete them.
- **Say what matters to you, not how to write HCL.** Size, tier, region, exposure, retention, and naming intent are useful. Kumoss applies your organization’s conventions for the rest.
- **Do not paste secrets.** Request text, the files the agent reads, and the plan are sent to the configured language model and stored in the tracing system. Reference secrets by name or vault path.
- **Prefer additive changes.** A standalone deletion is always denied by the compliance policy, even when you ask for it, and locks the session, see [Resolve a locked session](../resolve-a-locked-session/).

Examples that work well: "Create a private S3 bucket named `demo-platform-logs` with versioning and default encryption for application logs." "Open port 443 from the load balancer subnet to the web security group." "Upgrade the PostgreSQL flexible server in `envs/dev` to 16."

## Next steps

- [Follow a session](../follow-a-session/) once the session starts.
