# Notifications sidecar API

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/reference/api/notifications/

The notifications service delivers an event the core wants a human to see. The contract is deliberately **channel-agnostic**: a caller never names a channel. It describes an event and identifies an audience, and the implementation decides where that lands — which Slack channel, which Teams group, which mailing list, which pager rotation.

Contract: `contracts/openapi/notifications.v1.yaml`. Default endpoint: `http://notifications:8080`. Bearer token: the value of the variable named by `services.notifications.token_env`, `KUMOSS_NOTIFICATIONS_TOKEN` by default. The service is **optional** and ships disabled (`services.notifications.enabled: false`).

## Endpoints

Two paths.

| Endpoint | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /v1/notify` | Validates a notification and queues it for delivery. Answers `202 Accepted` as soon as the request is accepted — delivery happens out of band and is not guaranteed to have finished when the call returns. |
| `GET /healthz` | Liveness probe, answers `{"status":"ok"}`. Does not check downstream connectivity, so a `200` here does not mean Slack is reachable. |

Implementations are encouraged, but not required, to be idempotent on `kind` plus `subject` plus `body` within a short window so that a caller retry does not double-post.

## Request

```
{
  "kind": "iac.terraform.apply_completed",
  "severity": "info",
  "subject": "Apply completed for session a1b2c3",
  "body": "3 added, 1 changed, 0 destroyed.",
  "audience": ["someone@example.com"],
  "links": [{"label": "Pull request", "url": "https://github.com/..."}],
  "context": {"session_id": "a1b2c3"}
}
```

`kind`, `severity`, `subject`, and `body` are required. `additionalProperties` is `false`, so an undeclared field is a `422` rather than a silently ignored one.

| Field | Limits | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kind` | 1-128 chars | Event category. Free-form by design; the convention is dotted lowercase — `iac.terraform.plan_completed`, `iac.terraform.apply_completed`, `system.error`. An implementation may route on it. |
| `severity` | enum | One of `info`, `warning`, `error`, `critical`. |
| `subject` | 1-256 chars | Single-line summary, suitable as a notification title. |
| `body` | 1-16384 chars | The message. Markdown is permitted; whether it is rendered or passed through verbatim is the implementation’s choice. |
| `audience` | ≤256 items | Implementation-specific recipient identifiers — email addresses, Slack handles, Teams group ids. An implementation that routes by other means may ignore it. |
| `links` | ≤32 items | Structured links to render. Each is `{"label": …​, "url": …​}` with `label` 1-128 characters and `url` a URI of at most 2048. |
| `context` | free-form | Arbitrary structured context. An implementation must not assume any particular shape. |

## Responses

`202 Accepted` carries the delivery identifier:

```
{"delivery_id": "3f2504e0-4f89-11d3-9a0c-0305e82c3301"}
```

It identifies the **delivery attempt**, not a durable record the caller can later query: the contract has no endpoint that takes it back. Its value is correlating a core log line with the sidecar’s own.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | The body could not be parsed at the transport layer — malformed JSON, non-UTF-8 bytes, no `Content-Type`. May be a problem document or a framework-default body. |
| `401` | Missing or invalid bearer token. Carries a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` challenge. |
| `403` | The token is valid but not authorized for this endpoint. |
| `422` | Well-formed JSON that failed schema validation. |
| `502` | The downstream channel returned an error or could not be reached. |
| `503` | The service is running but not configured — no webhook URL, for example. |

## How the core uses it

The core never exposes this contract directly. Its own `POST /api/v1/notifications` route takes the same event description **minus** `audience`, and derives the recipient list server-side from the caller’s identity before forwarding. A client therefore cannot address a notification to somebody else. See [Core API](../core/).

The core also fires notifications of its own accord — an apply failure, for instance, is reported this way rather than raised. When the service is disabled the core’s route answers `503`; when a forward fails it answers `502`.

## The bundled implementation

`services/notifications/` posts to a single Slack channel through an incoming webhook. It exists to be useful out of the box and to be a readable worked example for anyone writing a Teams, email, or PagerDuty implementation of the same contract.

A notification becomes a Slack attachment, color-coded by severity, with an action button per link. Two limits shape the rendering, one Slack’s and one the service’s own:

- Slack allows five buttons per attachment, so links past the fifth continue in follow-up attachments.
- The service caps field values at 1000 characters, well under Slack’s own per-field limit, so one oversized value cannot push the rest of the card out of view. A context value over the cap is truncated and ends with an ellipsis; an audience list over it is cut at a recipient boundary and ends with `+N more`.

The bearer token is compared in constant time. If `KUMOSS_NOTIFICATIONS_TOKEN` is blank the service accepts every request — acceptable on an isolated workstation, not on a shared network.

A non-2xx answer from Slack, or an unreachable Slack, becomes `502` with an RFC 7807 body whose title is `Downstream channel error` and which carries **no** detail. That is deliberate: the webhook URL is the Slack credential, and the HTTP client embeds it in every error message, so echoing the underlying error would leak it into the core’s logs.

### Responses it never produces

The contract documents `400`, `403`, and `503`; this implementation emits none of them. Request validation runs before the handler, so a bad body is a `422` rather than a `400`. It has no authorization concept beyond the bearer token, so there is nothing to answer `403` with. And `503` is unreachable because the process refuses to boot without a webhook URL. Another implementation of the same contract may use all three, so a caller must still handle them.

### Configuration

| Variable | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` | yes | Slack incoming-webhook URL. The service refuses to start without it. |
| `KUMOSS_NOTIFICATIONS_TOKEN` | no | Bearer token clients must present. Blank accepts every request. |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | no | Root log level, default `INFO`. |

Configuration is asserted at startup: a missing webhook URL or an unknown log level raises a configuration error and the process exits, so a deployment that could not deliver anything fails at boot rather than on the first notification. Under `docker compose` that shows up as the `notifications` container exiting until `services/notifications/.env` sets the URL. The core treats its notifications as best-effort and keeps working.

### Troubleshooting

The service reports a problem in one place only — the `application/problem+json` response to the caller. It writes no log lines of its own, so `docker compose logs -f notifications` shows just the server’s access and error output. It does not trace deliveries.

- **The container exits at boot with a configuration error.** Set `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL`, and a valid `LOG_LEVEL`, in `services/notifications/.env`.
- **The core gets `401`.** `KUMOSS_NOTIFICATIONS_TOKEN` differs between `core/.env` and `services/notifications/.env`.
- **`502 Downstream channel error`.** Slack rejected the payload or was unreachable. Check the webhook URL is still valid in Slack.
- **Nothing arrives and the core logs `Failed to send '<kind>' notification`.** Check the `services.notifications` block in `config.yaml`, and that the core was restarted after the change — the file is read only at startup.

## Conformance

The implementation-agnostic Schemathesis suite at `contracts/conformance/notifications/` runs against any implementation of this contract:

```
cd contracts/conformance/notifications
uv sync
uv run pytest \
  --service-url=https://notifications.your.example \
  --service-token=$YOUR_TOKEN
```

`--service-token` is needed only if the implementation enforces authentication.

The suite generates requests from the OpenAPI document and checks that response bodies match the declared schemas and that invalid bodies do not produce undocumented `5xx` answers. It cannot check that a notification actually reached a human, so a green run on an implementation with a stale webhook URL is still possible.

## Next steps

- [Core API](../core/) for the core route that wraps this one.
- [the `services` section](../../configuration/#config-services) of the configuration reference for enabling the sidecar.
- [Deploy to production](../../../guides/deploy-to-production/) for the decision of whether to run the bundled implementation at all.

# Customize prompts

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/guides/customize-prompts/

Kumoss does not hard-code cloud knowledge. Its agents read your organization’s standards (naming, tagging, networking, permissions, intent rules, compliance policies, and exceptions) from **prompts** stored in [Langfuse](https://langfuse.com/docs/prompt-management). This guide shows what each prompt controls and how to change it. How the registry works underneath, including seeding and the shipped inventory, is in [Prompt registry](../../reference/prompt-registry/).

## Prerequisites

- Access to your deployment’s Langfuse with a role that can edit prompts; see [Monitor with Langfuse](../monitor-with-langfuse/) for where it runs and how to log in.
- Your deployment’s `environment` value (`development` by default). The core reads every prompt from the version carrying that label; see [Configuration](../../reference/configuration/).

## What you can customize

Every prompt is named `<scope>/<type>/<name>`, where the scope is `general` or a Terraform provider type such as `azurerm`. Provider prompts apply only to sessions whose root module uses that provider. For which agent reads each prompt, see [Which agent reads which prompt](../../reference/prompt-registry/#prompt-composition).

### General guidelines

| Prompt | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| `general/guidelines/terraform` | Organization-wide Terraform standards: structure, providers, state, and style. Followed by the code generator; no check reads it. Do not write into it bans a compliance policy enforces; see [Change a compliance policy](#compliance-policy). |
| `general/guidelines/requests` | Which requests the request filter accepts, declines, or answers. |
| `general/guidelines/targeting_policies` | Resources a partial drift round must never plan. Ships as a placeholder with no exclusions. |

### Provider guidelines

One set per provider, at `<provider>/guidelines/<name>`:

| Prompt | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| `resource_creation` | General conventions for creating resources: tags, naming, and defaults. Followed by the generator. |
| `networking` | Networking conventions: address plans, exposure rules, and private endpoints. Followed by the generator. |
| `permissions` | Identity and access conventions: least privilege and role assignment patterns. Followed by the generator. |
| `abbreviations` | Short prefixes for resource names. |
| `resources_list` | The catalog of resource prompts the session may use; see [Add a resource prompt](#add-a-resource-prompt). |
| `drift_exceptions` | What drift remediation must never touch; see [Write drift exception rules](#drift-exception-rules). |
| `import_exceptions` | Resource IDs an import must never bring under Terraform; see [Write the import exception list](#import-exception-list). |

### Resource prompts

`<provider>/resources/<name>` holds the default configuration of one resource type, such as `aws/resources/s3_bucket` or `azurerm/resources/storage_account`, used unless the request asks for something else. A session uses only the resource prompts its request needs, chosen from `resources_list`.

### Compliance prompts

| Prompt | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| `general/intent/rules` | The rules the intent check judges a plan against, each with a rule id and a severity: only whether the plan does what the session’s requests ask. Ships with `scope_exceeded` and `scope_incomplete`, both `error`. An `error` or `critical` finding locks the session. Its prompt type is `intent`. |
| `general/compliance/impact` | What counts as a low, medium, or high impact change. A high impact locks the session when `orchestration.block_on_high_impact` is `true`. |
| `general/policies/compliance` | The general deterministic compliance policy, in Rego, evaluated on every generate round; see [Change a compliance policy](#compliance-policy). |
| `<provider>/policies/compliance` | A provider’s compliance policy, in Rego, evaluated with the general policy when the root module declares that provider; see [Change a compliance policy](#compliance-policy). |

For how these checks decide whether a session is locked, see [How compliance works](../../architecture/compliance/); for what each one looks for, see [Why a session is locked](../resolve-a-locked-session/#why).

## Change a prompt

1. In Langfuse, go to **Prompts** and open the prompt, for example `azurerm/guidelines/resource_creation`.
2. Create a new version with your edited text. When Langfuse offers to set labels, leave your production environment’s label unticked.
3. Try the version on a deployment whose `environment` is `development` or `staging`: set that environment’s label on the new version and run a session that exercises the change.
4. Move your environment’s label to the new version. The next session uses it; no restart is needed.

To roll back, move the label back to the previous version. Keep earlier versions for that reason.

> **Warning**
> Never move or remove the `seed` label. It marks the version the
> seeder last pushed; without it, the next startup treats your latest
> version as its own. See
> [How seeding works](../../reference/prompt-registry/#how-seeding-works).

### Verify

Run a session that touches the change, and check that the generated code, the report, or the compliance findings follow it. If they do not, check that the label sits on the version you edited.

### What happens on upgrades

A Kumoss release that changes a shipped prompt only moves the environment labels that are still on the shipped version. Once you move a label to your own version, upgrades leave it there, and merging later shipped changes into your version is up to you.

## Add a resource prompt

A resource prompt is only used if `resources_list` names it. Add both in Langfuse:

1. Create a **text** prompt named `<provider>/resources/<name>`, for example `aws/resources/cloudfront_distribution`, with the default configuration as its body. Set your environment’s label on it.
2. Open `<provider>/guidelines/resources_list`, create a new version with one more line, and set your environment’s label on it: ``` - `cloudfront_distribution` — CloudFront distribution with HTTPS only and an origin access control. ``` The name must equal the `<name>` part of the prompt exactly. Follow the style of the existing lines; the Kubernetes list uses plain bullets without backticks.
3. Run a session that asks for the new resource.

Both prompts must exist: a resource prompt missing from `resources_list` is never selected, and a `resources_list` entry without a prompt contributes nothing.

### Ship it with the image instead

To make the prompt part of every new deployment, add it as seed files:

1. Create `core/prompts/seed/<provider>/resources/<name>.yaml` with `description` and `body`; see [Seed file conventions](../../reference/prompt-registry/#seed-files).
2. Add the `<name>` entry to `core/prompts/seed/<provider>/guidelines/resources_list.yaml`.
3. Rebuild the core image (`docker compose build core`) and start the stack. The seeder creates the new prompt, labeled with every environment.

## Write drift exception rules

`<provider>/guidelines/drift_exceptions` is the list of things drift remediation must never touch. A dedicated **drift exception filter** reads it on every drift round, full or partial, and on the drift pre-check inside every generate round, so a generate round cannot "fix" an excluded resource either. The filter receives the drift operations that remain after the session’s own changes are removed, and returns the ones no rule covers; only those are remediated.

Whatever it removes is reported in the drift report under **Left Alone by Exception Rules**, naming the change and the rule that covers it. Leaving an excluded change alone is the intended result, so it does not lower the report’s outcome. See [Read the drift report](../remediate-drift/#drift-report).

This is not the same as `general/guidelines/targeting_policies`, which decides which resources a **partial** drift round plans at all. Exception rules apply to the operations of every drift round, whatever produced them.

### How to write one

The body is prose, read by a model. Keep each exception on its own bullet, and name the resource address, type, attribute, tag, namespace, or naming pattern precisely enough to match a sentence like "In `main.tf`, for `azurerm_key_vault.kvt_001`: update the tag `owner` from `platform` to `payments`." Say what must not be reconciled, and why: the reason is what the report quotes back.

The shipped seed has three sections, the rule kinds the filter understands:

- **Provider quirks**: a permanent false diff the provider reports on every plan.
- **Resources managed outside Terraform**: something another system owns and changes on purpose.
- **Environment, team, and naming carve-outs**: whole slices of the estate a workload session must not touch.

The filter may also **trim** an operation: when one instruction bundles an excluded change with a legitimate one, it keeps the legitimate part. Rules that name a single attribute are therefore as useful as rules that name a whole resource.

### Example

```
## Provider quirks (permanent false diffs)
- The `azurerm` provider always reports a diff on the `created_at` tag
  written by the tagging policy; never reconcile that tag.

## Resources managed outside Terraform
- The values of `azurerm_key_vault_secret` are rotated by the secrets
  platform; never reconcile them.

## Environment, team and naming carve-outs
- Never reconcile resources in the `rg-shared-platform` resource
  group; the platform team owns them.
```

With these rules, a drift round that finds "Delete resource `azurerm_storage_account.sta_shared_001` in `rg-shared-platform`" remediates nothing and lists the resource under **Left Alone by Exception Rules**, quoting the carve-out, with the outcome still **Succeeded**.

## Write the import exception list

`<provider>/guidelines/import_exceptions` names the resources an import round must never bring under Terraform, even when they exist in the cloud scope and the state does not track them. Unlike every other prompt, it is not read by a model: the core parses it and removes the listed IDs from the scope before anything else sees it.

- The list applies on **every** import round, full scope or partial. A withheld resource never reaches the selection agent, the code generator, or `terraform import`, so neither a broad request nor a model can bring it back.
- Azure resource IDs match case-insensitively, so `/subscriptions/…​/resourceGroups/rg-a` also withholds `/resourcegroups/RG-A`. GCP and AWS IDs match exactly.
- Withheld resources are not an error: the import report names each one as skipped on purpose. When every unmanaged resource in the scope is withheld, the round ends with `Every unmanaged resource in the scope <scope> is on the import exception list.` and an empty report.
- An ID that is not in the scope, or is already managed, has no effect.

Only Azure, GCP, and AWS scopes can be listed for import, so the list is read for `azurerm`, `google`, and `aws` only.

### How to write one

Put each resource ID on its own Markdown bullet (`-` or `*`), exactly as the cloud’s scope listing returns it: the full ARM ID for Azure, the asset name without the `//service.googleapis.com/` prefix for GCP (for project IAM, the space-separated `<project-id> <role> <member>` entry), and the ARN for AWS. See [IaC sidecar API](../../reference/api/iac/) for the exact shapes. Backticks around the ID are optional. Every line that is not a bullet is ignored, so headings and explanations stay readable, but keep them in plain paragraphs: a bullet of prose would be read as an ID.

```
# Import Exception List — Azure

The shared platform resources are owned by the platform team and
must stay out of workload repositories.

- /subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/resourceGroups/rg-shared-platform
- `/subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/resourceGroups/rg-shared-platform/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/kvt-shared-001`
```

Each ID withholds that one resource only. Listing a resource group does not withhold the resources inside it, which the scope lists under their own IDs.

> **Note**
> Lists written as free text before the core parsed them are kept
> as they were, and any ID not written as a bullet is ignored. Rewrite
> such lists as bullets.

## Change a compliance policy

The compliance policies are Rego modules evaluated by Open Policy Agent, not read by a model: `general/policies/compliance` on every generate round, and `<provider>/policies/compliance` on the rounds whose root module declares that provider. Kumoss ships one for `aws`, `azurerm`, `google`, `kubernetes`, `oci`, and `vsphere`; give another provider a policy by creating its prompt in Langfuse. Change a policy like any other prompt, with the steps in [Change a prompt](#change-a-prompt), but test every version before you move the label: a broken version locks every generate round it applies to (every round for the general policy, every round of a module declaring the provider for a provider policy) until the label is on a working one. To write, test, and publish a rule, see [Write a policy rule](../write-a-policy-rule/); the input and decision a policy works with, and the shipped rules, are in [Compliance policy](../../reference/compliance-policy/).

What a policy enforces is not restated in the guideline and resource prompts. Those prompts feed only the IaC generator, and no check reads them, so a ban written there would be applied by the model at generation time, possibly differently from the policy, and never checked afterwards. The shipped prompts keep positive defaults (`allow_privilege_escalation = false`, S3 Block Public Access fully enabled, outputs carrying secrets marked `sensitive = true`) and leave the bans to Rego: they no longer tell the generator to avoid `null_resource`, provisioners and `data "external"`, internet-open ingress, basic roles or service account keys, `cluster-admin` or `Allow any-user` grants, or `allow_unverified_ssl`. A round that generates one of those is locked by a policy rather than written correctly in the first place. If you add a rule to a policy, do not also write it into a prompt; if you would rather the generator avoid a pattern up front, phrase the prompt as the default to produce, not as a prohibition.

## If something goes wrong

### A session stops without an error

A `general/*` prompt has no version carrying your environment’s label, or does not exist. The run stops with `prompt_name=<name>. No version labeled '<environment>'` in the core log, but the session shows no failure: it keeps its last status (for example `filtering`), no notification is sent, and the browser waits until its timeout. Set the label on a version of that prompt; a new request can be sent right away. This also happens after changing `environment` if prompts you created by hand do not carry the new label: set it on every such prompt before switching.

### Conventions are missing from a session

A provider prompt that is deleted, or has no version with your environment’s label, is skipped without an error: that provider’s conventions silently disappear from every session. Restore the prompt or its label.

### A resource prompt is never used

Its name is not in `<provider>/guidelines/resources_list`, or does not match the `<name>` part of the prompt exactly. See [Add a resource prompt](#add-a-resource-prompt).

## Checklist for operators

- Review every shipped prompt before relying on a deployment: the naming conventions, security defaults, and intent rules encode a policy, not yours.
- Write the prohibitions your organization needs as rules in the compliance policies: `<provider>/policies/compliance` for a provider’s resources, `general/policies/compliance` for rules that span providers. No prompt lists forbidden actions any more; the shipped policies deny standalone deletions, removed customer-managed keys and command execution, and three critical misconfigurations per shipped provider (public ingress, admin grants and the like), nothing else. Review them before relying on them.
- Do not restate a policy rule in a prompt; see [Change a compliance policy](#compliance-policy). Guidance the shipped prompts dropped along with those bans, and that no policy checks (no secrets in user data, Owner or User Access Administrator at narrower scopes, scoping other ingress to known CIDRs, tags or security groups, the alternatives to service account keys, credentials in the `vsphere` provider block, locking down the OCI default security list, OCI delete-protection defaults), is now checked by nothing: write it back into your own prompts, as a default, if you need it. `null_resource`, provisioners and `data "external"` are denied by the general policy’s `command_execution` rule only when the compliance check is on; see [Deploy to production](../deploy-to-production/).
- Decide who may edit prompts. Anyone who can edit prompts in the Langfuse project can change what the agents generate; give others a viewer role.
- Keep Langfuse reachable whenever the core starts; seeding is part of the boot.
- Back up `langfuse-db`; it holds your curated prompts.

## Next steps

- [Prompt registry](../../reference/prompt-registry/) for seeding, runtime lookup, and the shipped inventory.
- [Write a policy rule](../write-a-policy-rule/) to add a deterministic compliance rule.
- [Resolve a locked session](../resolve-a-locked-session/) for what users see when your compliance prompts lock a session.

# Deploy with Helm

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/guides/deploy-with-helm/

The chart in `charts/kumoss` deploys the same stack as `docker-compose.yml` on Kubernetes: the proxy, the core, the IaC and notifications sidecars, and the bundled backing services (two PostgreSQL databases, Redis, RustFS object storage, Langfuse and SearXNG). Every backing service can be switched off and replaced by an external one.

Each release publishes the chart as an OCI artifact, `oci://ghcr.io/inditextech/charts/kumoss`, with the same version as the release; its Kumoss image tags default to that version. Install it without a checkout:

```
helm upgrade --install kumoss oci://ghcr.io/inditextech/charts/kumoss \
  --version <version> -n kumoss --create-namespace \
  --set core.existingSecret=<secret with LLM / Git credentials>
```

The examples below use `charts/kumoss` from a checkout; the OCI reference works in its place everywhere.

The chart does not make a deployment production-ready on its own. The decisions in [Deploy to production](../deploy-to-production/) still apply; this page covers only how the chart maps them to Kubernetes.

## What the chart deploys

| Component | Kind | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `proxy` | Deployment + Service | The single entry point, as in Compose: port 80 serves the SPA and `/api` (including the event stream); port 9000 fronts the object store for presigned artifact URLs; port 3000 serves the Langfuse UI. |
| `core` | Deployment (1 replica, `Recreate`) | Mounts `config.yaml` from a ConfigMap and the shared `workspaces` volume. Probed on `GET /healthz`. |
| `iac` | Deployment (1 replica, `Recreate`) | Mounts the same `workspaces` volume as the core. |
| `notifications` | Deployment | Off by default: the service refuses to start without `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL`. |
| `core-db`, `langfuse-db` | StatefulSet (`postgres:17`) | Single instance each. Use a managed database or an operator in production. |
| `redis`, `object-storage`, `searxng` | Deployment / StatefulSet | Same images and settings as Compose. SearXNG runs the upstream image with the repository’s `settings.yml`. |
| `langfuse-web`, `langfuse-worker`, `langfuse-clickhouse`, `langfuse-redis` | Deployments, StatefulSet (ClickHouse) | Langfuse, as in Compose. An init container on `langfuse-web` creates its bucket on the object store; the worker and the core wait for `langfuse-web` to answer, so they start after its database migrations. The queue Redis is ephemeral, like the core’s. |

The repository’s `config.yaml`, `nginx/nginx.conf` and `services/searxng/settings.yml` are symlinked into `charts/kumoss/files`, so the chart always ships what Compose ships. At render time the chart replaces the Compose hostnames (`core`, `iac`, `langfuse-web`, …​) with the release’s Service names, then applies your `config` overrides on top.

## Values that matter

Value
Purpose

`publicUrl`

URL the browser uses to reach the proxy. It becomes the core’s only CORS origin (`http.cors_origins`).

`storagePublicUrl`

URL the browser uses to reach the proxy’s port 9000. The core signs artifact download links for this host (`storage.public_endpoint_url`).

`config`

Any `config.yaml` key, merged over the repository file. See [Configuration](../../reference/configuration/).

`core.existingSecret`

Secret loaded whole into the core: LLM credentials (see [LLM providers and models](../../reference/llm-providers/)), `GIT_USER`, `GIT_TOKEN`. `core.secretEnv` creates one from values instead, for local testing.

`iac.existingSecret`

Cloud provider credentials for plan and apply.

`caBundle.existingConfigMap`, `caBundle.certificates`

Extra CA roots (PEM) trusted for outbound HTTPS by every pod that calls out: the core, the IaC and notifications sidecars, and SearXNG. Needed behind a TLS-inspecting proxy; see [Behind a TLS-inspecting proxy](#tls-inspecting-proxy).

`secrets.*`

Service tokens and bundled-service passwords. Leave them blank: the chart generates them on first install and reuses them on upgrade. If the chart is rendered offline, see [Rendering offline (Argo CD, Flux, `helm template`)](#gitops).

`workspaces.accessMode`, `workspaces.storageClass`

The core and the IaC sidecar share this volume. With `ReadWriteOnce` (the default) the IaC pod is required to run on the core’s node and the core prefers the IaC pod’s node, so a rollout returns to the node that holds the volume. Setting `iac.affinity` or `core.affinity` replaces those rules: keep the equivalent `podAffinity` in yours. On a multi-node cluster, a `ReadWriteMany` class removes the constraint.

`<service>.enabled`, `<service>.externalUrl`

Replace a bundled backing service. `postgres.core.externalUrl` and `redis.externalUrl` take connection URLs; for object storage, disable it and set `config.storage.*` instead.

`<component>.serviceAccount`, `<component>.podLabels`

The Kubernetes identity each of `proxy`, `core`, `iac`, `notifications` and `mapping` runs as; see [Cloud credentials with workload identity](#workload-identity).

`notifications.enabled`

Off by default. Turning it on requires `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` in `notifications.secretEnv` or `notifications.existingSecret`; the chart refuses to render without it.

`mapping.enabled`, `mapping.env.MAPPING_PREFIX_IDENTIFIER`

On by default. The prefix a bare repository name typed in the wizard is appended to (`foo` → `<prefix>foo.git`); empty accepts full `https://` URLs only. Turn `mapping.enabled` off to use the input as the URL without a mapper, or point `config.services.mapping.endpoint` at your own implementation.

`<component>.resources`

CPU and memory requests and limits. Empty by default; set them for production, and on clusters that require them (GKE Autopilot fills in its own defaults otherwise).

`langfuse.publicUrl`

Where browsers reach the Langfuse UI (`http://localhost:3000` by default). Langfuse sends its login redirects there, and the admin panel’s **Langfuse** link opens it, so it must match how you expose the proxy’s port 3000: a port-forward, a NodePort (`proxy.service.nodePorts.langfuse`) or `ingress.langfuseHost`. The proxy is the only way in. Langfuse has its own login, but its traces hold full prompts and repository content: serve it over TLS in production.

`langfuse.adminEmail`, `secrets.langfuseAdminPassword`

The Langfuse admin, created on the first start (`admin@example.com` and a generated password by default; sign-up is off). Read the password with `kubectl get secret <release>-kumoss-internal -o jsonpath='{.data.LANGFUSE_ADMIN_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d`.

`langfuse.enabled`

With `false`, point `config.telemetry.langfuse_url` and `langfuse.publicUrl` at your own Langfuse and give the core that project’s key pair as `LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY` / `LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY` in `core.existingSecret`. The core seeds its prompts there at startup.

`langfuse.clickhouse.enabled`, `langfuse.redis.enabled`, postgres.langfuse., `langfuse.s3.`

Replace Langfuse’s bundled ClickHouse, Redis, database or bucket with your own; the settings to provide then (`CLICKHOUSE_*`, `REDIS_CONNECTION_STRING`, S3 keys) go in `langfuse.secretEnv` or `langfuse.existingSecret`. See the comments in `values.yaml` and [Langfuse’s configuration reference](https://langfuse.com/self-hosting/configuration).

`ingress.*`

Optional Ingress in front of the proxy. `ingress.storageHost` routes a second host to port 9000 for downloads; set `storagePublicUrl` to match. `ingress.langfuseHost` routes a third one to port 3000, the Langfuse UI; set `langfuse.publicUrl` to match.

`<component>.extraEnv`, `extraVolumes` and `extraVolumeMounts` cover everything else.

## Cloud credentials with workload identity

On a managed cluster, prefer workload identity over long-lived keys in Secrets: each pod runs as a Kubernetes ServiceAccount that the cloud maps to one of its identities, and the pod receives short-lived tokens automatically.

The chart creates one ServiceAccount per Kumoss component, so permissions stay separate. Two of them need cloud access:

- `core`: the LLM provider (Vertex AI, Azure AI, Bedrock) and, with `S3` storage, the artifacts store: leave the static keys blank and the default AWS credential chain picks up the identity. `STORAGE_ACCOUNT` storage does not use the pod identity; it still needs `STORAGE_ACCOUNT_KEY` (for example in `core.existingSecret`), because the core signs download links with the account key.
- `iac`: the permissions `plan` and `apply` need on the target infrastructure. This is the most privileged identity in the deployment; scope it accordingly.

Bind a ServiceAccount by annotating it (and, on AKS, labeling the pods):

```
# AKS — Azure Workload Identity. The webhook injects AZURE_* variables;
# the azurerm provider and import discovery read the ARM_* ones.
iac:
  serviceAccount:
    annotations:
      azure.workload.identity/client-id: <managed-identity-client-id>
  podLabels:
    azure.workload.identity/use: "true"
  env:
    ARM_USE_AKS_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY: "true"
    ARM_CLIENT_ID: <managed-identity-client-id>
    ARM_TENANT_ID: <tenant-id>

# EKS — IRSA (EKS Pod Identity needs no annotation: associate the
# ServiceAccount with the role in EKS instead). The webhook injects the
# role and token; only the region is yours to set.
iac:
  serviceAccount:
    annotations:
      eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::<account>:role/<role>
  env:
    AWS_REGION: <region>

# GKE — Workload Identity Federation, impersonating a service account.
# The provider finds the identity through the metadata server.
iac:
  serviceAccount:
    annotations:
      iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: <name>@<project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com
```

The per-cloud variables come from `services/iac/PROVIDERS.md`, which lists every supported credential form.

The cloud side (the managed identity or role, its permissions, and the trust that lets this ServiceAccount assume it) is set up outside the chart. The trust is keyed on the namespace and ServiceAccount name: `<release>-kumoss-<component>` by default (`kumoss-iac` for a release named `kumoss`), or set `serviceAccount.name`. To use a ServiceAccount you manage yourself, set `serviceAccount.create: false` and `serviceAccount.name`.

Kumoss does not call the Kubernetes API, so the pods do not mount a Kubernetes API token (`serviceAccount.automount: false`). The workload-identity token is injected separately and is unaffected.

## Rendering offline (Argo CD, Flux, `helm template`)

The chart reads its generated credentials back from the cluster with Helm’s `lookup`, which only works when Helm talks to the cluster (`helm install` / `helm upgrade`). Tools that render the chart offline get nothing back, so every render would generate new passwords, and the databases, initialized with the first ones, would reject them.

Manage that Secret yourself instead (with Sealed Secrets, External Secrets, SOPS…​) and set `secrets.existingSecret` to its name. The chart then renders no credentials of its own. The Secret needs every key the generated one has:

| Key | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `KUMOSS_IAC_TOKEN`, `KUMOSS_NOTIFICATIONS_TOKEN`, `KUMOSS_MAPPING_TOKEN` | Bearer tokens between the core and the sidecars (any random string) |
| `CORE_DB_PASSWORD`, `LANGFUSE_DB_PASSWORD` | Passwords the bundled databases are initialized with |
| `KUMOSS_SQL_DATABASE_URL`, `LANGFUSE_DATABASE_URL` | Connection URLs, e.g. `postgresql://postgres:<password>@<release>-kumoss-core-db:5432/kumoss`. Percent-encode the password. |
| `LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY`, `LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY` | The Langfuse project key pair, provisioned by `langfuse-web` and used by the core; `pk-lf-` and `sk-lf-` followed by a random string |
| `LANGFUSE_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | The Langfuse admin’s password |
| `LANGFUSE_NEXTAUTH_SECRET`, `LANGFUSE_SALT`, `LANGFUSE_CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD`, `LANGFUSE_REDIS_PASSWORD` | Any random strings |
| `LANGFUSE_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | 64 hex characters (`openssl rand -hex 32`). Never change it once Langfuse has stored data, nor `LANGFUSE_SALT`. |
| `KUMOSS_REDIS_URL` | e.g. `redis://<release>-kumoss-redis:6379/0` |
| `RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY`, `RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY` | Credentials of the bundled object store |
| `SEARXNG_SECRET` | SearXNG’s secret key (any random string) |

Keys for components you disabled can be omitted. Pods do not restart when this Secret changes; restart them after rotating it.

## Try it on kind

[kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/) runs a Kubernetes cluster as Docker containers on your workstation. The steps below give a single-node cluster whose host ports 80 and 9000 reach the proxy, so the browser uses the same URLs as with Compose and the default `publicUrl` / `storagePublicUrl` work unchanged. Run them from the repository root.

`charts/kind-up.sh` runs all of them in one idempotent command; re-run it to upgrade. It reads the credentials from a Compose-style `.env` (stripping the quotes `kubectl --from-env-file` would keep), and with `CA_DIR` set it also does the [TLS-inspecting proxy](#tls-inspecting-proxy) steps:

```
ENV_FILE=core/.env charts/kind-up.sh
# Behind a TLS-inspecting proxy:
ENV_FILE=core/.env CA_DIR=/usr/local/share/ca-certificates charts/kind-up.sh
# Other host ports, or the published chart instead of the checkout:
HTTP_PORT=8080 STORAGE_PORT=9900 LANGFUSE_PORT=3300 charts/kind-up.sh
CHART=oci://ghcr.io/inditextech/charts/kumoss CHART_VERSION=<version> charts/kind-up.sh
```

Its header lists every setting; arguments after them go to `helm upgrade --install`. The manual steps:

1. Create the cluster. The port mappings forward host ports 80, 9000 and 3000 to the node ports the proxy is exposed on in step 4: ``` cat <<'EOF' | kind create cluster --name kumoss --config - kind: Cluster apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4 nodes: - role: control-plane extraPortMappings: - { containerPort: 30080, hostPort: 80 } - { containerPort: 30900, hostPort: 9000 } - { containerPort: 30300, hostPort: 3000 } EOF ```
2. Make the images available. The chart’s image tags follow the chart version, so a chart from a release pulls that release’s images and nothing needs doing. To run your checkout instead, build the images you changed and load them into the node, which has its own image store: ``` docker build -f core/Dockerfile --build-context host-certs=docker/certs \ -t kumoss-core:dev . kind load docker-image kumoss-core:dev --name kumoss ``` Then point the component at it with `--set core.image.repository=kumoss-core,core.image.tag=dev,core.image.pullPolicy=Never`.
3. Store the LLM credentials the configured models need (here, the default Vertex AI models) and, optionally, the Git credentials: ``` kubectl create namespace kumoss kubectl -n kumoss create secret generic kumoss-credentials \ --from-literal=VERTEXAI_PROJECT=my-project \ --from-literal=VERTEXAI_LOCATION=europe-west1 \ --from-file=VERTEXAI_CREDENTIALS=./service-account.json \ --from-literal=GIT_USER=<user> \ --from-literal=GIT_TOKEN=<token> ```
4. Install, exposing the proxy on the node ports mapped in step 1: ``` helm upgrade --install kumoss charts/kumoss -n kumoss \ --set proxy.service.type=NodePort \ --set proxy.service.nodePorts.http=30080 \ --set proxy.service.nodePorts.storage=30900 \ --set proxy.service.nodePorts.langfuse=30300 \ --set core.existingSecret=kumoss-credentials \ --wait --timeout 10m helm test kumoss -n kumoss ```
5. Open `http://localhost`. Langfuse is at `http://localhost:3000`; log in as `admin@example.com` with the password from the internal Secret (`helm status kumoss -n kumoss` prints the command).

### Behind a TLS-inspecting proxy

The proxy re-signs HTTPS with a corporate root that neither the kind node nor the images trust. Two things change, matching the [Compose setup](../development/#tls-inspecting-proxy); `charts/kind-up.sh` does both when `CA_DIR` is set.

- **Image pulls.** The node fails to pull with `x509: certificate signed by unknown authority` (`ImagePullBackOff`). Pull the images on the host and copy them in, all in one archive. Save a single platform, because `kind load docker-image` fails on multi-platform images: ``` images=$(helm template kumoss charts/kumoss | sed -n 's/^ *image: *"\{0,1\}\([^"]*\)"\{0,1\}$/\1/p' | sort -u) for i in $images; do docker pull -q "$i"; done docker save --platform linux/amd64 -o /tmp/kumoss-images.tar $images kind load image-archive /tmp/kumoss-images.tar --name kumoss ``` Render with the same `--set` flags you install with: enabling `notifications` adds its image. The list includes the `curlimages/curl` image `helm test` runs.
- **Outbound HTTPS from the pods.** Put your corporate roots (PEM) in a ConfigMap and point `caBundle.existingConfigMap` at it: ``` kubectl -n kumoss create configmap corporate-ca-roots \ --from-file=/usr/local/share/ca-certificates helm upgrade --install kumoss charts/kumoss -n kumoss ... \ --set caBundle.existingConfigMap=corporate-ca-roots ``` Or pass the certificates inline with `--set-file caBundle.certificates=corp-root.pem` and the chart creates the ConfigMap. Every pod that calls out gets an init container that combines its image’s public roots with yours into one bundle, pointed at by `SSL_CERT_FILE`, `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE`, `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` and `AWS_CA_BUNDLE`. A file may hold several PEM certificates: | Pod | Outbound HTTPS | | --- | --- | | `core` | LLM providers, Git hosts, web pages read by `web_search`. The roots are also mounted at `KUMOSS_CA_DIR`, so the entrypoint imports them into Chromium’s store. | | `iac` | The OpenTofu registry and provider downloads (`tofu init`). Without the roots, the pod starts and passes its probes, but every plan fails. | | `notifications` | Slack. | | `searxng` | The search engines. | Pods do not restart when an `existingConfigMap` changes; restart them after editing it. Earlier versions of this guide mounted the roots through `core.extraVolumes` and `searxng.extraVolumes`; remove those when switching to `caBundle`. When building the core image, pass the same directory as the `host-certs` build context instead of `docker/certs`.

### Troubleshooting kind

`kube-proxy` crash-looping with `too many open files`, followed by CoreDNS and the `local-path-provisioner` failing, means the host ran out of inotify instances. Every kind node on the host shares the per-user limit, so it shows up with several clusters. Raise it, and persist it if your distribution reads `/etc/sysctl.d`:

```
sudo sysctl fs.inotify.max_user_instances=512
echo 'fs.inotify.max_user_instances=512' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-kind.conf
```

Then delete the crashed pods so they restart immediately, for example `kubectl -n kube-system delete pod -l k8s-app=kube-proxy`.

## Upgrades and removal

- `config.yaml` changes roll the core automatically (the pod carries a checksum of the rendered file). Changes to `secrets.*`, the external service URLs, or a component’s `secretEnv` roll every pod that reads them the same way. A Secret you reference through `existingSecret` is managed outside the chart: after rotating it, restart its readers (`kubectl rollout restart deploy/<release>-kumoss-core`). The same goes for `caBundle.existingConfigMap`; inline `caBundle.certificates` roll the pods on change.
- Generated passwords and tokens are read back from the existing Secret on every upgrade. Changing a database password in values after the first install does not change it inside an initialized database.
- `helm uninstall` keeps the data: the `workspaces` claim, the StatefulSets' data claims, and the `<release>-kumoss-internal` Secret holding the passwords that data was initialized with (both carry `helm.sh/resource-policy: keep`). Reinstalling the same release in the same namespace picks all three up again. To start from scratch, delete them explicitly: ``` kubectl -n kumoss delete pvc -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=kumoss kubectl -n kumoss delete secret kumoss-internal ```

# Development

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/guides/development/

This guide covers contributing to Kumoss itself — running the repository’s own test suites, checks, and tooling. It does not cover deploying or operating Kumoss; for that, see [Quickstart](../../quickstart/) and [Deploy to production](../deploy-to-production/).

## Prerequisites

Before contributing, read [Contributing](../../contributing/) for the Contributor License Agreement, the code of conduct, and the process for proposing a change.

## Repository layout

The repository is a monorepo: the FastAPI core in `core/`, the IaC and notifications sidecar services in `services/`, the React web application in `client/web/`, the sidecar OpenAPI contracts in `contracts/`, and the Helm chart in `charts/kumoss/`. See [Architecture](../../architecture/) for how they fit together.

## Running the stack for development

Copy each `env.sample` to a `.env` next to it (`core/.env` is required), set the two model strings in `config.yaml`, and run `docker compose up --build`. [Quickstart](../../quickstart/) is the step-by-step guide. `--build` matters: without it, Compose runs the published release images (`ghcr.io/inditextech/kumoss-*`) instead of your checkout. A `docker compose pull` later replaces locally built images with the published ones again.

After a code change, rebuild and recreate the affected service, for example `docker compose up -d --build core`. An edit to `config.yaml` needs only `docker compose restart core`, because Compose bind-mounts that file.

### Local Compose overrides

Settings that belong to your machine rather than to the project go in `docker-compose.override.yml`, which Compose loads automatically and git ignores. `docker-compose.override.example.yml` is the tracked template — copy it rather than editing it in place:

```
cp docker-compose.override.example.yml docker-compose.override.yml
```

### Behind a TLS-inspecting proxy

On a corporate network that inspects HTTPS, most outbound container requests fail while a few domains keep working: `web_search` returns engine snippets instead of page content, and `docker compose logs core` shows the reads failing before any HTTP request is sent.

```
Page read for '<url>' failed, falling back to the engine snippet:
PageReadError("could not render '<url>'")
(RuntimeError('[SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify
failed: self-signed certificate in certificate chain'))
```

The proxy terminates TLS and re-signs it with its own root, which the containers do not trust; the domains that still work are the ones the proxy passes through untouched. Confirm it by looking at who signed what you received:

```
docker compose exec core sh -c \
  'echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 \
   -servername example.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer'
```

An `issuer` naming your company rather than a public CA confirms the interception. The fix is two-part, both wired in the override template above, and keeps the certificates on your machine:

- **Build** — the images fetch their dependencies over HTTPS, so the roots are needed at build time too. The override points the `host-certs` build context at the host directory holding them.
- **Runtime** — the override mounts that directory at `KUMOSS_CA_DIR`, and each entrypoint merges its certificates into a bundle and points the HTTP clients at it before starting the server.

A **hostname mismatch** is not a trust problem: the proxy is sinkholing that domain under its filtering policy, and the certificate honestly belongs to the sinkhole. No configuration fixes that one.

## Core tests

Python 3.15, `uv`. `pytest` and `pytest-cov` are part of the `tooling` dependency group, so sync the project first:

```
cd core
uv sync --frozen --group tooling
uv run --no-sync pytest tests/
```

Async tests use `unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase` (no pytest-asyncio plugin, no `--asyncio-mode` flag). `core/tests/conftest.py` supplies placeholder values for the LLM credential, the database URL and the mandatory `KUMOSS_IAC_TOKEN` that the configuration module validates at import; suites that talk to PostgreSQL or Redis need the compose stack (or point `KUMOSS_SQL_DATABASE_URL` and `KUMOSS_REDIS_URL` at your own instances).

## Compliance policy tests

The seed policies (`core/prompts/seed/*/policies`: the general policy and one per provider) have Rego tests in `core/tests/policies`; see [Testing commands](../../reference/compliance-policy/#testing). From the `core` directory, with the OPA version of the core image:

```
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/core:ro" -w /core \
  openpolicyagent/opa:1.22.4-static \
  test prompts/seed/*/policies tests/policies
```

`opa fmt --diff --fail` and `opa check` on the same directories must pass too.

## Type checking

`basedpyright` lives in the `tooling` dependency group, which the project install above does not include; install the group first:

```
cd core
uv pip install --system --group tooling -r pyproject.toml
basedpyright
```

`pyrightconfig.json` only includes `src/` — tests are not type-checked.

## Frontend checks

Node 24:

```
cd client/web
npm ci
npm run lint
npm run test:ci
npm run build
```

## Sidecar tests

Each sidecar service has its own `tooling` dependency group with `pytest` and its test helpers (the exact set differs per service):

```
cd services/<name>
uv sync --group tooling
uv run pytest
```

## Linting and formatting

`pre-commit run --all-files` runs Ruff (`ruff check` and `ruff format`), the REUSE check, and gitleaks secret scanning. Install the hooks once with `pre-commit install`.

## Continuous integration

Pull requests run Repolinter, the REUSE compliance check, the Conventional Commits check, and an offline Markdown link and anchor check, plus a Verify workflow: frontend type check, tests, and production build, the pytest suite of each sidecar service, and the compliance policy job (`opa fmt`, `opa check` and `opa test`). **The core suite is not run in CI**, so run it locally against the compose stack before opening a pull request. **Neither is the Helm chart**: after changing it, or the `config.yaml`, `nginx/nginx.conf`, or `services/searxng/settings.yml` it renders, run `helm lint charts/kumoss` and install it on a kind cluster with `charts/kind-up.sh` ([Try it on kind](../deploy-with-helm/#try-it-on-kind)). Publishing a release lints the chart and pushes it to `oci://ghcr.io/inditextech/charts/kumoss`.

## Regenerating sidecar clients

Changing a sidecar’s behavior means updating its spec in `contracts/openapi/`, its conformance suite in `contracts/conformance/`, and regenerating the core’s client for that service. From `core/`, once per service:

```
uv run --group tooling openapi-python-client generate \
  --path ../contracts/openapi/<service>.v1.yaml \
  --config ../contracts/openapi-python-client.yaml \
  --meta none \
  --output-path src/clients/<service> \
  --overwrite
```

Regeneration drops the SPDX headers from the generated files; re-add them afterwards. Do not hand-edit anything under `core/src/clients/{authz,iac,mapping,notifications}/`.

## Pull requests

Once your change is ready, [Contributing](../../contributing/) covers the pull-request process and the checks it must pass.

# Merge and apply

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/guides/merge-and-apply/

Once you have reviewed a session’s results, this guide takes you from the session branch to applied infrastructure: you open the pull request, get it reviewed, merge it, and apply exactly the plan you reviewed. If a **Deployment Blocked** screen opens on the way, see [If the session is locked](#session-locked).

## Prerequisites

- A session with results, reached by following [Follow a session](../follow-a-session/).
- The `developer` role; see [Roles and permissions](../../reference/roles-and-permissions/).

## Steps

1. In the results view, choose **Create PR**. Kumoss writes the title and description and opens the pull request from the session branch on your Git provider. This can take a minute. When it is ready you see "Here is your Pull Request."
2. Choose **View Pull Request** and review it with your team. The button appears when the link points at a recognized Git host; otherwise copy the link from the session details. Your team’s normal review and CI apply. To make changes, type them as a follow-up request: the new round pushes to the same branch and updates the pull request.
3. When the review is done, choose **Approve PR and Apply**, then **Confirm and Apply**. The confirmation asks you to confirm that you read and understood the report and the proposed changes. **Confirm and Apply** merges the pull request into the default branch and starts the apply; to ask for help instead, choose **Request Review**, which sends a support request. The engine executes exactly the plan you reviewed; it is not re-planned. The apply-results screen shows **Succeeded**, **Partially Applied**, or **Failed**, with the execution summary, the resources created, updated, destroyed, or failed, and recommendations.

> **Note**
> In drift-remediation and import sessions the button reads **Approve and Merge PR** and only merges: the merge is the remediation, an import is
> already in the state, and no apply follows. See
> [Comparing the operating modes](../../reference/operating-modes/#compare-modes).

## If the session is locked

If the **Deployment Blocked** screen opens instead of the merge controls, the session is locked: you can still create the pull request, but merge and apply are refused. Expand **Why** to see what locked it.

[![Deployment Blocked screen listing the high-impact reason and two blocking compliance findings](../../_images/deployment-blocked.png)](../../_images/deployment-blocked.png)

Figure 1. The Deployment Blocked screen with **Why** expanded: a high-impact verdict, a `critical_deletion` finding from the compliance policy, and a `scope_exceeded` finding from the intent check

See [Resolve a locked session](../resolve-a-locked-session/) for what each cause means and how to get the session unlocked.

## Verify

- The apply-results screen shows **Succeeded**.
- The pull request shows as merged into the default branch on your Git provider.

The session’s own status is not a reliable check: a failed apply also ends the session normally. A failed apply is not retried and nothing is rolled back; read the error on the apply-results screen and start a new request.

After an apply the reviewed plan is consumed. To change anything else, send a new request; a fresh plan is produced and reviewed before the next apply.

## Next steps

- [Make a request](../make-a-request/) to start a new session for the next change.
- [Resolve a locked session](../resolve-a-locked-session/) if a later round locks the session.
- [Remediate drift](../remediate-drift/) to bring changed infrastructure back in line with its code.

# Resolve a locked session

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/guides/resolve-a-locked-session/

Kumoss checks every generate round before it lets you merge and apply. When a check fails, the session is locked: you can keep working on it, but merge and apply are refused until the lock is cleared. This guide explains why a session gets locked, what you see, and the two ways to get it unlocked.

## Prerequisites

- A session whose latest generate round finished, reached by following [Follow a session](../follow-a-session/).
- To unlock a session yourself, the panel role `editor` or `admin`; see [Roles and permissions](../../reference/roles-and-permissions/). Without it, you need a follow-up request or a reviewer who has it.

## Why a session is locked

Three independent checks run at the end of every generate round, and any one of them can lock the session. Only the first is deterministic: the same plan always gets the same verdict. The other two are judgments made by a language model, because they depend on what you asked for and on what a change means, which no fixed rule over the plan can capture. For the mechanism as a whole, see [How compliance works](../../architecture/compliance/). Drift and import rounds are never checked and never lock a session.

| Check | Deterministic | Defined in | How to adapt it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Compliance policy](#compliance-policy) | Yes | Rego policies `general/policies/compliance` and `<provider>/policies/compliance`, evaluated by Open Policy Agent | Write or change rules in Rego; see [Write a policy rule](../write-a-policy-rule/) |
| [Intent check](#intent-check) | No | Prompt `general/intent/rules`, read by a model | Edit the intent rules in prose; see [Compliance prompts](../customize-prompts/#compliance-prompts) |
| [High impact](#high-impact) | No | Prompt `general/compliance/impact`, read by the report model | Edit the impact criteria in prose; see [Compliance prompts](../customize-prompts/#compliance-prompts) |

All three are prompts in Langfuse, seeded from `core/prompts/seed/general/` (and, for the provider policies, from `core/prompts/seed/<provider>/`). A change takes effect on the next generate round once its new version carries your environment’s label. Which checks run at all is set by your operator with the `orchestration` switches; see [Configuration](../../reference/configuration/).

### Compliance policy (deterministic)

**What locks.** Open Policy Agent evaluates your organization’s [compliance policies](../../reference/compliance-policy/), Rego modules, against the plan’s JSON: the general policy, and one policy for each provider the module declares. Any `deny` finding locks the session; `warn` findings are reported but do not.

- The general policy’s `critical_deletion` rule denies any resource that is destroyed without being recreated, **even when you asked for the deletion**. Replacements are allowed.
- The other shipped rules deny removing a customer-managed key, having Terraform run commands (provisioners, `null_resource`, external data sources), and provider-specific risks such as public ingress or wildcard admin roles; see [The shipped rules](../../reference/compliance-policy/#shipped-rules).
- If a policy cannot be evaluated at all, the round gets a `policy_unavailable` finding and is locked too: the policies [fail closed](../../reference/compliance-policy/#failure).

Findings from this check carry a **policy** badge.

**Why it is deterministic.** No model is involved: the rules are code that reads resource types, actions, and attribute values from the plan. The same plan always gets the same verdict, and every rule can be tested with `opa test` before it is rolled out.

**Where to change it.** The general policy is the Langfuse prompt `general/policies/compliance`, and each provider’s is `<provider>/policies/compliance`, seeded from `core/prompts/seed/<scope>/policies/compliance.rego`. To add a rule, such as allowed regions, no public storage, or no owner role assignments, write it in the policy of the provider it concerns (or in the general policy when it spans providers), test it, and publish it as a new version in Langfuse; see [Write a policy rule](../write-a-policy-rule/). The input a policy receives and the decision it must return are in [Compliance policy](../../reference/compliance-policy/).

Use the policies for every rule you can state as a condition on the plan: they are the only check that cannot miss a case or flag one by mistake.

### Intent check (not deterministic)

**What locks.** A language-model agent judges only whether the plan does what the requests of the session ask, every request and not just the first. It reports violations with a rule id and a severity; a finding of severity `error` or `critical` locks the session, and `warning` is reported only. The shipped rules, both of severity `error`, are:

- `scope_exceeded`: the plan changes something you did not ask for, for example it removes a block or sets an attribute to null. A removal is never accepted as a side effect of an addition.
- `scope_incomplete`: part of your request has no matching change in the plan.

The intent check does not judge safety, conventions, deletions, or versions, and a change you asked for is never an intent violation. Your organization’s conventions only guide generation: nothing checks a plan against them afterwards except the rules of the compliance policy.

Findings from this check carry an **intent** badge.

**Why it is not deterministic.** Whether a change is "what you asked for" depends on the meaning of your request, written in natural language; there is no attribute in the plan to test. A model can read it, but two runs on the same plan can disagree, so a finding can be wrong. When you think it is, rephrase the request to be explicit about what must change and what must stay, or ask a reviewer to check it.

**Where to adapt it.** The prompt `general/intent/rules` defines the rules, each with a `rule_id` and a severity. Edit `scope_exceeded` and `scope_incomplete` to match how strict your organization wants to be, or add your own rules about intent in the same format; see [Compliance prompts](../customize-prompts/#compliance-prompts).

To enforce a convention, such as a mandatory tag, write it as a rule of the [compliance policy](../../reference/compliance-policy/): it then always holds, without depending on the model.

### High impact (not deterministic)

**What locks.** While writing the report, the report model groups the changes and labels each group `low`, `medium`, or `high`, and the report shows the overall level as its impact banner. When the level is `high` and your deployment enables `orchestration.block_on_high_impact`, the session is locked. The banner is shown on every report either way.

**Why it is not deterministic.** Whether a change causes downtime or touches something critical depends on the resource, the attribute, and its context: renaming a tag and changing a firewall rule are both in-place updates in the plan. A model makes that judgment from written criteria, so the same plan can be rated differently on two runs.

**Where to adapt it.** The criteria are the prompt `general/compliance/impact`. The shipped criteria are: high for destructive actions, restarts, service downtime, or critical networking changes; medium for configuration updates that change behavior without guaranteed downtime; low for isolated new resources or non-disruptive updates such as tags or locks. Rewrite them to match your organization’s change-management standards, for example to rate any change to a production network as high; see [Compliance prompts](../customize-prompts/#compliance-prompts).

If a specific change must always be stopped, such as any change to a firewall, write it as a rule of the [compliance policy](../../reference/compliance-policy/): a high-impact verdict is a model’s judgment and is not guaranteed.

## What you see

When you continue to the pull request, the **Deployment Blocked** screen opens instead of the merge controls; see the screenshot in [Merge and apply](../merge-and-apply/#session-locked).

- Expand **Why** to see the cause: **High impact** with the impact summary, **Compliance** with each blocking finding (severity, rule id, resource, and a **policy** or **intent** badge), or both. **Show all findings** adds the warnings and the suggested fixes.
- **Check again** reads the lock state again, for example after a reviewer unlocked the session.
- **Back to Report** returns to the report. **Contact Team** sends a support request.

The full compliance report, including the rules that passed, is also in the session details, as the round’s **Compliance Check** artifact.

While locked, you can still read everything, continue the conversation, and create the pull request so reviewers can read the diff. Merge and apply are refused with `409`. Your sessions list shows the lock in the **Apply** column.

## Who is notified

When the notifications sidecar is enabled, Kumoss sends a "Compliance check failed" notification, a "High impact changes detected" notification, or both. They go to you and to every user with the panel role `editor` or higher, so a reviewer usually knows about the lock before you ask.

If your browser tab is hidden when the round finishes, you also get a "Session blocked" browser notification.

## Unlock the session

Choose one of the two ways:

1. **Fix the request.** Read the findings under **Why**, then send a follow-up request that addresses them, for example "keep the existing bucket and only add the tag". When the new round passes all three checks, the lock clears and the merge controls return.
2. **Ask a reviewer.** A user with the panel role `editor` or `admin` reviews the findings in the admin panel and unlocks the session; see [Lock or unlock the apply of a session](../administer-users-and-locks/#unlock-a-session). When they are done, choose **Check again**. [![Admin panel Sessions tab with the locked session’s detail panel open and the Apply Locked button highlighted](../../_images/admin-unlock-session.png)](../../_images/admin-unlock-session.png) Figure 1. A reviewer opens the locked session from the admin panel’s Sessions tab and presses **Apply Locked** to unlock it

> **Note**
> A reviewer’s unlock lasts only until your next generate round on
> the session. That round runs the checks again and sets the lock afresh.

## Verify

The **Deployment Blocked** screen no longer opens when you continue to the pull request, the **Apply** column of your sessions list shows the session unlocked, and **Approve PR and Apply** is available. Continue with [Merge and apply](../merge-and-apply/).

## Next steps

- [Merge and apply](../merge-and-apply/) to merge the pull request and apply the plan.
- [Compliance policy](../../reference/compliance-policy/) to write your own policy rules.
- [Customize prompts](../customize-prompts/) to change the conventions that guide generation, or the intent rules.

# Write a policy rule

Source: https://inditextech.github.io/kumoss/stable/main/guides/write-a-policy-rule/

The compliance policies hold your organization’s hard rules for infrastructure changes, such as "no public storage" or "only these regions", and Kumoss checks every generate round’s plan against them: the general policy, `general/policies/compliance`, on every round, and a provider’s policy, `<provider>/policies/compliance`, on the rounds whose root module declares that provider. This guide adds a rule to the Azure policy that stops storage accounts with public network access, tests it, and publishes it. The exact input and decision a policy works with are in [Compliance policy](../../reference/compliance-policy/).

## Prerequisites

- Access to Langfuse prompt management for your deployment; see [Customize prompts](../customize-prompts/).
- Docker, to run the `openpolicyagent/opa:1.22.4-static` image, or OPA 1.22.4 installed locally. 1.22.4 is the version in the core image.
- `orchestration.enable_compliance_checker` set to `true`, the shipped default; see [Configuration](../../reference/configuration/).
- A rough idea of the plan JSON your engine produces with `terraform show -json` or `tofu show -json`.

## How a rule works

Each policy is one Rego module: `package kumoss.compliance` for the general policy, `package kumoss.providers.<provider>` for a provider’s. The general policy’s `critical_deletion` rule shows every part a rule needs:

```
package kumoss.compliance

rules contains "critical_deletion" (1)

deny contains finding if { (2)
	some change in input.plan.resource_changes (3)
	change.mode == "managed"
	change.change.actions == ["delete"] (4)
	finding := { (5)
		"rule_id": "critical_deletion",
		"severity": "critical",
		"resource": change.address,
		"message": sprintf(
			"%s is destroyed without being recreated; standalone deletions are never allowed, even when requested.",
			[change.address],
		),
	}
}
```

| **1** | Registers the rule id, so the report lists the rule as passed when it finds nothing. |
| --- | --- |
| **2** | Adds a finding to `deny`, the set of blocking findings, for every case where all the lines in the body hold. `warn` works the same way but does not block. |
| **3** | Loops over the plan’s resource changes. `input.plan` is the plan JSON, unchanged. |
| **4** | The condition: the resource is destroyed and not recreated. |
| **5** | The finding: a rule id, a severity (`error` or `critical`), the resource address, and a message for the user. |

In Rego, the lines of a body are joined by "and": if any line is false or refers to a value that does not exist, the rule produces nothing for that change.

## Steps

1. Create a working folder with this layout: ``` policy-work/ ├── general.rego ├── azurerm.rego └── tests/ └── storage_test.rego ```
2. In Langfuse, open `azurerm/policies/compliance`, and copy the text of the version your environment uses into `azurerm.rego`. Keep the existing rules: the policy is one module, and every new version replaces the whole text. Copy `general/policies/compliance` into `general.rego` the same way; you will not change it, but a round evaluates both together. A rule that concerns one provider’s resources goes in that provider’s policy, which only runs for modules that declare the provider. A rule that spans providers goes in the general policy. For a provider that has no policy yet, create its `<provider>/policies/compliance` prompt with `package kumoss.providers.<provider>`.
3. Add your rule at the end of `azurerm.rego`: ``` rules contains "azurerm_storage_public_access" deny contains finding if { some change in input.plan.resource_changes change.mode == "managed" change.type == "azurerm_storage_account" change.change.after.public_network_access_enabled == true finding := { "rule_id": "azurerm_storage_public_access", "severity": "error", "resource": change.address, "message": sprintf("%s allows public network access; set public_network_access_enabled = false.", [change.address]), } } ``` Every policy sees the whole plan, so the rule matches on its own resource `type`. A deleted resource has no `after` values, so the rule only matches creates and updates. Prefix the rule id with the provider, as the shipped rules do.
4. (Optional) To report something without blocking, add a rule to `warn` instead of `deny`. This one flags Azure resources without a `cost-center` tag: ``` rules contains "azurerm_cost_center_tag" warn contains finding if { some change in input.plan.resource_changes change.mode == "managed" startswith(change.type, "azurerm_") some action in change.change.actions action in {"create", "update"} tags := object.get(change.change.after, "tags", {}) not tags["cost-center"] finding := { "rule_id": "azurerm_cost_center_tag", "resource": change.address, "message": sprintf("%s has no cost-center tag.", [change.address]), } } ```
5. Write a test for the rule in `tests/storage_test.rego`: ``` package kumoss.providers.azurerm_test import data.kumoss.providers.azurerm storage(public) := { "plan": {"resource_changes": [{ "address": "azurerm_storage_account.logs", "mode": "managed", "type": "azurerm_storage_account", "change": { "actions": ["create"], "after": {"public_network_access_enabled": public, "tags": {"cost-center": "analytics"}}, }, }]}, "kumoss": {"schema": "kumoss.compliance.input/v1", "providers": ["azurerm"]}, } test_public_storage_is_denied if { some finding in azurerm.deny with input as storage(true) finding.rule_id == "azurerm_storage_public_access" } test_private_storage_is_allowed if { count(azurerm.deny) == 0 with input as storage(false) } ```
6. From `policy-work/`, run the tests: ``` docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/w:ro" -w /w \ openpolicyagent/opa:1.22.4-static test -v general.rego azurerm.rego tests ``` Every test reports `PASS` (timings omitted): ``` tests/storage_test.rego:18: data.kumoss.providers.azurerm_test.test_public_storage_is_denied: PASS tests/storage_test.rego:23: data.kumoss.providers.azurerm_test.test_private_storage_is_allowed: PASS -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- PASS: 2/2 ```
7. Check the decision against a real plan from one of your root modules. Wrap its `show -json` in the input document and evaluate it the way the core does: ``` terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json jq '{plan: ., kumoss: {schema: "kumoss.compliance.input/v1", providers: ["azurerm"]}}' \ plan.json > input.json docker run --rm -i -v "$PWD:/w:ro" -w /w openpolicyagent/opa:1.22.4-static \ eval --stdin-input --strict-builtin-errors --format pretty \ -d general.rego -d azurerm.rego data.kumoss.providers.azurerm < input.json ``` Query `data.kumoss` instead to see the general policy’s decision too, as the core reads it. For a plan that creates a public storage account without a `cost-center` tag, the Azure policy’s decision contains: ``` { "deny": [ { "message": "azurerm_storage_account.logs allows public network access; set public_network_access_enabled = false.", "resource": "azurerm_storage_account.logs", "rule_id": "azurerm_storage_public_access", "severity": "error" } ], "rules": [ "azurerm_cost_center_tag", "azurerm_host_command", "azurerm_public_inbound", "azurerm_storage_public_access", "azurerm_subscription_owner" ], "warn": [ { "message": "azurerm_storage_account.logs has no cost-center tag.", "resource": "azurerm_storage_account.logs", "rule_id": "azurerm_cost_center_tag" } ] } ```
8. Publish the rule: in Langfuse, create a new version of `azurerm/policies/compliance` with the full text of `azurerm.rego`, then move your environment’s label to it. The next generate round uses it. To roll back, move the label to the previous version. See [Change a prompt](../customize-prompts/#change-a-prompt). > **Warning** > One version serves every generate session of the environment > that the policy applies to: every session for the general policy, every > session whose module declares the provider for a provider policy. A > syntax error or a rule that fails at run time does not skip the policy: > it locks each of those rounds with `policy_unavailable` until the label > is on a working version. Move the label only after the tests pass.

## Verify

Send a request that creates a storage account with public network access. The round is locked, and **Why** on the **Deployment Blocked** screen lists `azurerm_storage_public_access` with a **policy** badge; see [If the session is locked](../merge-and-apply/#session-locked).

## Things to keep in mind

- **A rule sees the session’s targets only.** The plan is a `-target` plan, so a rule cannot reason about resources outside the session.
- **Values known only after apply are not in `after`.** They are listed in `after_unknown`; a rule cannot check their final value.
- **Never put attribute values in a message.** The plan JSON carries sensitive values unmasked, and messages end up in the compliance report, the session’s artifacts, and the notification. Name the resource address and the attribute instead.
- **Keep rule ids stable.** They appear in reports, and they are what reviewers and users search for.
- **Do not restate a rule in a prompt.** The guideline and resource prompts feed only the code generator, so a ban written there would be applied a second time, by a model, possibly differently from the policy; see [Change a compliance policy](../customize-prompts/#compliance-policy).
- **Use the policies for conditions on the plan only.** Rules that depend on what the user asked for belong in the intent check; see [Intent check](../resolve-a-locked-session/#intent-check).

## Next steps

- [Compliance policy](../../reference/compliance-policy/) for the full input and decision contract, and every reason a policy can fail to evaluate.
- [Resolve a locked session](../resolve-a-locked-session/) for what users see when your rule denies a plan.
